options.text: Crate three packet mirroring policies: one for each zone. Create one group of collector instances for the us-west2 region. Configure each packet mirroring policy to match traffic for its zone based on instance-tags, and create a filter for TCP traffic.

Create one packet mirroring policy for the us-west2 region. Create one group of collector instances for the us-west2 region. Configure the packet mirroring policy to match traffic for web server instances based on instance-tags, and create a filter for TCP traffic.

Create three packet mirroring policies: one for each zone. Create three groups of collector instances: one group for each zone. Configure each policy to match traffic for its zone based on instance-tags, and create a filter for TCP traffic.

Create three packet mirroring policies: one for each zone. Create three groups of collector instances: one group for each zone. Configure each policy to match traffic for its zone based on subnets, and create a filter for TCP traffic.

questions.explanation:
Packet Mirroring can select sources using network tags and can filter by protocol, so tags can target only the web-server instances and a TCP filter captures their web traffic without mirroring UDP game-server traffic. Because mirrored traffic that travels between zones incurs egress charges, deploying a collector group in each source zone and directing that zone’s policy to its local collector group minimizes inter-zonal egress costs.

**Learn more:** [Packet Mirroring | Virtual Private Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/packet-mirroring?hl=en) · [Use Packet Mirroring | Virtual Private Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/using-packet-mirroring?hl=en)

You need to create a GKE cluster in an existing VPC that can be accessed from on-premises. You must satisfy these requirements:  
  
- IP ranges for Pods and Services must be as small as possible.  
- The nodes and master must not be accessible from the internet.  
- You must be able to run `kubectl` commands from on-premises subnets to manage the cluster.  
  
How should you create the GKE cluster?
questions.explanation:
A VPC-native GKE cluster using user-managed secondary IP ranges lets the administrator define the Pod and Service CIDRs, including /24 ranges. Enabling the private control-plane endpoint disables external control-plane access, and master authorized networks can allow the required on-premises source CIDRs. A network proxy provides a controlled path for administrative access while keeping the cluster endpoints off the public internet.

**Learn more:** [Create a VPC-native cluster](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/alias-ips) · [Customize your network isolation in GKE](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/latest/network-isolation)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have set up an HTTP(S) load-balanced service and need to confirm that the backend instances are responding correctly.  
  
How should you configure the health check?

options.text: Set request-path to a specific URL used for health checking, and set proxy-header to PROXY_V1.
Set request-path to a specific URL used for health checking, and set host to include a custom host header that identifies the health check.
Set request-path to a specific URL used for health checking, and set response to a string that the backend service will always return in the response body.
Set proxy-header to the default value, and set host to include a custom host header that identifies the health check.

questions.explanation:
HTTP(S) health checks can target a specific request path and require an expected response string. A backend is considered healthy when it returns HTTP 200 and the expected string is found in the response body, so a stable health endpoint and known response content provide a reliable health signal.

**Learn more:** [Use health checks | Cloud Load Balancing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/health-checks)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company uses web application firewall (WAF) capabilities from a third-party cloud WAF provider. The WAF provider proxies every HTTPS connection from internet clients, applies security policies, and then opens a new HTTPS connection to the public IP address of your global Application Load Balancer in Google Cloud. Your Google Cloud workloads are the backends for this global Application Load Balancer. Cloud Am1or is currently not configured.  
  
You need to create a Cloud Armor security policy that blocks sessions originating from internet clients whose source IP addresses belong to the `IP_RANGE_BLOCK` IP range. The block must be enforced by the Cloud Armor security policy; the third-party cloud WAF provider will not perform it. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create a new Cloud Armor network edge security policy. In the policy, set the userIpRequestHeaders[] attribute.2. Add a policy rule that denies traffic that matches inIpRange(origin.user_ip, 'IP_RANGE_BLOCK') statement.3. Apply the policy to the backend service that includes all your Google Cloud workloads.

1. Create a new Cloud Armor network edge security policy. In the policy, set the userIpRequestHeaders[] attribute.2. Add a policy rule that denies traffic that matches the inIpRange(origin.ip, 'IP_RANGE_BLOCK') statement.3. Apply the policy to the backend service that includes all your Google Cloud workloads.

1. Create a new Cloud Armor backend security policy. In the policy, set the userIpRequestHeaders[] attribute.2. Add a policy rule that denies traffic that matches the inIpRange(origin.user_ip, 'IP_RANGE_BLOCK') statement.3. Apply the policy to the backend service that includes all your Google Cloud workloads.

1. Create a new Cloud Armor backend security policy. In the policy, set the userIpRequestHeaders[] attribute.2. Add a policy rule that denies traffic that matches the inIpRange(origin.ip, 'IP_RANGE_BLOCK') statement.3. Apply the policy to the backend service that includes all your Google Cloud workloads.

questions.explanation:
A trusted upstream proxy causes `origin.ip` to contain the proxy’s address rather than the original internet client’s address. Configuring `userIpRequestHeaders[]` enables Cloud Armor to populate `origin.user_ip` from the client-IP header supplied by that proxy, so `inIpRange(origin.user_ip, 'IP_RANGE_BLOCK')` blocks the intended clients. A backend security policy is the appropriate policy type to attach to the backend service; edge security policies do not support `origin.user_ip`.

**Learn more:** [User IP addresses | Google Cloud Armor](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/user-ip-overview) · [Configure custom rules language attributes | Google Cloud Armor](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/rules-language-reference)

A multi-region VPC has long used HA VPN in "region 1" to connect to your corporate network. You plan to add two 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect connections and VLAN attachments in "region 2" to connect to that same corporate network. You must plan VPC-to-corporate-network connectivity so that traffic uses the Dedicated Interconnect connections as the primary path and the HA VPN as the secondary path. What should you do?

options.text: Enable regional dynamic routing mode on the VPC. Configure BGP associated with the HA VPN in
Enable regional dynamic routing mode on the VPC. Configure BGP associated with the HA VPN in
Enable global dynamic routing mode on the VPConfigure BGP associated with the HA VPN in
Enable global dynamic routing mode on the VPC. Configure BGP associated with the HA VPN in

questions.explanation:
Global dynamic routing allows dynamically learned and advertised routes to be used across VPC regions. A Cloud Router BGP session’s base advertised priority becomes its MED value, and a lower MED has higher preference. Setting the Dedicated Interconnect VLAN attachments to 100 and the HA VPN to 20000 makes Dedicated Interconnect the preferred path while retaining HA VPN for failover; corresponding MED values on the on-premises routers maintain that preference in the opposite direction.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud: Learned routes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/concepts/learned-routes?hl=en) · [Google Cloud: Update the base route priority](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/updating-priority?hl=en)

You manage a hybrid cloud environment that connects your on-premises data center to a Google Cloud VPC through Cloud VPN. Your on-premises DNS servers are authoritative for the `corp.example.com` zone, while a Cloud DNS private zone is authoritative for the `gcp.example.com` zone.  
  
You need to configure a Google-recommended solution that lets Google Cloud VMs resolve on-premises hostnames and, conversely, lets on-premises hosts resolve hostnames in your Google Cloud VPC. What should you do?

options.text: • Create a Cloud DNS outbound server policy that forwards all DNS queries from the VPC to your on-premises DNS servers.• Configure your on-premises servers to handle resolution for gcp.example.com and public domains on behalf of the VPC.
• Configure your on-premises DNS servers to use Google Cloud's public DNS (8.8.8.8) for all queries.• Update your Google Cloud instances to use Cloud DNS for internal resolution.
• Deploy a Compute Engine VM in the VPC to run a DNS forwarder, such as BIND or Unbound.• Configure this VM to handle bi-directional forwarding between the on-premises DNS servers and Cloud DNS.

• Create a Cloud DNS forwarding zone for corp.example.com that points to your on-premises DNS servers.• Configure a private Cloud DNS zone for gcp.example.com. Create a Cloud DNS inbound server policy, and configure on-premises DNS servers to forward queries for gcp.example.com to it.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud DNS forwarding zone for `corp.example.com` sends VPC DNS queries for the on-premises zone to its authoritative on-premises DNS servers. An inbound DNS server policy exposes the VPC’s Cloud DNS resolution service through internal entry-point IP addresses reachable over Cloud VPN, allowing on-premises DNS servers to forward `gcp.example.com` queries to the Cloud DNS private zone.

**Learn more:** [Create a forwarding zone | Cloud DNS](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones/forwarding-zones) · [DNS server policies | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/server-policies-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying an application running on Compute Engine instances and need to decide how to expose it to a new customer. Ensure that the application meets these requirements:  
  
- Maps multiple existing reserved external IP addresses to the instance  
- Processes IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) traffic  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure a target pool, and create protocol forwarding rules for each external IP address.
Configure a backend service, and create an external network load balancer for each external IP address.
Configure a target instance, and create a protocol forwarding rule for each external IP address to be mapped to the instance.
Configure the Compute Engine instances’ network interface external IP address from None to Ephemeral. Add as many external IP addresses as required.

questions.explanation:
External protocol forwarding uses a target instance that references one VM and can use multiple external forwarding rules to map multiple external IP addresses to that VM. External protocol forwarding supports ESP traffic. Target pool-based load balancing supports only TCP and UDP traffic.

**Learn more:** [Protocol forwarding overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/protocol-forwarding) · [Forwarding rules overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/forwarding-rule-concepts)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company runs Compute Engine instances exposed to the public internet. Each compute instance has one network interface and one public IP address. You need to block every connection attempt originating from internet clients whose IP addresses belong to the `BGP_ASN_TOBLOCK` BGP ASN. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new Cloud Armor backend security policy, and use the --network-src-asns parameter.
Create a new Cloud Armor network edge security policy, and use the --network-src-asns parameter.
Create a new Cloud Armor edge security policy, and use the --network-src-asns parameter.
Create a new firewall policy ingress rule, and use the --network-src-asns parameter.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Armor network edge security policies protect VMs with public IP addresses and support matching a source IP address’s BGP autonomous system number with `--network-src-asns`. A deny rule using that parameter blocks connection attempts from the specified ASN.

**Learn more:** [Configure network edge security policies | Google Cloud Armor](https://cloud.google.com/armor/docs/network-edge-policies)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a highly resilient, secure connection between an on-premises data center and Google Cloud for a financial services company. The company requires 10 Gbps of bandwidth and requires all traffic to be encrypted end-to-end between its on-premises network and its Google Cloud VPC. You have already provisioned two 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect connections. You need to choose an encryption strategy that satisfies these requirements and provides redundancy.  
  
What action should you take?

options.text: Deploy four HA VPN gateways on each Dedicated Interconnect connection.
Deploy two HA VPN gateways on each Dedicated Interconnect connection.
Configure MACsec on each of the Dedicated Interconnect connections.
Use one Dedicated Interconnect for traffic and an HA VPN over the internet for backup.

questions.explanation:
HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect provides IPsec encryption between the on-premises network and the VPC. Each HA VPN tunnel has 3 Gbps of bandwidth, and Google recommends four tunnels for each 10-Gbps VLAN attachment, with eight tunnels across two attachments to preserve capacity during failover. Two HA VPN gateways per Dedicated Interconnect connection provide the tunnel capacity and redundant encrypted paths required. MACsec protects only the segment between the on-premises router and Google's edge router, so it is not end-to-end encryption to the VPC.

**Learn more:** [Configure HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/configure-ha-vpn-interconnect) · [MACsec for Cloud Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/macsec-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization requires all SMTP traffic to its cloud environment to be blocked, except traffic originating from the corporate network. It also requires that only specific VPCs across its Google Cloud projects permit SMTP access from that corporate network. You need to configure a security policy to enable this connectivity. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Configure an ingress hierarchical firewall rule with priority 10000 specifying the 0.0.0.0/0 source, TCP port 25, and the deny action.2. Configure an egress hierarchical firewall rule with priority 10010 specifying the source of your corporate network as TCP port 25 and the goto_next action.3. Associate the hierarchical firewall policy at the organization level.4. Configure firewall policy rules allowing TCP port 25 in the firewall policies associated with the respective VPCs that require that access.

1. Configure an ingress hierarchical firewall rule with priority 10000 specifying the 0.0.0.0/0 source, TCP port 25, and the allow action.2. Associate the hierarchical firewall policy at the organization level.3. Configure firewall policy rules to deny TCP port 25 in the firewall policies associated with the respective VPCs that do not require that access.

1. Configure an ingress hierarchical firewall rule with priority 10000 specifying the source of your corporate network, TCP port 25, and the goto_next action.2. Configure an ingress hierarchical firewall rule with priority 10010 specifying the 0.0.0.0/0 source, TCP port 25, and the deny action.3. Associate the hierarchical firewall policy at the organization level.4. Configure firewall policy rules allowing TCP port 25 in the firewall policies associated with the respective VPCs that require that access.

1. Configure an ingress hierarchical firewall rule with priority 10000 specifying the 0.0.0.0/0 source, TCP port 25, and the deny action.2. Associate the hierarchical firewall policy at the organization level.3. Configure firewall policy rules allowing TCP port 25 in the firewall policies associated with the respective VPCs that require that access.

questions.explanation:
Hierarchical firewall policies are evaluated before VPC firewall rules, and a `goto_next` action delegates matching traffic to lower-level VPC rules. An organization-level ingress `goto_next` rule for corporate-network TCP port 25 permits only the selected VPCs to make the final allow decision, while the subsequent ingress deny rule for TCP port 25 from `0.0.0.0/0` blocks all other SMTP traffic. [Hierarchical firewall policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies) [Firewall policy evaluation order](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies-rule-eval-order)

At your company, two departments have separate GCP projects (`code-dev` and `data-dev`) in the same organization and need to permit complete cross-communication among all their GCP virtual machines. Each department has one VPC in its project and requires full control of its own network. Neither department plans to recreate its existing compute resources. You want to implement a solution that minimizes cost.  
  
Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Connect both projects using Cloud VPN.
Connect the VPCs in project code-dev and data-dev using VPC Network Peering.
Enable Shared VPC in one project (e. g., code-dev), and make the second project (e. g., data-dev) a service project.
Enable firewall rules to allow all ingress traffic from all subnets of project code-dev to all instances in project data-dev, and vice versa.
Create a route in the code-dev project to the destination prefixes in project data-dev and use nexthop as the default gateway, and vice versa.

questions.explanation:
VPC Network Peering provides private connectivity between VPC networks in separate projects while leaving each VPC administratively independent. It automatically exchanges private subnet routes, but it does not exchange firewall rules. Therefore, ingress firewall rules must allow traffic from the peer VPC’s subnet ranges in each direction. Shared VPC centralizes network administration and existing instances cannot simply be reconfigured to use its shared subnets.

**Learn more:** [VPC Network Peering](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering) · [Shared VPC](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a containerized application environment on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You deployed a microservice using a Kubernetes Service manifest that defines a named port, `http-api`, for its primary endpoint. You are now configuring an external HTTP(S) load balancer to expose this microservice. You must ensure that the configuration is independent of the actual port number and follows best practices.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a backend service that uses the GKE node instance group as its backend, and configure the named port http-api in the backend service.
Reference the GCE_VM_IP_PORT network endpoint group (NEG) in the backend configuration that was automatically created for your Kubernetes service, and specify http-api named port for traffic.
Add an annotation to your Kubernetes service manifest to create a GCE_VM_IP network endpoint group (NEG), and configure the backend service to use this NEG.
Add an annotation in your Kubernetes ingress manifest to specify the http-api port number directly, and configure the backend service to use this hardcoded port number.

questions.explanation:
GKE container-native load balancing uses `GCE_VM_IP_PORT` NEGs containing Pod endpoints, avoiding the additional NodePort and kube-proxy hops of instance-group backends. An Ingress backend can reference the Kubernetes Service port by its name, such as `http-api`, rather than a numeric port. Compute Engine backend-service named ports apply only to instance-group backends, not `GCE_VM_IP_PORT` NEGs.

**Learn more:** [GKE Ingress for Application Load Balancers](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ingress) · [About GKE Ingress routing and security](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ingress-routing-security)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster for a rapidly growing microservices application. The application will contain thousands of pods and hundreds of services. It requires internal pod-to-pod communication and internal service exposure. You want to follow Google’s recommended approach to ensure efficient IP address use in your existing Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) subnet while using Google Cloud’s native networking capabilities.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Deploy a route-based GKE cluster and rely on GKE-managed routing tables for all pod and service communication.
Allocate a primary IP address range for the entire cluster to encompass both node, pod, and service IP addresses.
Configure the GKE cluster to use a VPC-native mode with the main subnets primary IP range for nodes, and separate secondary IP ranges for pods and services.
Implement a mesh of Istio service proxies on every pod to manage all internal pod-to-pod communication and service discovery.

questions.explanation:
VPC-native GKE uses the subnet’s primary IPv4 range for node addresses and secondary IP ranges for Pod addresses and, when using user-managed Service ranges, Service `ClusterIP` addresses. This provides native VPC routing for Pods and independently planned address capacity for the large Pod and Service populations.

**Learn more:** [VPC-native clusters | GKE networking](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/alias-ips)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company provides a popular gaming service. Its instances use private IP addresses, with external access provided through a global load balancer. The company has recently contracted a traffic-scrubbing service and needs to restrict its origin so that it accepts connections only from that traffic-scrubbing service.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Armor Security Policy that blocks all traffic except for the traffic-scrubbing service.
Create a VPC Firewall rule that blocks all traffic except for the traffic-scrubbing service.
Create a VPC Service Control Perimeter that blocks all traffic except for the traffic-scrubbing service.
Create IPTables firewall rules that block all traffic except for the traffic-scrubbing service.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Armor security policies protect services behind supported external load balancers and can filter requests by incoming source IP address or CIDR range. An allow rule for the traffic-scrubbing service’s addresses, with a default deny rule for all other traffic, ensures that only traffic delivered by that service reaches the load-balanced backend.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Armor security policy overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/security-policy-overview) · [Example Cloud Armor security policies](https://cloud.google.com/armor/docs/example-policies)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Applications in your Google Cloud environment and AWS cloud environment frequently exchange large data volumes, and the current Cloud VPN connections do not meet the required throughput and reliability. You need to establish high-performance, low-latency, highly available connectivity between your Google Cloud environment and AWS cloud environment. You also need to create a dedicated, private connection between your Google Cloud VPC and AWS VPC.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Establish a Partner Interconnect connection with a service provider that has direct presence in both Google Cloud and AWS regions.
Configure multiple dedicated Cloud VPN tunnels in an active/active configuration between the Google Cloud VPC and AWS VPC.
Provision a Cross-Cloud Interconnect connection between your Google Cloud project and your AWS account, and configure Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) peering over the dedicated connection.
Use a Google Cloud Dedicated Interconnect and an AWS Direct Connect and route traffic through a co-location provider.

questions.explanation:
Cross-Cloud Interconnect provides dedicated, high-bandwidth physical connectivity between Google Cloud and AWS and supports private connectivity between a Google Cloud VPC and AWS resources. It uses Cloud Router and BGP sessions over VLAN attachments to exchange routes; redundant connections can be provisioned for high availability.

**Learn more:** [Connect to Amazon Web Services — Cloud Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/cci/aws/connectivity-overview) · [Cross-Cloud Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/cci-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a Cloud Storage bucket in Google Cloud project XYZ that holds sensitive data. You need to design a solution that ensures only instances belonging to VPCs under project XYZ can access the data stored in this Cloud Storage bucket. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Private Google Access to privately access the Cloud Storage service using private IP addresses.
Configure a VPC Service Controls perimeter around project XYZ, and include storage.googleapis.com as a restricted service in the service perimeter.
Configure Cloud Storage with projectPrivate Access Control List (ACL) that gives permission to the project team based on their roles.
Configure Private Service Connect to privately access Cloud Storage from all VPCs under project XYZ.

questions.explanation:
VPC Service Controls creates a service perimeter around Google Cloud resources and supported services such as Cloud Storage. Including project XYZ and restricting `storage.googleapis.com` limits access across the perimeter, helping ensure that Cloud Storage data is accessible only from the trusted resources and networks within the perimeter. Private connectivity and ACLs do not by themselves impose this service-perimeter access boundary.

**Learn more:** [Overview of VPC Service Controls](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/overview) · [Set up a service perimeter by using VPC Service Controls](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/set-up-service-perimeter)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization uses a Shared VPC design with one host project and three service projects. Compute Engine instances are located in the service projects, and critical workloads run in your on-premises data center. You need to ensure that the Google Cloud instances can resolve on-premises hostnames through the Dedicated Interconnect deployed for hybrid connectivity. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create a Cloud DNS private forwarding zone in the host project of the Shared VPC that forwards the private zone to the on-premises DNS servers.2. In your Cloud Router, add a custom route advertisement for the IP 35.199.192.0/19 to the on-premises environment.

1. Create a Cloud DNS private forwarding zone in the host project of the Shared VPC that forwards the Private zone to the on-premises DNS servers.2. In your Cloud Router, add a custom route advertisement for the IP 169.254 169.254 to the on-premises environment.

1. Configure a Cloud DNS private zone in the host project of the Shared VPC.2. Set up DNS forwarding to your Google Cloud private zone on your on-premises DNS servers to point to the inbound forwarder IP address in your host project3. In your Cloud Router, add a custom route advertisement for the IP 169.254 169 254 to the on-premises environment.

1.Configure a Cloud DNS private zone in the host project of the Shared VPC.2. Set up DNS forwarding to your Google Cloud private zone on your on-premises DNS servers to point to the inbound forwarder IP address in your host project.3. Configure a DNS policy in the Shared VPC to allow inbound query forwarding with your on-premises DNS server as the alternative DNS server.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud DNS private forwarding zone in the Shared VPC host project can forward queries for the on-premises private domain to on-premises DNS servers, making it available to workloads that use the authorized Shared VPC network. Cloud DNS sends queries to on-premises forwarding targets from `35.199.192.0/19`; advertising that prefix through Cloud Router over the Interconnect supplies the on-premises return path for DNS responses.

**Learn more:** [Cloud DNS overview](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/overview) · [Best practices for Cloud DNS](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/best-practices)

Your company operates an enterprise platform on-premises with virtual machines (VMs). Its internet customers have created tens of thousands of DNS domains that point to public IP addresses assigned to the VMs. Customers generally hard-code your IP addresses in their DNS records.  
  
You are planning to migrate the platform to Compute Engine and want to use Bring Your Own IP. You want to minimize disruption to the platform. What should you do?

options.text: Create a VPC and request static external IP addresses from Google Cloud. Assign the IP addresses to the Compute Engine instances. Notify your customers of the new IP addresses so they can update their DNS records.
Verify ownership of your IP addresses. After the verification, Google Cloud advertises and provisions the IP prefix for you. Assign the IP addresses to the Compute Engine instances.
Create a VPC with the same IP address range as your on-premises network. Assign the IP addresses to the Compute Engine instances.
Verify ownership of your IP addresses. Use live migration to import the prefix. Assign the IP addresses to the Compute Engine instances.

questions.explanation:
Bring Your Own IP preserves the existing public IP addresses, avoiding the need for customers to change hard-coded DNS records. Google Cloud requires ownership validation for an imported public advertised prefix; after validation and provisioning, Google Cloud can advertise the prefix and the addresses can be assigned to supported Compute Engine resources.

**Learn more:** [Bring your own IP addresses](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/bring-your-own-ip) · [Create a public advertised prefix](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/create-pap)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You created a new VPC network named Dev with one subnet. You added a firewall rule for the Dev network that permits only HTTP traffic and enabled logging.  
  
When you attempt to sign in to an instance in the subnet through Remote Desktop Protocol, the sign-in fails. You search for Firewall rules logs in Stackdriver Logging, but find no entries for blocked traffic. You want to view logs for blocked traffic.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Check the VPC flow logs for the instance.
Try connecting to the instance via SSH, and check the logs.
Create a new firewall rule to allow traffic from port 22, and enable logs.
Create a new firewall rule with priority 65500 to deny all traffic, and enable logs.

questions.explanation:
VPC firewall logging does not support the implied ingress deny rule, so RDP traffic denied by that implied rule produces no firewall log entry. A logging-enabled explicit deny-all rule at priority 65500 matches traffic not already allowed by the HTTP rule and records the denied RDP attempts.

**Learn more:** [VPC firewall rules logging overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/vpc-firewall-rules-logging-overview?authuser=0) · [Google Cloud Firewall Rules Logging: How and why you should use it](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-firewall-rules-logging-how-and-why-you-should-use-it)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to create a new VPC network that lets instances have IP addresses in both the `10.1.1.0/24` network and the `172.16.45.0/24` network.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure global load balancing to point 172.16.45.0/24 to the correct instance.
Create unique DNS records for each service that sends traffic to the desired IP address.
Configure an alias-IP range of 172.16.45.0/24 on the virtual instances within the VPC subnet of 10.1.1.0/24.
Use VPC peering to allow traffic to route between the 10.1.0.0/24 network and the 172.16.45.0/24 network.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud alias IP ranges allow a VM network interface with a primary IP address from a subnet’s primary CIDR range to also use addresses from a secondary CIDR range on that same subnet. Configuring `172.16.45.0/24` as the alias range for instances in the `10.1.1.0/24` subnet provides addresses from both networks.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud: Alias IP ranges](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/alias-ip) · [Google Cloud: Configure alias IP ranges](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-alias-ip-ranges?hl=en)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a security-focused network architecture on Google Cloud. Your company has deployed a central inspection VPC containing a fleet of Cloud Next Generation Firewall (NGFW) appliances. The inspection VPC has a default route whose next hop points to the passthrough Network Load Balancer, with NGFW appliances as its backends.  
  
You also have two application VPCs (App-A and App-B) that must not communicate directly with one another, and neither VPC has a default route. You need to make sure that all traffic originating from App-A and App-B is forced through the inspection VPC for analysis by the Cloud NGFW appliances.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use VPC Network Peering to create a full mesh by peering all three VPCs with each other, and then use firewall rules to deny all traffic between App-A and App-B.
Create a Network Connectivity Center hub in mesh topology, connect all three VPCs as spokes, and configure the inspection VPC to advertise the default route.

Create a Network Connectivity Center hub in star topology. Configure the inspection VPC spoke as a center group that advertises a default route, and configure the application VPCs as edge spokes to use that route for inter-VPC traffic.
Create two separate VPC Network Peering connections: One between the inspection VPC and App-A, and another between the inspection VPC and App-B.

questions.explanation:
A Network Connectivity Center hub using star topology separates center and edge spoke route tables. Edge spokes can have routes to center spokes, but Network Connectivity Center prohibits edge-group routes that provide connectivity between different edge spokes. Making the inspection VPC a center spoke and App-A and App-B edge spokes therefore sends their default-routed traffic to the inspection VPC and prevents direct App-A-to-App-B routing. A static route in a VPC spoke can use an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer in another spoke as its next hop when the relevant NCC connectivity requirements are met.

**Learn more:** [Preset connectivity topologies](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/connectivity-topologies) · [Static routes overview](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/static-routes-overview)

questions.question:
You need to configure a static route to an on-premises resource behind a Cloud VPN gateway configured for policy-based routing by using the `gcloud` command.  
  
Which next hop should you select?

options.text: The default internet gateway
The IP address of the Cloud VPN gateway
The name and region of the Cloud VPN tunnel
The IP address of the instance on the remote side of the VPN tunnel

questions.explanation:
A policy-based Classic VPN uses static routing, and static routes created with the Google Cloud CLI use the Cloud VPN tunnel as the next hop. The tunnel is specified by its name and region, rather than by the VPN gateway address or a remote instance address.\
\
**Learn more:** [Networks and tunnel routing | Cloud VPN](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/choosing-networks-routing) · [Order of routes | Cloud VPN](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/order-of-routes)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question:
You need to configure a static route to an on-premises resource behind a Cloud VPN gateway configured for policy-based routing by using the `gcloud` command.  
  
Which next hop should you select?

options.text: You have not configured compression in Cloud CDN.
You have configured the web servers and Cloud CDN with different compression types.
The web servers behind the load balancer are configured with different compression types.
You have to configure the web servers to compress responses even if the request has a Via header.

questions.explanation:
External HTTP(S) load balancers add a `Via` header to requests forwarded to the origin. Some web servers disable compression by default for proxied requests containing that header, so the web servers must be configured to compress responses even when a `Via` header is present.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot Cloud CDN](https://cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/troubleshooting-steps)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services

options.text: Use Network Load Balancing
Use TCP Proxy Load Balancing with PROXY protocol enabled
Use External HTTP(S) Load Balancing with URL Maps and custom headers
Use External HTTP(S) Load Balancing with URL Maps and an X-Forwarded-For header

questions.explanation:
An external Application Load Balancer provides global HTTP(S) load balancing with URL maps for host- and path-based routing, supports IPv4 and IPv6 client frontends, and can use global backend services spanning multiple regions for availability and low-latency delivery. It passes client address information to backends by appending the client IP address and load-balancer IP address to the `X-Forwarded-For` request header.

**Learn more:** [External Application Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/https) · [Use URL maps](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/url-map)

You manage a Google Cloud VPC network with multiple Cloud VPN tunnels connected to one branch office for redundancy. One tunnel is a new, high-performance link, while the other is an older, less reliable link.  
  
You need to configure dynamic routing to influence how your on-premises network routes traffic, so that it prefers sending traffic to Google Cloud through the new, high-performance tunnel. The older tunnel must remain available as a backup. What should you do?

options.text: Adjust the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED) attribute advertised by the Cloud Router for the preferred VPN tunnel to a lower value.
Configure static routes with different priorities on your on-premises router to point to the two different Cloud VPN tunnel interfaces in Google Cloud.
On the Cloud Router, configure custom route advertisements to send a shorter prefix route over the new, high-performance tunnel.
For the BGP session associated with the new tunnel, configure a higher advertised route priority (a lower numerical value) on the Cloud Router.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Router assigns each BGP session a base advertised route priority, which it uses as the BGP MED value advertised to the on-premises router. Setting a lower numerical advertised route priority for the new tunnel makes its route more preferable, while the older tunnel’s higher-priority-value route remains available for failover.

**Learn more:** [Update the base route priority | Cloud Router](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/updating-priority?hl=en) · [Advertised routes | Cloud Router](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/concepts/advertised-routes)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You ordered Dedicated Interconnect in the GCP Console and must provide the Letter of Authorization/Connecting Facility Assignment (LOA-CFA) to your cross-connect provider to finish the physical connection.  
  
Which two actions can do this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Open a Cloud Support ticket under the Cloud Interconnect category.
Download the LOA-CFA from the Hybrid Connectivity section of the GCP Console.
Run gcloud compute interconnects describe <interconnect>.
Check the email for the account of the NOC contact that you specified during the ordering process.
Contact your cross-connect provider and inform them that Google automatically sent the LOA/CFA to them via email, and to complete the connection.

questions.explanation:
For a Dedicated Interconnect order, Google emails the LOA-CFA to both the specified NOC technical contact and the user who submitted the order. The LOA-CFA can also be downloaded in the Google Cloud console from the Dedicated Interconnect physical connections area, then provided to the vendor that will install the cross-connect.

**Learn more:** [Retrieve LOA-CFAs | Cloud Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/retrieving-loas) · [Order a Dedicated Interconnect connection | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/ordering-dedicated-interconnect?hl=en)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You created a firewall with rules that permit traffic only over HTTP, HTTPS, and SSH ports. During testing, you intentionally attempt to reach the server using several ports and protocols; however, no denied connections appear in the firewall logs. You want to fix the issue.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Enable logging on the default Deny Any Firewall Rule.
Enable logging on the VM Instances that receive traffic.
Create a logging sink forwarding all firewall logs with no filters.
Create an explicit Deny Any rule and enable logging on the new rule.

questions.explanation:
VPC firewall logging must be enabled on the explicit rule that matches the traffic. The implied deny-ingress rule does not support firewall-rule logging, so denied traffic that falls through to it is not logged. An explicit deny-all rule with logging enabled records matching denied TCP and UDP connection attempts.

**Learn more:** [VPC firewall rules logging overview](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/vpc-firewall-rules-logging-overview) · [Manage VPC firewall rules logging](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/manage-vpc-firewall-rules-logging)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are the Organization Admin for your company. An engineer is responsible for configuring multiple host projects across multiple folders and sharing subnets with service projects. You need to configure the engineer's Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions so they can complete this work with the fewest steps. What should you do?

options.text: Set up the engineer with Compute Shared VPC Admin IAM role at the folder level.
Set up the engineer with Compute Shared VPC Admin IAM role at the organization level.
Set up the engineer with Compute Shared VPC Admin IAM role and Project IAM Admin role at the folder level.
Set up the engineer with Compute Shared VPC Admin IAM role and Project IAM Admin role at the organization level.

questions.explanation:
A Shared VPC Admin requires both the Compute Shared VPC Admin (`roles/compute.xpnAdmin`) and Project IAM Admin (`roles/resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin`) roles to administer Shared VPC host projects, attach service projects, and delegate subnet access. Assigning these roles at the organization level grants the necessary access throughout all folders, avoiding separate role assignments for each folder.

**Learn more:** [Provision Shared VPC](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/provisioning-shared-vpc) · [Shared VPC overview](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc)

Your company’s streaming application, deployed on Google Cloud, supports multiple languages. The application development team asks how to split audio and video traffic into separate backend Google Cloud Storage buckets. They want to use URL maps while minimizing operational overhead. They currently use this directory structure:  
  
```text  
/fr/video  
/en/video  
/es/video  
/../video  
/fr/audio  
/en/audio  
/es/audio  
/../audio  
```  
  
Which solution do you recommend?

options.text: Rearrange the directory structure, create a URL map and leverage a path rule such as /video/* and /audio/*.
Rearrange the directory structure, create DNS hostname entries for video and audio and leverage a path rule such as /video/* and /audio/*.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud URL-map path rules support exact paths and prefix matches ending in `/*`; they do not accept regular expressions or a leading wildcard for matching the language segment. Placing the media type first in the path lets one URL map route `/video/*` and `/audio/*` to separate backend buckets, independent of language, without DNS-based routing overhead.

**Learn more:** [URL maps overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/url-map-concepts)

You are designing the DNS topology for an enterprise migrating its applications to Google Cloud. The company has a robust on-premises Active Directory and DNS infrastructure that remains authoritative for its existing internal domains. New Google Cloud applications will require their own private DNS records.  
  
You need to provide seamless resolution for all internal resources across both on-premises and cloud workloads, without publicly exposing internal DNS records, while minimizing the administrative effort of DNS management in the hybrid environment.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Deploy dedicated DNS proxy servers within the Google Cloud VPC, and configure these proxy servers to forward all DNS queries to the on-premises DNS servers. Concurrently configure the on-premises DNS servers to send cloud-specific DNS queries back to the Google Cloud proxy servers.

Configure Cloud DNS server policies in Google Cloud VPCs to enable:• inbound DNS queries from on-premises for cloud-hosted private zones.• outbound DNS forwarding to on-premises DNS servers for on-premises domains.

Use Cloud VPN or Interconnect to establish hybrid connectivity between the on-premises network and the Google Cloud VPThen configure custom route tables on all instances to direct DNS queries to the appropriate DNS server based on the domain.
Migrate all existing on-premises DNS records to private Cloud DNS zones, and configure all on-premises and cloud workloads to use Cloud DNS as their primary DNS resolver.

questions.explanation:
Cloud DNS server policies support managed hybrid name resolution. Inbound DNS forwarding lets on-premises resolvers query private Cloud DNS zones through internal forwarding entry points, and outbound DNS forwarding lets VPC workloads use on-premises DNS servers for existing internal domains. This keeps private records private and retains the on-premises DNS service as authoritative without operating self-managed DNS proxy servers or migrating all existing records.

**Learn more:** [Configure DNS server policies](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/policies) · [DNS server policies overview](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/server-policies-overview)

You are investigating connectivity problems between Google Cloud and a public SaaS provider. The two environments connect through the public internet. Your users report intermittent connection errors when they use TCP to connect, but ICMP tests show no failures. Users state that the errors happen at roughly the same time each day.  
  
You want to troubleshoot and collect information by using Google Cloud tools that are most likely to provide insight into what is happening within Google Cloud. What should you do?

options.text: Enable and review Cloud Logging for Cloud Armor. Look for logs with errors matching the destination IP address of the public SaaS provider.
Enable and review Cloud Logging on your Cloud NAT gateway. Look for logs with errors matching the destination IP address of the public SaaS provider.
Enable the Firewall Insights API. Set the deny rule insights observation period to one day. Review the insights to assure there are no firewall rules denying traffic.

Create a Connectivity Test by using TCP, the source IP address of your test VM, and the destination IP address of the public SaaS provider. Review the live data plane analysis and take the next steps based on the test results.

questions.explanation:
Cloud NAT logging records NAT connections and errors for TCP and UDP traffic. It can log outbound packets dropped because no NAT port is available, and its connection data includes the destination IP address and port. Reviewing these error logs around the recurring failure time can reveal Cloud NAT port-allocation or related egress translation problems affecting connections to the SaaS provider.

**Learn more:** [Logs and metrics | Cloud NAT](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/monitoring) · [Connectivity Tests overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/connectivity-tests/concepts/overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An instance in your VPC is configured to run using only a private IP address. You need to ensure that, even if the instance is deleted, its present private IP address is not automatically assigned to another instance.  
  
In the GCP Console, what should you do?

options.text: Assign a public IP address to the instance.
Assign a new reserved internal IP address to the instance.
Change the instance's current internal IP address to static.
Add custom metadata to the instance with key internal-address and value reserved.

questions.explanation:
An ephemeral internal IP address is returned to the available address pool when its instance is deleted. Promoting the instance’s existing internal IP address to a static address reserves that specific address, preventing automatic reassignment and allowing it to persist beyond the instance’s lifetime.

**Learn more:** [Configure static internal IP addresses](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/ip-addresses/configure-static-internal-ip-address)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization operates a hub-and-spoke architecture with critical Compute Engine instances in its Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs). You are responsible for designing Cloud DNS in Google Cloud. You need to resolve Cloud DNS private zones from the on-premises data center and enable on-premises name resolution from the hub-and-spoke VPC design. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Configure a private DNS zone in the hub VPC, and configure DNS forwarding to the on-premises server.2. Configure DNS peering from the spoke VPCs to the hub VPC.
1. Configure a DNS policy in the hub VPC to allow inbound query forwarding from the spoke VPCs.2. Configure the spoke VPCs with a private zone, and set up DNS peering to the hub VPC.

1. Configure a DNS policy in the spoke VPCs, and configure your on-premises DNS as an alternate DNS server.2. Configure the hub VPC with a private zone, and set up DNS peering to each of the spoke VPCs.
1. Configure a DNS policy in the hub VPC, and configure the on-premises DNS as an alternate DNS server.2. Configure the spoke VPCs with a private zone, and set up DNS peering to the hub VPC.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud DNS server policy in the hub VPC supports hybrid DNS: inbound forwarding lets on-premises resolvers query Cloud DNS, and alternative name servers provide outbound resolution to the on-premises DNS infrastructure. Private zones in the spoke VPCs with DNS peering to the hub extend name resolution across the hub-and-spoke design. The inbound policy must be in the VPC that receives the hybrid connection, and DNS peering is required to resolve records in peered VPCs.

**Learn more:** [Cloud DNS best practices: hybrid hub-and-spoke architecture](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/best-practices) · [Cloud DNS server policies](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/server-policies-overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to limit access to your load-balanced Google Cloud application so that connections are accepted only from specified IP addresses.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a secure perimeter using the Access Context Manager feature of VPC Service Controls and restrict access to the source IP range of the allowed clients and Google health check IP ranges.
Create a secure perimeter using VPC Service Controls, and mark the load balancer as a service restricted to the source IP range of the allowed clients and Google health check IP ranges.
Tag the backend instances
Label the backend instances

questions.explanation:
A VPC ingress firewall rule can limit traffic to backend instances to the allowed client source ranges while also permitting Google health-check probe ranges. Network tags can target the backend instances for that firewall rule; labels cannot be used as firewall targets. VPC Service Controls does not provide this type of load-balancer client IP restriction.

**Learn more:** [Firewall rules — Cloud Load Balancing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/firewall-rules) · [Use health checks — Cloud Load Balancing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/health-checks)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have applications operating in the `us-west1` and `us-east1` regions. You want to create a highly available VPN with 99.99% availability that connects your applications in your project to cloud services offered by your partner's project, while minimizing the required infrastructure. Your partner's services also run in the `us-west1` and `us-east1` regions. You want to use the simplest solution. What should you do?

options.text: Create one Cloud Router and one HA VPN gateway in each region of your VPC and your partner's VPC. Connect your VPN gateways to the partner's gateways. Enable global dynamic routing in each VPC.

Create one Cloud Router and one HA VPN gateway in the us-west1 region of your VPC. Create one OpenVPN Access Server in each region of your partner's VPC. Connect your VPN gateway to your partner's servers.
Create one OpenVPN Access Server in each region of your VPC and your partner's VPConnect your servers to the partner's servers.

Create one Cloud Router and one HA VPN gateway in the us-west1 region of your VPC and your partner's VPC. Connect your VPN gateways to the partner's gateways with a pair of tunnels. Enable global dynamic routing in each VPC.

questions.explanation:
Two Google Cloud VPC networks can achieve the 99.99% HA VPN availability SLA with one HA VPN gateway in each VPC deployed in the same region and two tunnels that connect corresponding gateway interfaces. VPC networks are global, so gateways in one region can connect resources in both regions; global dynamic routing distributes dynamically learned routes across the VPC. A single same-region gateway pair with two tunnels therefore meets the availability requirement with the least infrastructure.

**Learn more:** [HA VPN topologies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/topologies) · [Networks and tunnel routing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/choosing-networks-routing)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing your organization’s architecture so that clients can connect to specific Google APIs. Your plan must provide connectivity to Cloud Storage and BigQuery. You must also ensure that traffic does not traverse the internet. You want a cloud-first solution that requires the fewest configuration steps. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Private Google Access on the VPC resource. Create a default route to the internet.
Configure Private Google Access on the subnet resource. Create a default route to the internet.
Configure Cloud NAT, and remove the default route to the internet.
Configure a global Secure Web Proxy, and remove the default route to the internet.

questions.explanation:
Private Google Access is configured on the subnet used by the clients, enabling internal-IP workloads to reach Google APIs, including Cloud Storage and BigQuery. The VPC needs an appropriate route whose next hop is the default internet gateway; traffic to Google APIs using that route remains on Google's network and does not traverse the public internet.

**Learn more:** [Configure Private Google Access | Virtual Private Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access)

Your end users are near `us-east1` and `europe-west1`. Their workloads must communicate with one another, and you want to minimize cost while improving network efficiency.  
  
How should this topology be designed?

options.text: Create 2 VPCs, each with their own regions and individual subnets. Create 2 VPN gateways to establish connectivity between these regions.
Create 2 VPCs, each with their own region and individual subnets. Use external IP addresses on the instances to establish connectivity between these regions.
Create 1 VPC with 2 regional subnets. Create a global load balancer to establish connectivity between the regions.
Create 1 VPC with 2 regional subnets. Deploy workloads in these subnets and have them communicate using private RFC1918 IP addresses.

questions.explanation:
A Google Cloud VPC is a global network composed of regional subnets. Workloads in subnets within the same VPC can communicate using internal RFC 1918 IP addresses over Google’s network; appropriate ingress firewall rules must allow the traffic. This provides direct private cross-region connectivity without VPN gateways, public external IP addresses, or a load balancer.

**Learn more:** [VPC networks | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc) · [Subnets | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/subnets)

questions.domain: Configuring, implementing and managing a cloud network security solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has one project containing multiple Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs). You need to secure API access to your Cloud Storage buckets and BigQuery datasets by permitting API access only from resources in your corporate public networks. What should you do?

options.text: Create an access context policy that allows your VPC and corporate public network IP ranges, and then attach the policy to Cloud Storage and BigQuery.
Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter for your project with an access context policy that allows your corporate public network IP ranges.
Create a firewall rule to block API access to Cloud Storage and BigQuery from unauthorized networks.
Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter for each VPC with an access context policy that allows your corporate public network IP ranges.

questions.explanation:
A VPC Service Controls perimeter can restrict Cloud Storage and BigQuery APIs for the project, while an Access Context Manager access level permits requests originating from the specified corporate public IP ranges. Firewall rules govern network traffic to VPC resources and do not enforce access to these Google-managed service APIs.

**Learn more:** [Set up a service perimeter by using VPC Service Controls](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/set-up-service-perimeter) · [Allow access to protected resources from outside a perimeter](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/use-access-levels)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has recently migrated to Google Cloud in a single region. You configured distinct Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks for two departments: Department A and Department B. Department A has requested access to resources that belong to Department B's VPC. You need to configure traffic from private IP addresses to flow between the VPCs by using multi-NIC virtual machines (VMs) to meet security requirements. The configuration must also:  
  
- Support both TCP and UDP protocols  
- Provide fully automated failover  
- Include health checks  
- Require minimal manual intervention on the client VMs  
  
Which approach should you use?

options.text: Create the VMs in the same zone, and configure static routes with IP addresses as next hops.
Create the VMs in different zones, and configure static routes with instance names as next hops.
Create an instance template and a managed instance group. Configure a single internal load balancer, and define a custom static route with the internal TCP/UDP load balancer as the next hop.

Create an instance template and a managed instance group. Configure two separate internal TCP/UDP load balancers for each protocol (TCP/UDP), and configure the client VMs to use the internal load balancers’ virtual IP addresses.

questions.explanation:
An internal passthrough Network Load Balancer can be configured as the next hop for a custom static route, distributing TCP and UDP traffic to a pool of multi-NIC VM appliances. Its health checks select healthy backends for new connections, and a managed instance group created from an instance template provides automated recovery and scaling. Routing through the load balancer as the static route's next hop avoids requiring client VMs to be individually configured to use load-balancer virtual IP addresses.

**Learn more:** [Internal passthrough Network Load Balancers as next hops](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/internal/ilb-next-hop-overview) · [Internal passthrough Network Load Balancer overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/internal)

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have two VPCs: VPC A in Project A and VPC B in Project B. The VPCs are peered, and each VPC contains VM instances across four zones. You are using the Network Intelligence Center Performance Dashboard to investigate packet loss for traffic flows that begin in VPC A and end in VPC B. You need the reported packet-loss metric to have at least a 90% confidence level. What should you do?

options.text: Ensure that each zone in each of the VPC networks has at least 10 compute instances. Look in Project A for the reported metric.
Ensure that each zone in each of the VPC networks has at least 9 compute instances. Look in Project B for the reported metric.
Ensure that each zone in each of the VPC networks has at least 9 compute instances. Look in Project A for the reported metric.
Ensure that each zone in each of the VPC networks has at least 10 compute instances. Look in Project B for the reported metric.

questions.explanation:
A 90% packet-loss confidence level requires 2.5 VMs multiplied by the number of zones in the project, in each zone. With four zones, each zone needs at least 10 VM instances. For peered VPC networks in different projects, Performance Dashboard exposes packet-loss data in the destination project; traffic terminating in VPC B is therefore reported in Project B.

**Learn more:** [Performance Dashboard metrics and views](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/performance-dashboard/concepts/metrics-views?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization uses Google Cloud Network Connectivity Center. A VPC spoke includes subnet-corp-prod (`10.10.1.0/24`) and subnet-corp-test (`192.168.1.0/24`). You must ensure that only the subnet-corp-prod range is advertised to the Network Connectivity Center hub, including if new subnets are created in the VPC. You want the most direct and precise way to control route advertisements from this spoke. What should you do?

options.text: Create a custom static route in the Network Connectivity Center hub with the next hop as the VPC spoke for the 10.10.1.0/24 range.
Add 192.168.1.0/24 to the exclude export ranges filter in the VPC spoke configuration.
Set the include export ranges filter to 10.10.1.0/24 in the VPC Spoke configuration, and ensure no other ranges are included.
Create a VPC firewall rule with a DENY action for the 192.168.1.0/24 range.

questions.explanation:
VPC spoke export filters determine which subnet ranges are advertised to the Network Connectivity Center hub. Configuring `10.10.1.0/24` as the only include export range creates an allowlist: that subnet is exported, while all other current and future subnet ranges are excluded unless explicitly added. An exclude-only filter would block only the specified test range and could still allow future subnets to be advertised.

**Learn more:** [Spoke filters overview | Network Connectivity Center](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/spoke-filters-overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are performing a canary test of a new version of an online retailer’s main application, named app-v2, which is configured as a separate backend service from the current version, app-v1. You must send 10% of traffic for the `/shop` path to app-v2 and the remaining 90% to app-v1.  
  
The app-v2 service supports requests on both `/shop/v2` and `/shop`, whereas the app-v1 service supports requests only on `/shop`. You need to implement the most efficient solution to achieve this traffic split and path rewrite.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: • Create a path rule for /shop in the URL map.• Configure its route action with weightedBackendServices to split traffic 90% to app-v1 and 10% to app-v2.

• Create a single URL map rule for the /shop path.• In the rule’s route action, configure weightedBackendServices to split traffic 90/10 between app-v1 and app-v2.• Configure a urlRewrite to change the path to /shop/v2.

• Create two URL map rules with the same /shop path.• Configure the first rule with a higher priority to route traffic to app-v2, and perform a urlRewrite to /shop/v2.• Configure the second rule with a lower priority to route traffic to app-v1 without a rewrite.

• Create two separate route rules in the URL map.• The first rule, with a higher priority, matches traffic based on a specific HTTP header and routes it to app-v2 with a URL.• The second rule, with a lower priority, routes all other traffic to app-v1.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud URL-map route actions can use `weightedBackendServices` to split requests for the same matching URL across backend services according to assigned weights. Because both backends can receive `/shop` only app-v1 requires that path, the correct configuration preserves `/shop` and assigns app-v1 a weight of 90 and app-v2 a weight of 10. Rewriting the path to `/shop/v2` would send an unsupported path to app-v1 traffic.

**Learn more:** [URL maps overview | Cloud Load Balancing](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/url-map-concepts)

questions.domain: Configuring, implementing and managing a cloud network security solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A new VPC was created for the development team. Access to resources in this VPC must be permitted only through SSH.  
  
How should the firewall rules be configured?

options.text: Create two firewall rules: one to block all traffic with priority 0, and another to allow port 22 with priority 1000.
Create two firewall rules: one to block all traffic with priority 65536, and another to allow port 3389 with priority 1000.
Create a single firewall rule to allow port 22 with priority 1000.
Create a single firewall rule to allow port 3389 with priority 1000.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud VPC firewall evaluation includes an implied deny for ingress traffic to VM network interfaces. Therefore, allowing inbound TCP port 22—the SSH port—with a priority of 1000 permits SSH while other inbound traffic remains denied. Priority 1000 is the default VPC firewall-rule priority; a lower numeric priority has higher precedence, so an explicit deny-all rule at priority 0 would also block SSH.

**Learn more:** [VPC firewall rules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls) · [Evaluation order for firewall policies and rules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies-rule-eval-order)

questions.question:
You want to create a dedicated connection to Google that can reach Cloud SQL through a public IP address and does not require a third-party service provider.  
  
Which connection type should you select?

options.text: Enable negative caching for the backend bucket.
Change the cache mode to Force cache all content.C Configure a Cloud Storage bucket permission that gives allUsers the Storage Legacy Object Reader role.
Increase the default time-to-live (TTL) for the backend service.

questions.explanation:
`USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS` honors the origin's caching directives, and `Cache-Control: private` prevents Cloud CDN from caching the object. Requests therefore continue to reach the private Cloud Storage origin, which returns 403. `FORCE_CACHE_ALL` caches successful responses while overriding `private` and `no-store` directives; it is appropriate for a backend containing static Cloud Storage content.

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has resources in two separate VPCs, each in a different Google Cloud project, that need connectivity between them. You have already confirmed that no IP address ranges overlap; however, one VPC uses privately used public IP (PUPI) ranges. You want to enable connectivity between these resources by using a lower-cost, higher-performance method. What should you do?

options.text: Create a HA VPN between the two VPCs that includes the PUPI ranges in the Custom Route Advertisements of the Cloud Router. Create the necessary ingress VPC firewall rules that target the specific resources by using network tags as the source filter.

Create a HA VPN between the two VPCs that includes the PUPI ranges in the Custom Route Advertisements of the Cloud Router. Create the necessary ingress VPC firewall rules that target the specific resources by using IP ranges as the source filter.

Create a VPC Peering between the two VPCs that allows the export and import of custom routes. Create the necessary ingress VPC firewall rules that target the specific resources by using service accounts as the source filter.

Create a VPC Peering between the two VPCs that allows the export and import of subnet routes with public IP addresses. Create the necessary ingress VPC firewall rules that target the specific resources by using IP ranges as the source filter.

questions.explanation:
VPC Network Peering provides private connectivity between VPC networks across different projects. Subnet routes that use privately used public IPv4 addresses are not imported automatically, so the peering configuration must explicitly export and import subnet routes with public IP addresses. Cross-VPC firewall rules cannot use network tags or service accounts from the peer VPC as source selectors; the allowed traffic must be filtered by source IP ranges.

**Learn more:** [VPC Network Peering](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering?hl=en) · [Set up and manage VPC Network Peering](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/using-vpc-peering?hl=en)

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) with two Dedicated Interconnect connections in separate regions: `us-west1` and `us-east1`. Each Dedicated Interconnect connection is connected to a Cloud Router in its own region through a VLAN attachment.  
  
A high-availability failover path is required. By default, all ingress traffic from the on-premises environment must reach the VPC through the `us-west1` connection. If `us-west1` becomes unavailable, traffic must be redirected to `us-east1`. How should the multi-exit discriminator (MED) values be configured to provide this failover path?

options.text: Use regional routing. Set the us-east1 Cloud Router to a base priority of 100, and set the us-west1 Cloud Router to a base priority of 1
Use global routing. Set the us-east1 Cloud Router to a base priority of 100, and set the us-west1 Cloud Router to a base priority of 1
Use regional routing. Set the us-east1 Cloud Router to a base priority of 1000, and set the us-west1 Cloud Router to a base priority of 1
Use global routing. Set the us-east1 Cloud Router to a base priority of 1000, and set the us-west1 Cloud Router to a base priority of 1

questions.explanation:
Global dynamic routing lets each Cloud Router advertise subnet routes from both regions. Cloud Router advertises MED using the base priority, adding an inter-regional cost for remote subnet ranges; on-premises routing prefers the lower MED. Setting `us-west1` to 1 and `us-east1` to 1000 ensures the `us-west1` path is preferred for ingress traffic, with `us-east1` used when the preferred connection is unavailable.

**Learn more:** [Advertised routes | Cloud Router | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/concepts/advertised-routes) · [Update the base route priority | Cloud Router | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/updating-priority)

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],The company is exhausting network capacity for a critical application in its on-premises data center and wants to migrate that application to GCP. The company must also ensure that the Security team retains its ability to monitor traffic to and from Compute Engine instances.  
  
Which two products should be included in the solution? (Choose two.)

options.text: VPC flow logs
Firewall logs
Cloud Audit logs

1. Configure a VPC firewall rule to allow TCP port 22 for your corporate IP address with priority 1.2. Configure a VPC firewall rule to deny TCP port 22 for all IP addresses with priority 0.

1. Configure a hierarchical firewall policy to the organization node to allow TCP port 22 for your corporate IP address with priority 12. Configure a hierarchical firewall policy to the organization node to deny TCP port 22 for all IP addresses with priority 0.

questions.explanation:
Hierarchical firewall policies associated with the organization are inherited by VPC networks throughout the organization, and lower-level rules cannot override a matching higher-level rule. Firewall policy rules are evaluated from the lowest numeric priority upward, with 0 as the highest priority. Allowing TCP port 22 from the corporate IP address at priority 0 and denying TCP port 22 from all addresses at priority 1 therefore preserves corporate SSH access while blocking SSH from all other sources.

**Learn more:** [Hierarchical firewall policies](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies) · [Create hierarchical firewall policies and rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/using-firewall-policies)
