You are deploying a VPC architecture for your organization by using a Network Connectivity Center hub-and-spoke topology:  
  
- There is one Network Connectivity Center hybrid spoke that receives on-premises routes.  
- There is one VPC spoke that must be added as a Network Connectivity Center spoke.  
  
Your organization has limited routable IP space for its cloud environment (`192.168.0.0/20`). The Network Connectivity Center spoke VPC connects to on-premises through a Cloud Interconnect connection in the `us-east4` region. The on-premises IP range is `172.16.0.0/16`. You must reach on-premises resources from multiple Google Cloud regions (`us-west1`, `europe-central1`, and `asia-southeast1`) while minimizing the IP addresses used. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Configure a Private NAT gateway and NAT subnet in us-west1(192.168.1.0/24), europe-central1(192.168.2.0/24) and asia-southeast1(192.168.3.0/24).2. Add the VPC as a spoke and configure an export include policy to advertise only 192.168.1.0/24, 192.168.2.0/24, and 192.168.3.0/24 to the hub.3. Enable global dynamic routing to allow resources in us-west1, us-central1 and asia-southeast1 to reach the on-premises location through us-east4.

1. Configure a Private NAT gateway instance in us-west1(172.16.1.0/24), europe-central1(172.16.2.0/24), and asia-southeast1(172.16.3.0/24).2. Add the VPC as a spoke and configure an export include policy on the VPC spoke to advertise only the NAT subnets 172.16.1.0/24, 172.16.2.0/24, and 172.16.3.0/24 to the hub.3. Enable global dynamic to allow resources in us-west1, us-central1, and asia-southeast1 to reach the on-premises location through us-east4.

1. Configure a Private NAT gateway instance in us-east4(192.168.1.0/24).2. Add the VPC as a spoke and configure an export include policy on the VPC spoke to advertise 192.168.1.0/24 to the hub.3. Enable global dynamic routing to allow resources in us-west1, us-central1 and asia-southeast1 to reach the on-premises location through us-east4.

1. Configure a Private NAT gateway instance in us-west1(192.168.1.0/24), europe-central1(192.168.2.0/24), and asia-southeast1(192.168.3.0/24).2. Add the VPC as a spoke and configure an export exclude policy on the VPC spoke to advertise only the NAT subnets 192.168.1.0/24, 192.168.2.0/24, and 192.168.3.0/24 to the hub.3. Enable global dynamic routing to allow resources in us-west1, us-central1, and asia-southeast1 to reach the on-premises location through us-east4.

questions.explanation:
Private NAT is regional: a gateway provides NAT for eligible VM interfaces that use subnets in its region, and its Private NAT addresses must come from a Private NAT subnet in the same region and VPC. Separate NAT subnets in the three workload regions are therefore required. The `192.168.x.0/24` ranges are within the available cloud address space and do not overlap the on-premises `172.16.0.0/16` range. An export include filter restricts the VPC spoke to exporting precisely those NAT subnet routes, and global dynamic routing permits cross-region access to hybrid connectivity in `us-east4`.

**Learn more:** [Private NAT](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/private-nat) · [Private NAT for NCC spokes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/about-private-nat-for-ncc)

You have recently assumed responsibility for your organization’s Google Cloud network security configurations. You want to review your Cloud Next Generation Firewall (Cloud NGFW) configurations to make sure that no rules allow ingress traffic from the internet to your VMs and services. You want to avoid manual work. What should you do?

options.text: Export all your Cloud NGFW rules into a CSV file and search for 0.0.0.0/0.
Use Firewall Insights, and enable insights for Overly permissive rules.
Run Connectivity Tests from multiple external sources to confirm that traffic is not allowed to ingress to your most critical services in Google Cloud.
Review Network Analyzer insights on the VPC network category.

questions.explanation:
Firewall Insights can automatically generate overly permissive rule insights for allow rules with overly permissive IP address or port ranges. These insights help identify firewall rules whose scope is broader than necessary, enabling review of potential internet-accessible ingress rules without manually exporting and searching the rule set.

**Learn more:** [Firewall Insights overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/firewall-insights/concepts/overview) · [Firewall Insights categories and states](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/firewall-insights/concepts/insights-categories-states?hl=en)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A web application is currently hosted in the `us-central1` region. Users encounter high latency while traveling in Asia. You configured a network load balancer, but users have seen no performance improvement. You want to reduce the latency.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure a policy-based route rule to prioritize the traffic.
Configure an HTTP load balancer, and direct the traffic to it.
Configure Dynamic Routing for the subnet hosting the application.
Configure the TTL for the DNS zone to decrease the time between updates.

questions.explanation:
An external HTTP load balancer is a global Layer 7 service for HTTP(S) traffic. In the Premium Network Service Tier, it terminates HTTP(S) traffic as close as possible to users and routes requests to an appropriate healthy backend over Google's network, which reduces latency for users far from a `us-central1` application backend.

**Learn more:** [External Application Load Balancer overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/https) · [Optimize application latency with load balancing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/tutorials/optimize-app-latency)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your global website runs on Google Cloud. Static website assets, including images and CSS files, are kept in a Cloud Storage bucket, while dynamic content is delivered by a managed instance group (MIG).  
  
You want to enhance website performance, lower latency, and build an efficient, cost-conscious solution that uses Cloud CDN to cache static assets as near to users as possible. You also need requests for dynamic content to be routed directly to the MIG. What should you do?

options.text: Create two separate global external HTTPS Application Load Balancers. One for the Cloud Storage bucket with Cloud CDN enabled, and another for the MIG without Cloud CDN.
Create a Media CDN service, and configure it to pull content from both the Cloud Storage bucket and the MIG.

Configure a single global external HTTPS Application Load Balancer with a backend bucket for the Cloud Storage assets and a backend service for the MIG. Enable Cloud CDN on the backend bucket configuration.
Enable the static website hosting feature on the Cloud Storage bucket.

questions.explanation:
A global external HTTPS Application Load Balancer can use a URL map to route static paths to a Cloud Storage backend bucket and dynamic paths to a MIG-backed backend service. Cloud CDN enabled on the backend bucket caches the static Cloud Storage objects at Google edge locations; dynamic requests routed to the backend service continue directly to the MIG.

**Learn more:** [Backend buckets overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/backend-bucket) · [Use URL maps](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/url-map)

You are designing a Shared VPC architecture. Your network and security team enforces strict controls over the routes exposed between departments. The Production and Staging departments can communicate with one another, but only through specific networks. You want to follow Google-recommended practices.  
  
How should you design this topology?

options.text: Create 2 shared VPCs within the shared VPC Host Project, and enable VPC peering between them. Use firewall rules to filter access between the specific networks.
Create 2 shared VPCs within the shared VPC Host Project, and create a Cloud VPN/Cloud Router between them. Use Flexible Route Advertisement (FRA) to filter access between the specific networks.
Create 2 shared VPCs within the shared VPC Service Project, and create a Cloud VPN/Cloud Router between them. Use Flexible Route Advertisement (FRA) to filter access between the specific networks.
Create 1 VPC within the shared VPC Host Project, and share individual subnets with the Service Projects to filter access between the specific networks.

questions.explanation:
A single VPC network in the Shared VPC host project can selectively share individual subnets with service projects. This keeps network, route, and security administration centralized while limiting each department to its approved subnets; firewall rules can govern communication between the resources using those subnets. This is the Shared VPC model intended for centrally controlled networks used by multiple projects.

**Learn more:** [Shared VPC](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc) · [Provision Shared VPC](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/provisioning-shared-vpc)

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question:
You are using the `gcloud` command-line tool to create a new custom role in a project by copying a predefined role. You receive the following error message:  
  
`INVALID_ARGUMENT: Permission resourcemanager.projects.list is not valid`  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Add the resourcemanager.projects.get permission, and try again.
Try again with a different role with a new name but the same permissions.
Remove the resourcemanager.projects.list permission, and try again.
Add the resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy permission, and try again.

questions.explanation:
Project-level custom roles cannot include permissions that are applicable only at organization or folder scope. `resourcemanager.projects.list` lists projects and is not valid for inclusion in a project-level custom role, so it must be removed before creating the role.\
\
**Learn more:** [Create and manage custom roles](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/creating-custom-roles)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question:
You are using the `gcloud` command-line tool to create a new custom role in a project by copying a predefined role. You receive the following error message:  
  
`INVALID_ARGUMENT: Permission resourcemanager.projects.list is not valid`  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Establish a Private Service Connect endpoint between your application's VPC and the Google-managed service producer network.
Deploy a private Compute Engine instance with a custom proxy server in your application's VPC, and route all Cloud SQL traffic through this proxy.
Establish a Private Service Access connection between your application’s VPC and the Google-managed service producer network.
Use Cloud SQL connector to connect to the Cloud SQL instance.

questions.explanation:
Private Service Connect lets clients use an internal endpoint IP address in their VPC to access a Cloud SQL instance privately, with traffic staying within Google Cloud. It avoids the dedicated allocated IP range required by Private Service Access, making it the more IP-efficient private connectivity option with less network setup overhead.

**Learn more:** [Connect to an instance using Private Service Connect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/configure-private-service-connect) · [Configure private services access](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/configure-private-services-access)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization operates a highly available, non-HTTP application. The application listens on multiple TCP ports and is hosted across multiple regions. You must design a solution to load balance the application within the same Shared VPC where the service will be accessed. The IP address header must include the client’s actual source IP address. Public internet access is not needed. What should you do?

options.text: Configure multiple regional internal proxy Network Load Balancers and enable global access. Use DNS routing policies to balance traffic across regions.
Configure multiple regional internal Application Load Balancers and enable global access. Use DNS routing policies to balance traffic across regions.
Configure a single cross region internal proxy Network Load Balancer.
Configure multiple regional internal passthrough Network Load Balancers and enable global access. Use DNS routing policies to balance traffic across regions.

questions.explanation:
Internal passthrough Network Load Balancers are internal Layer 4 load balancers that preserve the original client packet source IP address and can forward TCP traffic on multiple ports. Their backends are regional, so a multi-region deployment requires regional load balancers; global access permits clients from other regions, and DNS routing distributes traffic among the regional load balancer addresses.

**Learn more:** [Internal passthrough Network Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/internal) · [Passthrough Network Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/passthrough-network-load-balancer)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization recently rearchitected its cloud environment to use Network Connectivity Center. However, an error occurred when you attempted to add a new VPC, named `vpc-dev`, as a spoke. The error indicated an issue involving an existing spoke and the IP space of a VPC, named `vpc-pre-prod`. You must complete the migration quickly and efficiently. What should you do?

options.text: Delete the VMs associated with the conflicting subnets, then delete the conflicting subnets in vpc-dev. Recreate the subnets with a new IP range and redeploy the previously-deleted VMs in the new subnets. Add the VPC spoke for vpc-dev.
Exclude the conflicting IP range by using the --exclude-export-ranges flag when creating the VPC spoke for vpc-dev.
Exclude the conflicting IP range by using the --exclude-export-ranges flag in the hub when attaching the VPC spoke for vpc-dev.
Remove the conflicting VPC spoke for vpc-pre-prod from the set of VPC spokes in Network Connectivity Center. Add the VPC spoke for vpc-dev. Add the previously removed vpc-pre-prod as a VPC spoke.

questions.explanation:
Network Connectivity Center prohibits conflicting subnet IP ranges from being exported by VPC spokes connected to the same hub. An export filter on a VPC spoke can prevent the conflicting subnet range from being shared with the hub; specify that filter with `--exclude-export-ranges` when creating the `vpc-dev` VPC spoke. This avoids disruptive subnet and VM recreation or removal of the existing spoke.

**Learn more:** [Spoke administration overview — Subnet route uniqueness](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/vpc-spoke-admin?hl=en) · [gcloud network-connectivity spokes linked-vpc-network create](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/network-connectivity/spokes/linked-vpc-network/create)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an HTTP API hosted on a Compute Engine virtual machine instance that must be called only by multiple clients in the same Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). You want the clients to be able to obtain the service's IP address. What should you do?

options.text: Reserve a static external IP address and assign it to an HTTP(S) load balancing service's forwarding rule. Clients should use this IP address to connect to the service.
Ensure that clients use Compute Engine internal DNS by connecting to the instance name with the url https://[INSTANCE_NAME].[ZONE].c.[PROJECT_ID].internal/.

Reserve a static external IP address and assign it to an HTTP(S) load balancing service's forwarding rule. Then, define an A record in Cloud DNS. Clients should use the name of the A record to connect to the service.
Ensure that clients use Compute Engine internal DNS by connecting to the instance name with the url https://[API_NAME]/[API_VERSION]/.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine internal DNS creates a name that resolves to a VM’s internal IP address, and VMs in the same VPC can use that name for private instance-to-instance communication. A zonal internal DNS name has the form `[INSTANCE_NAME].[ZONE].c.[PROJECT_ID].internal`, so clients can connect using that hostname without using a public IP address.

**Learn more:** [Access VMs using internal DNS](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/networking/using-internal-dns)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are adding steps to an existing working automation that uses a service account for authentication. You need to give the automation the ability to retrieve files from a Cloud Storage bucket. Your organization requires the least privilege possible.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Grant the compute.instanceAdmin to your user account.
Grant the iam.serviceAccountUser to your user account.
Grant the read-only privilege to the service account for the Cloud Storage bucket.
Grant the cloud-platform privilege to the service account for the Cloud Storage bucket.

questions.explanation:
A service account must have read access to the Cloud Storage bucket’s objects to retrieve files. Bucket-scoped read-only access grants the necessary object-viewing capability without broader project, platform, Compute Engine, or service-account impersonation permissions. Google Cloud documents the Storage Object Viewer role as providing the permissions needed to download objects from a bucket.

**Learn more:** [Download objects | Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/downloading-objects) · [IAM roles for Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam-roles)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s logo is published as an image file on multiple websites hosted by the company. Cloud CDN has been implemented, but you want to improve the cache hit ratio for this image file. What should you do?

options.text: Configure custom cache keys for the backend service that holds the image file, and clear the Host and Protocol checkboxes.
Configure the default time to live (TTL) as 0 for the image file.
Configure versioned URLs for each domain to serve users the image file before the cache entry expires.
Configure Cloud Storage as a custom origin backend to host the image file, and select multi-region as the location type.

questions.explanation:
A custom Cloud CDN cache key that excludes the Host and Protocol components allows identical logo requests from different domains and protocols to use the same cache entry. This avoids unnecessarily splitting the cache and increases the cache hit ratio when the image content does not vary by host or protocol.

**Learn more:** [Content delivery best practices | Cloud CDN](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/best-practices) · [Customize cache keys | Cloud CDN](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/using-cache-keys?hl=en)

You are designing a secure, multi-VPC environment with a Network Connectivity Center (NCC) hub. A `landing-zone-vpc` contains the VLAN attachments for a Dedicated Interconnect, configured as hybrid spokes on the NCC hub. The `prod-vpc` and `landing-zone-vpc` are connected as VPC spokes. Critical Cloud SQL databases are deployed in `us-central1`, hosted in the `prod-vpc`, and exposed through Private Service Connect (PSC) endpoints.  
  
On-premises users, whose traffic enters through the Dedicated Interconnect in `us-west1`, report that they cannot connect to the database’s PSC endpoint. You need to enable this connectivity while following Google-recommended best practices.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create additional PSC endpoints in us-central1 within the landing-zone-vpc using the Cloud SQL database service attachments found using the command gcloud sq1 instances describe.
Create additional PSC endpoints in us-west1 within the landing-zone-vpc using the Cloud SQL database service attachments found using the command gcloud sq1 instances describe.
Enable PSC connection propagation on the Network Connectivity Center hub. Specify the landing-zone-vpc as the target VPC network.
Enable PSC connection propagation on the Network Connectivity Center hub. Update the Cloud SQL PSC endpoints to enable global access.

questions.explanation:
NCC PSC connection propagation makes PSC services in one VPC spoke reachable from other spokes, including on-premises networks reached through hybrid spokes when the routing VPC is also a VPC spoke. Propagated connections are regional by default; enabling global access on the Cloud SQL PSC endpoints permits traffic arriving in `us-west1` to reach endpoints in `us-central1`.

**Learn more:** [Private Service Connect connection propagation through NCC](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/psc-propagated-connection-overview) · [About propagated connections](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/about-propagated-connections)

Which GKE resource should you use?

You need to apply a new Cloud Armor policy to an application deployed in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You need to determine which target to use for the Cloud Armor policy.  
  
Which GKE resource should you use?

options.text: Promote the internal IP addresses to static assignments for all database VMs.
Create a firewall rule to allow only traffic to the IP addresses allocated to your database VMs.
Define a maintenance window to shut down the database VMs one at a time, promote the internal IP address to a static assignment, and restart the VM.
Define an organization policy to allow only statically allocated IP addresses for VMs. Ensure the prefix matches your database VMs.

questions.explanation:
An in-use ephemeral internal IP address can be promoted to a static internal IP address. Promotion reserves the VM’s current address without requiring the VM to be stopped or restarted, so existing operations remain uninterrupted.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your product team operates web servers in both the `us-east1` and `us-west1` regions in the `prod-servers` project. Your security team intends to deploy an intrusion detection system (IDS) in its own Google Cloud project to inspect incoming network traffic. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new project and a VPC for the security team.Peer the new VPC with the web servers’ VPC in the prod-servers project.Create an internal load balancer and the IDS system in both us-east1 and us-west1.Enable Packet Mirroring, and create packet mirroring policies inside the new project.

Create a host project and a Sharad VPC for the security team.Make prod-servers a service project, and relocate the web servers to shared subnets in both regions.Enable IP forwarding on all the web servers.Create the IDS system in a non-shared subnet of us-east1 or us-west1.Configure the web servers to forward the packets to the IDS system.C. Create a new project and a VPC for the security team.Peer the new VPC with the web servers’ VPC in the prod-servers project.Enable IP forwarding on all the web servers.Install the IDS system in both us-east1 and us-west1.Configure the web servers to forward the packets to the IDS system.

Create a host project and a Shared VPC for the security team.Make prod-servers a service project, and relocate the web servers to shared subnets in both regions.Create an internal load balancer and the IDS system in a subnet in either us-east1 or us-west1.Enable Packet Mirroring, and create a packet mirroring policy inside the host project.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Packet Mirroring sends copies of VM traffic to an internal passthrough load balancer that distributes it to IDS collector instances. Mirrored sources for a policy must be in the same project, VPC network, and region, and the collector destination must be in that same region. A peered security VPC with regional internal load balancers and IDS collectors in both `us-east1` and `us-west1` satisfies those requirements.

**Learn more:** [Packet Mirroring](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/packet-mirroring) · [Use Packet Mirroring](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/using-packet-mirroring)

Your organization is introducing a security policy to control how firewall rules govern flows between virtual machines (VMs). Following Google-recommended practices, you need to configure a firewall rule that strictly controls traffic between VM A and VM B.  
  
Ensure that communication can flow only from VM A to VM B within the VPC, with no other communication paths permitted. No other firewall rules exist in the VPC. Which firewall rule should you configure to allow only this communication path?

options.text: Firewall rule direction: ingressAction: allow -Target: VM B service account -Source ranges: VM A service accountPriority: 1000
Firewall rule direction: ingressAction: allow -Target: specific VM B tag -Source ranges: VM A tag and VM A source IP addressPriority: 1000
Firewall rule direction: ingressAction: allow -Target: VM A service account -Source ranges: VM B service account and VM B source IP addressPriority: 100
Firewall rule direction: ingressAction: allow -Target: specific VM A tag -Source ranges: VM B tag and VM B source IP addressPriority: 100

questions.explanation:
An ingress allow rule must target VM B, because VM B is receiving the connection, and must restrict the source to VM A. Using service accounts identifies the VMs by workload identity and is the recommended, more precise approach than network tags. VPC firewall rules are stateful, so connection tracking permits response traffic for an allowed VM A-to-VM B connection; with no other rules, the implied deny-ingress rule prevents other inbound paths.

**Learn more:** [VPC firewall rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls) · [Use VPC firewall rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/using-firewalls)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a critical application that depends on a Dedicated Interconnect connection between your on-premises data center and your Google Cloud VPC. Users report intermittent slowness while accessing the application. You need to verify the Dedicated Interconnect connection’s health and performance and identify any bottlenecks.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Audit the BGP routing table on your Cloud Router to ensure all routes are being advertised on the dedicated link correctly.
Use VPC Flow Logs to analyze the traffic patterns between your on-premises network and the Google Cloud VPC.
Review Cloud Logging entries for the Dedicated Interconnect-related events to detect connection flaps.
Examine Cloud Monitoring metrics for the Dedicated Interconnect connection, focusing on ingress/egress bytes, packet loss, and latency.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Interconnect sends Dedicated Interconnect connection and VLAN-attachment metrics to Cloud Monitoring. These metrics let operators assess traffic utilization against capacity and inspect sent/received traffic together with error and drop signals, which are the appropriate indicators for finding connection-level performance bottlenecks.

**Learn more:** [Monitor connections | Cloud Interconnect | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/monitoring?hl=en)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You administer the network for a large enterprise with two geographically separated on-premises data centers: datacenter-east and datacenter-west. You also have a Google Cloud VPC called hub-vpc. You must establish secure, high-bandwidth private network communication between datacenter-east and datacenter-west by using your existing Google Cloud network.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: • Create Dedicated Interconnects between hub-vpc and datacenter-east, and hub-vpc and datacenter-west.• Create a proxy VM to proxy traffic from one region to another.

• Create an NCC hub and add hub-vpc as a VPC spoke.• Create an HA-VPN between hub-vpc and datacenter-east, and hub-vpc and datacenter-west.• Add the HA-VPNs as hybrid spokes to the NCC hub with site-to-site data transfer set to On.

• Create an HA-VPN between hub-vpc and datacenter-east, and hub-vpc and datacenter-west.• Configure Cloud Storage buckets in your Google Cloud project, and use them as an intermediary to transfer data between datacenter-east and datacenter-west.

• Create an NCC hub and add hub-vpc as a VPC spoke.• Create Dedicated Interconnects between hub-vpc and datacenter-east, and hub-vpc and datacenter-west.• Add the Dedicated Interconnects as hybrid spokes to the NCC hub with site-to-site data transfer set to On.

questions.explanation: Dedicated Interconnect supplies private, high-bandwidth connectivity from each on-premises data center to Google Cloud. An NCC hub can use hub-vpc as a VPC spoke and the Dedicated Interconnect connections as hybrid spokes; enabling site-to-site data transfer permits traffic to transit between the two connected on-premises sites through the NCC topology.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an HA VPN connection with two tunnels configured in active/passive mode between your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) and on-premises network. Traffic across the connection has recently risen from 1 gigabit per second (Gbps) to 4 Gbps, and you observe dropped packets. You need to configure your VPN connection to Google Cloud to support 4 Gbps. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the remote autonomous system number (ASN) to 4096.
Configure a second Cloud Router to scale bandwidth in and out of the VPC.
Configure the maximum transmission unit (MTU) to its highest supported value.
Configure a second set of active/passive VPN tunnels.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud VPN tunnel supports up to 250,000 packets per second for combined ingress and egress traffic, which is approximately 1–3 Gbps depending on average packet size. An active/passive configuration uses one tunnel for normal traffic, so its capacity can be exceeded at 4 Gbps. Bandwidth is increased by adding another active/passive tunnel pair, providing an additional active tunnel to carry traffic while retaining failover capacity.

**Learn more:** [HA VPN topologies to increase bandwidth](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/topologies-increase-bandwidth) · [Cloud VPN overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for enabling Private Google Access so that virtual machine (VM) instances in your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) can access Google APIs. All VM instances have only private IP addresses and must access Cloud Storage. You need to ensure that all VM traffic is routed back to your on-premises data center for traffic scrubbing through your existing Cloud Interconnect connection. However, VM traffic to Google APIs must remain in the VPC. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Delete the default route in your VPC.2. Create a private Cloud DNS zone for googleapis.com, create a CNAME for *.googleapis.com to restricted googleapis.com, and create an A record for restricted googleapis com that resolves to the addresses in 199.36.153.4/30.3. Create a static route in your VPC for the range 199.36.153.4/30 with the default internet gateway as the next hop.

1. Delete the default route in your VPC and configure your on-premises router to advertise 0.0.0.0/0 via Border Gateway Protocol (BGP).2. Create a public Cloud DNS zone with a CNAME for *.google.com to private googleapis com, create a CNAME for * googleapis.com to private googleapis com, and create an A record for Private googleapis.com that resolves to the addresses in 199.36.153 8/30.3. Create a static route in your VPC for the range 199 .36.153.8/30 with the default internet gateway as the next hop.

1. Configure your on-premises router to advertise 0.0.0.0/0 via Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) with a lower priority (MED) than the default VPC route.2. Create a private Cloud DNS zone for googleapis.com, create a CNAME for * googieapis.com to private googleapis com, and create an A record for private.googleapis.com that resolves to the addresses in 199 .36.153.8/30.3. Create a static route in your VPC for the range 199.36. 153.8/30 with the default internet gateway as the next hop.

1. Delete the default route in your VPC and configure your on-premises router to advertise 0.0.0.0/0 via Border Gateway Protocol (BGP).2. Create a private Cloud DNS zone for googleapis.com, create a CNAME for * googieapis.com to Private googleapis.com, and create an A record for private.googleapis.com that resolves to the addresses in 199.36.153.8/30.3. Create a static route in your VPC for the range 199.36.153.8/30 with the default internet gateway as the next hop.

questions.explanation:
`private.googleapis.com` uses `199.36.153.8/30` and requires private DNS records in a private `googleapis.com` zone, including a wildcard CNAME to `private.googleapis.com`. After the default VPC route is removed, an on-premises BGP-advertised `0.0.0.0/0` route sends general traffic through Cloud Interconnect for scrubbing. A more-specific static route for `199.36.153.8/30` with the default internet gateway as its next hop overrides that default route; traffic to Google APIs remains on Google’s network.

**Learn more:** [Configure Private Google Access](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access) · [Routes](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/routes)

Your company is collaborating with a partner to deliver a solution for a customer. Both your company and the partner organization use GCP. Applications in the partner's network need access to certain resources in your company's VPC. The VPCs have no overlapping CIDR ranges.  
  
Which two solutions can you implement to meet the required outcome without compromising security? (Choose two.)

options.text: VPC peering
Shared VPC
Cloud VPN
Dedicated Interconnect
Cloud NAT

questions.explanation:
VPC Network Peering provides private internal connectivity between two VPC networks, including networks in projects belonging to different organizations, and it requires their subnet ranges not to overlap. Cloud VPN provides secure site-to-site IPsec connectivity and can connect two VPC networks, encrypting traffic in transit.

**Learn more:** [VPC Network Peering](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering?hl=en) · [Cloud VPN overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have just deployed infrastructure on Google Cloud and now must configure DNS to meet these requirements:  
  
- Your on-premises resources must resolve your Google Cloud zones.  
- Your Google Cloud resources must resolve your on-premises zones.  
- You must be able to resolve `.internal` zones provisioned by Google Cloud.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure an outbound server policy, and set your alternative name server to be your on-premises DNS resolver. Configure your on-premises DNS resolver to forward Google Cloud zone queries to Google's public DNS 8.8.8.8.

Configure both an inbound server policy and outbound DNS forwarding zones with the target as the on-premises DNS resolver. Configure your on-premises DNS resolver to forward Google Cloud zone queries to Google Cloud's DNS resolver.

Configure an outbound DNS server policy, and set your alternative name server to be your on-premises DNS resolver. Configure your on-premises DNS resolver to forward Google Cloud zone queries to Google Cloud's DNS resolver.
Configure Cloud DNS to DNS peer with your on-premises DNS resolver. Configure your on-premises DNS resolver to forward Google Cloud zone queries to Google's public DNS 8.8.8.8.

questions.explanation:
An inbound DNS server policy provides Cloud DNS entry points that an on-premises resolver can use to resolve Google Cloud zones. Forwarding zones can direct Google Cloud queries for on-premises zones to the on-premises DNS resolver. This avoids using an outbound server policy with alternative name servers, which makes Google Cloud-provisioned `.internal` names unavailable.

**Learn more:** [DNS server policies](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/server-policies-overview) · [DNS policies overview](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/policies-overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are overseeing the integration of a newly acquired company. The primary corporate VPC (`vpc-corp`) and the acquired company’s VPC (`vpc-acquired`) have overlapping subnet CIDR ranges. You must enable a private connection that lets the monitoring service in `vpc-corp` initiate traffic to application servers in `vpc-acquired`, while preventing all other connections.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a Network Connectivity Center hub. On the vpc-acquired spoke, configure Private NAT to translate its addresses for inbound traffic.
Create a Network Connectivity Center hub, connect both VPCs as spokes, and deploy a proxy instance in the hub.
Deploy Cloud NAT gateway in vpc-corp. Configure Cloud NAT to translate traffic outbound. Configure an external load balancer in vpc-acquired to accept the connections from Cloud NAT.
Create a Network Connectivity Center hub. On the vpc-corp spoke, configure Private NAT to translate its source address range for outbound traffic.

questions.explanation:
Private NAT for Network Connectivity Center translates egress traffic from VM instances in the selected source subnet ranges when the destination spoke belongs to the same hub. Placing Private NAT on `vpc-corp` and limiting its source range to the monitoring service enables the required one-way initiated connectivity across overlapping CIDRs without enabling other source ranges.

**Learn more:** [Private NAT for NCC spokes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/about-private-nat-for-ncc)

options.text: Place your NVAs behind an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer named ILB1. Add the global network firewall policy rules to allow traffic through your NVAs. Create a policy-based route (PBR) with the source IP range of the backend VM subnet, destination IP range of the frontend VM subnet, and the next hop of ILB1. Scope the PBR to the VMs with the backend network tag. Add a backend network tag to your backend servers.

Create a custom static route with the destination IP range of the backend VM subnet, frontend instance tag, and the next hop of ILB1. Add a frontend network tag to your frontend VMs.

Create a policy-based route (PBR) with the source IP range of the frontend VM subnet, destination IP range of the backend VM subnet, and the next hop of ILB1. questions.explanation:
Google Cloud policy-based routes can match source and destination IP ranges, apply only to VMs identified by network tags, and redirect matching traffic to an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer that fronts firewall appliances. Matching the frontend subnet as the source and the backend subnet as the destination, while scoping the route to frontend-tagged VMs, inserts the NVAs into the frontend-to-backend path. Since the full-proxy NVA source-NATs allowed traffic, return traffic is sent to the NVA without requiring a backend-to-frontend policy-based route.

**Learn more:** [Use policy-based routes | Virtual Private Cloud | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/use-policy-based-routes) · [Policy-based routes | Virtual Private Cloud | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/policy-based-routes)

Your company is implementing new outbound internet-traffic rules in its Google Cloud environment. You must design a configuration that routes all outbound internet traffic from virtual machines tagged `production-critical` through a Secure Web Proxy (SWP) for inspection, while allowing every other virtual machine to egress directly to the internet. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway configured to translate and forward traffic from production-critical VMs to the internet.
Configure a custom static route with a destination of 0.0.0.0/0 for the production-critical network tag with the SWP IP address as a next hop.
Configure a policy-based route with a destination of 0.0.0.0/0 for the production-critical network tag with the SWP IP as a next hop.
Configure a policy-based route with a source set as the subnets of the production-critical VMs and a destination of 0.0.0.0/0 with the SWP IP as the next hop.

questions.explanation:
A static route with destination `0.0.0.0/0`, the Secure Web Proxy IP as its next hop, and the `production-critical` network tag applies only to VMs bearing that tag. Their outbound internet traffic is therefore sent to the SWP, while VMs without the tag continue to use the normal default route to the internet. Google Cloud Secure Web Proxy next-hop documentation specifically requires network tags for static routes and uses `0.0.0.0/0` to redirect all internet traffic.

**Learn more:** [Deploy Secure Web Proxy as next hop](https://cloud.google.com/secure-web-proxy/docs/deploy-next-hop)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are reviewing and tuning Secure Web Proxy at your organization, Mount Kirk Games. Users report that they cannot access the documents they require on the Terram Earth website (`https://www.terramearth.com/docs/*`). The Secure Web Proxy rules configuration is as follows:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783887377648-i1ff2093.png)  
  
You need to enable access to these documents. What should you do?

options.text: Delete the updates-limiter rule.
Modify the updates-1 rule to perform the TLS inspection.
Review Cloud Logging for errors with Cloud NAT. If there are no errors, assign the VM a public IP address.
Modify the priority of the updates-limiter rule to 1000.

questions.explanation:
For HTTPS traffic, a Secure Web Proxy rule that uses an application matcher such as `request.path.contains('/docs/')` must have TLS inspection enabled. With inspection enabled, the priority-1002 allow rule can evaluate the encrypted request path and allow `/docs/` requests before the lower-priority priority-1050 deny rule for `terramearth.com` is reached. [Google Cloud: Enable TLS inspection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/secure-web-proxy/docs/enable-tls-inspection)

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud: Enable TLS inspection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/secure-web-proxy/docs/enable-tls-inspection) · [Google Cloud: Rule evaluation order](https://docs.cloud.google.com/secure-web-proxy/docs/tls-rule-evaluation)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are setting up a new application that will be exposed behind an external load balancer with both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and must support TCP pass-through on port 443. Backends will run in two regions: us-west1 and us-east1. You want to deliver content with the lowest possible latency while maintaining high availability and autoscaling. Which configuration should you use?

options.text: Use global SSL Proxy Load Balancing with backends in both regions.
Use global TCP Proxy Load Balancing with backends in both regions.
Use global external HTTP(S) Load Balancing with backends in both regions.
Use Network Load Balancing in both regions, and use DNS-based load balancing to direct traffic to the closest region.

questions.explanation:
A regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer delivers TCP packets to its backends without proxying or terminating the client connection. Because this load balancer is regional, deploying one in each region and using DNS-based routing directs clients toward the closest regional endpoint while each regional backend group can provide health-based availability and autoscaling. TCP Proxy, SSL Proxy, and HTTP(S) load balancers are proxy-based services that terminate client connections, so they do not provide TCP pass-through.

**Learn more:** [Regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/network/networklb-backend-service) · [IPv6 for Application Load Balancers and proxy Network Load Balancers](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/ipv6)

questions.question:
You need to configure load balancing for an internet-facing, standard voice-over-IP (VOIP) application.  
  
Which load balancer type should you use?

options.text: HTTP(S) load balancer
Network load balancer
Internal TCP/UDP load balancer
TCP/SSL proxy load balancer

questions.explanation:
An external Network Load Balancer supports Layer 4 UDP traffic used by standard VoIP applications and can accept internet traffic. HTTP(S) load balancers handle web traffic, internal TCP/UDP load balancers are for private connectivity, and TCP/SSL proxy load balancers do not provide UDP support.\
\
**Learn more:** [Choose a load balancer — Cloud Load Balancing](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/choosing-load-balancer) · [Cloud Load Balancing overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/load-balancing-overview)

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question:
You need to configure load balancing for an internet-facing, standard voice-over-IP (VOIP) application.  
  
Which load balancer type should you use?

options.text: Query the dynamic_routes/learned_routes/dropped_unique_destinations metric and review the global routing_mode metric attribute.
Query the dynamic_routes/learned_routes/unique_destinations_limit metric and review the global routing_mode metric attribute.
Query the dynamic_routes/learned_routes/any_dropped_unique_destinations metric and review the regional routing_mode metric attribute.
Query the dynamic_routes/learned_routes/dropped_unique_destinations metric and review the regional routing_mode metric attribute.

questions.explanation:
The `dynamic_routes/learned_routes/dropped_unique_destinations` metric reports the number of unique route destinations dropped in a network region after a route quota is exceeded. Its `routing_mode` label identifies routes learned from remote regions as `global` and locally learned routes as `regional`. Routes advertised through `us-west1` and needed in `us-east4` are remote-region routes, so inspect the metric using the `global` routing-mode attribute. [Google Cloud metrics: P through Z](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/api/metrics_gcp_p_z?hl=en)

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud metrics: P through Z](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/api/metrics_gcp_p_z?hl=en) · [Troubleshoot BGP routes and route selection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/support/troubleshoot-bgp-routes?hl=en)

Your organization has run Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters in several distinct Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) for the last year, with one GKE cluster in each VPC. Although the GKE nodes use unique IP address space for every cluster, Pod IP ranges have been reused among the VPCs. The VPCs are spokes in a Network Connectivity Center hub that uses mesh topology. Pod IP ranges have been excluded from the Network Connectivity Center VPC spokes.  
  
Although this setup appears to work and Compute Engine instances in the VPCs can access services, Pods cannot access services in other VPCs. You need to enable communication between Pods in separate VPCs. What should you do?

options.text: Ensure that the IP masquerade agent is installed correctly and performing source NAT for Pod traffic destined to services outside of the cluster.
Delete the GKE clusters, create a new pair of VMs in the subnets used by the GKE clusters, and test the connectivity. Recreate the GKE clusters.
Delete the Network Connectivity Center hub and VPC spokes. Connect all VPCs by using Cloud VPNs.
Delete the Network Connectivity Center hub and VPC spokes. Peer all VPCs by using VPC Network Peering.

questions.explanation:
When Pod IP ranges are reused across clusters, they cannot be uniquely routed between VPCs. GKE’s IP masquerade agent can apply source NAT to Pod traffic leaving a cluster, replacing the overlapping Pod source address with the cluster’s unique node IP address. Return traffic can then be routed correctly while the Pod CIDRs remain excluded from Network Connectivity Center advertisements.

**Learn more:** [Manage IP address migration in GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/gke-ip-address-mgmt-strategies) · [IP masquerade agent](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ip-masquerade-agent)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],To provide subnet-level isolation, you need to force instance-A in one subnet to route through a security appliance named instance-B in another subnet.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a more specific route than the system-generated subnet route, pointing the next hop to instance-B with no tag.
Create a more specific route than the system-generated subnet route, pointing the next hop to instance-B with a tag applied to instance-A.
Delete the system-generated subnet route and create a specific route to instance-B with a tag applied to instance-A.
Move instance-B to another VPC and, using multi-NIC, connect instance-B's interface to instance-A's network. Configure the appropriate routes to force traffic through to instance-A.

questions.explanation:
A more-specific custom route that uses instance-B as its next hop and targets the network tag on instance-A directs only instance-A’s matching traffic through the security appliance. Network tags scope custom routes to selected VM instances; an untagged route would apply to all applicable instances. Subnet routes are system-managed and cannot be deleted separately from their corresponding subnet.

**Learn more:** [Use routes | Virtual Private Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/using-routes) · [Routes | Virtual Private Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/routes)

questions.domain: Configuring, implementing and managing a cloud network security solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company provides a popular gaming service. Its instances use private IP addresses, and a global load balancer provides external access. You think you have identified a potential malicious actor, but you are not sure that you have the right client IP address. You need to identify this actor while minimizing disruption for legitimate users.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Armor Policy rule that denies traffic and review necessary logs.
Create a Cloud Armor Policy rule that denies traffic, enable preview mode, and review necessary logs.
Create a VPC Firewall rule that denies traffic, enable logging and set enforcement to disabled, and review necessary logs.
Create a VPC Firewall rule that denies traffic, enable logging and set enforcement to enabled, and review necessary logs.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Armor security policies protect traffic reaching a global external Application Load Balancer. A deny rule in preview mode logs matching requests and the proposed action without enforcing the block, so the suspected client IP can be validated without interrupting legitimate users. [Cloud Armor security policy overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/security-policy-overview?authuser=6)

**Learn more:** [Cloud Armor security policy overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/security-policy-overview?authuser=6)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must provide every member of the network operations team with least-privilege access to create, modify, and delete Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachments.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Assign each user the editor role.
Assign each user the compute.networkAdmin role.
Give each user the following permissions only: compute.interconnectAttachments.create, compute.interconnectAttachments.get.
Give each user the following permissions only: compute.interconnectAttachments.create, compute.interconnectAttachments.get, compute.routers.create, compute.routers.get, compute.routers.update.

questions.explanation:
The Compute Network Admin role (`roles/compute.networkAdmin`) grants permissions to create, modify, and delete networking resources, including Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachments. It includes the required `compute.interconnectAttachments.create`, `compute.interconnectAttachments.update`, and `compute.interconnectAttachments.delete` permissions without granting the broad project-wide access of the Editor role.

**Learn more:** [Compute Engine roles and permissions](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/compute)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying a Shared VPC network for your organization, which includes distributed teams. An application developer who works across multiple teams notices they can deploy applications into subnets reserved for another application's service projects. You want to ensure that developers can deploy resources only in the subnets reserved for their own service project. What should you do?

options.text: Specify which Shared VPC subnets each application's service projects can access by using the constraints/compute.restrictSharedVpcSubnetworks organizational constraint.
Grant the compute.NetworkViewer role to the developer in the Shared VPC host project.
Restrict another application's project from accessing specific subnets in the host project by using the constraints/compute.restrictSharedVpcHostProject organizational constraint.
Grant the compute.NetworkUser role to the developer in the specific Shared VPC service project.

questions.explanation:
The `constraints/compute.restrictSharedVpcSubnetworks` organization-policy constraint defines the Shared VPC subnetworks that eligible resources in a service project can use. Applying an allowlist for each service project prevents new resources from using subnets reserved for other projects.

**Learn more:** [Shared VPC documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc) · [Provision Shared VPC documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/provisioning-shared-vpc)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s web application has just been deployed to Compute Engine VMs in multiple Google Cloud regions. You created multiple instance groups and need to distribute traffic across these VMs. You want users to automatically connect to the backend in the closest region while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create one global external Application Load Balancer and multiple backend services. Ensure that each backend service contains one backend. Point each backend to a different instance group.
Create one global external Application Load Balancer and one backend service with multiple backends. Point each backend to a different instance group.
Create two global external Application Load Balancers with one backend service and one backend. Point each back end to a different instance group.
Create two global external Application Load Balancers with multiple backend services. Ensure that each backend service contains one backend. Point each backend to a different instance group.

questions.explanation:
A global external Application Load Balancer supports multi-region backends and attempts to route requests to the closest healthy backend with available capacity. One global backend service can include multiple instance-group backends, allowing each regional instance group to participate in the same globally distributed application service.

**Learn more:** [External Application Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/https) · [Backend services overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/backend-service)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is moving workloads from AWS to Google Cloud. Since one especially critical workload will require more time to migrate, you must configure Google Cloud CDN and direct it to the existing application in AWS. What should you do?

options.text: • Create an internet NEG that points to the existing FQDN of the application.• Map the NEG to an Application Load Balancer as a backend service.• Enable Cloud CDN on the backend service.
• Create a hybrid NEG that points to the existing IP of the application.• Map the NEG to a passthrough Network Load Balancer as a target pool.• Enable Cloud CDN on the target pool.
• Create an internet NEG that points to the existing FQDN of the application.• Map the NEG to a passthrough Network Load Balancer as a backend service.• Enable Cloud CDN on the backend service.
• Create a hybrid NEG that points to the existing IP of the application.• Map the NEG to an Application Load Balancer as a backend service.• Enable Cloud CDN on the backend service.

questions.explanation:
Cloud CDN can cache content from an external origin hosted in another cloud by using an internet NEG attached to an external Application Load Balancer backend service. Defining the origin by its FQDN is the recommended configuration because it accommodates changes to the origin IP address. Hybrid NEGs are intended for backends reached through Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect, rather than a public AWS application origin.

**Learn more:** [External backends specified by using internet NEGs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/external-backends-internet-neg-overview) · [Set up an external backend with an internet NEG](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/set-up-external-backend-internet-neg)

Your company uses Network Connectivity Center to link its VPCs in Google Cloud. It plans to connect its on-premises data center to one of these VPCs using HA VPN. The CIDR range of the on-premises network overlaps with IP addresses in Google Cloud. You want Google Cloud VMs to connect directly to the IP addresses of the on-premises hosts. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a subnet of purpose REGIONAL_MANAGED_PROXY and use a Google Cloud application load balancer.
Configure a subnet of purpose REGIONAL_MANAGED_PROXY and use a Google Cloud TCP proxy load balancer.
Configure a subnet of purpose PRIVATE_NAT and use Private NAT for the Network Connectivity Center spokes.
Configure a subnet of purpose PRIVATE_NAT and use Hybrid NAT.

questions.explanation:
Private NAT for Network Connectivity Center spokes supports NAT between a VPC spoke and an on-premises network reached through a hybrid spoke, including when subnet IP ranges overlap. It uses a custom NAT rule that references the NCC hub and a NAT IP range from a subnet whose purpose is `PRIVATE_NAT`.

**Learn more:** [Private NAT for NCC spokes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/about-private-nat-for-ncc)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently deployed your application in Google Cloud. Before deploying your on-premises workloads, you need to validate your Google Cloud network configuration. You want to ensure that the configuration permits traffic to flow from cloud resources to your on-premises network. The validation must also analyze and diagnose possible failure points in Google Cloud network configurations without sending any data-plane test traffic. What should you do?

options.text: Use Network Intelligence Center's Connectivity Tests.
Enable Packet Mirroring on your application and send test traffic.
Use Network Intelligence Center's Network Topology visualizations.
Enable VPC Flow Logs and send test traffic.

questions.explanation:
Network Intelligence Center's Connectivity Tests performs static configuration analysis of the expected packet-forwarding path through Google Cloud resources, including VPC networks, Cloud VPN tunnels, and VLAN attachments. It detects configuration problems that can prevent reachability without relying on live data-plane probes.

**Learn more:** [Connectivity Tests overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/connectivity-tests/concepts/overview) · [Detect invalid or inconsistent configurations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/connectivity-tests/concepts/detecting-configs)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You configured one IPSec Cloud VPN tunnel between your organization and a third-party customer. You verified that the VPN tunnel is established. However, the BGP session status indicates that BGP is not configured. The customer provided these BGP settings:  
  
- Local BGP address: 169.254.11.1/30  
- Local ASN: 64515  
- Peer BGP address: 169.254.11.2  
- Peer ASN: 64517  
- Base MED: 1000  
- MD5 Authentication: Disabled  
  
You must configure the local BGP session for this tunnel using the settings supplied by the customer. The Cloud Router is already associated with the Cloud VPN Tunnel. Which settings should you use for the BGP session?

options.text: Peer ASN: 64517 -Advertised Route Priority (MED): 100Local BGP IP: 169.254.11.2 -Peer BGP IP: 169.254.11.1 -MD5 Authentication: Disabled
Peer ASN: 64515 -Advertised Route Priority (MED): 100Local BGP IP: 169.254.11.1 -Peer BGP IP: 169.254.11.2 -MD5 Authentication: Disabled
Peer ASN: 64515 -Advertised Route Priority (MED): 100Local BGP IP: 169.254.11.2 -Peer BGP IP: 169.254.11.1 -MD5 Authentication: Disabled
Peer ASN: 64515 -Advertised Route Priority (MED): 1000Local BGP IP: 169.254.11.2 -Peer BGP IP: 169.254.11.1 -MD5 Authentication: Enabled

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Router BGP peer uses the external router’s ASN and address: the customer’s local ASN is 64515 and its local BGP address is 169.254.11.1. The Cloud Router therefore uses 169.254.11.2 as its local BGP IP and 169.254.11.1 as its peer BGP IP, with MD5 authentication disabled. The customer’s base MED is its own advertisement setting; Cloud Router’s default advertised route priority is 100 unless explicitly changed.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot BGP sessions | Cloud Router](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/support/troubleshoot-bgp-sessions) · [Update the base route priority | Cloud Router](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/updating-priority?hl=en)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s web server administrator is migrating an application’s on-premises backend servers to GCP. Libraries and configurations vary substantially across these backend servers. The move to GCP will be a lift-and-shift migration, and a single network load balancer frontend will serve all requests to the servers.  
  
You want to use a GCP-native solution whenever possible.  
  
How should you deploy this service on GCP?

options.text: Create a managed instance group from one of the images of the on-premises servers, and link this instance group to a target pool behind your load balancer.
Create a target pool, add all backend instances to this target pool, and deploy the target pool behind your load balancer.
Deploy a third-party virtual appliance as frontend to these servers that will accommodate the significant differences between these backend servers.
Use GCP's ECMP capability to load-balance traffic to the backend servers by installing multiple equal-priority static routes to the backend servers.

questions.explanation:
A target pool is a GCP-native backend grouping for a regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer and can contain individual VM instances. This supports lift-and-shift deployment of heterogeneous backend servers without requiring them to share a single managed-instance-group image or configuration.

**Learn more:** [Using target pools | Cloud Load Balancing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/target-pools) · [Target pool-based regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/network/networklb-target-pools)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are implementing firewall controls to protect your compute resources in a newly created VPC. To simplify managing and controlling protection, you have defined hierarchical firewall policies, global network firewall policies, and VPC firewall rules. The rule configuration has these characteristics:  
  
- The hierarchical firewall policy, bound at the organization level, allows or denies specific external traffic.  
- A global network firewall policy has rules that enforce intrusion prevention system (IPS) capabilities for specific external inbound and outbound traffic.  
- The VPC firewall rules permit internal communication from RFC 1918-defined subnets.  
- The VPC firewall includes an explicit deny rule with logging enabled.  
  
This configuration succeeded in multiple preexisting VPCs. However, when reviewing a newly created VPC, you noticed that the logs were missing. All external communications are hanging, while internal traffic works as expected. You want to resolve the connectivity issue.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a new VPC and migrate existing resources to the new VPC. Delete the old VPC, and reapply the firewall policies and rules in the newVPC.
Raise the priority numbers of the firewall policy rules and lower the priority numbers of the VPC firewall rules.
Review the order in which the VPC firewall rules and policies are evaluated. If the VPC firewall rules are being evaluated before firewall policies, switch the order.
Lower the priority numbers of the firewall policy rules and raise the priority numbers of the VPC firewall rules.

questions.explanation:
A VPC can use an enforcement order in which classic VPC firewall rules are evaluated before global network firewall policies. In that order, an explicit VPC deny rule can block matching external traffic before the global policy’s IPS rules are evaluated. Configuring the global network firewall policy to be evaluated before classic VPC firewall rules ensures that the IPS policy takes precedence. Hierarchical firewall policies remain evaluated before both.

**Learn more:** [Evaluation order for firewall policies and rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies-rule-eval-order)

Your company has just completed its migration to Google Cloud and configured an architecture with three Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks: one for Sales, one for Finance, and one for Engineering. Each VPC has more than 100 Compute Engine instances, and developers using instances in the Sales VPC and the Finance VPC now need private connectivity with one another. You need to enable communication between Sales and Finance without compromising performance or security. What should you do?

options.text: Configure an HA VPN gateway between the Finance VPC and the Sales VPC.
Configure the instances that require communication between each other with an external IP address.
Create a VPC Network Peering connection between the Finance VPC and the Sales VPC.
Configure Cloud NAT and a Cloud Router in the Sales and Finance VPCs.

questions.explanation:
VPC Network Peering connects the Sales and Finance VPC networks so their resources can communicate through internal IP addresses. Peering traffic has the same latency, throughput, and availability as traffic within a single VPC, while the VPC networks remain administratively separate and retain their own firewall controls.

**Learn more:** [VPC Network Peering](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering) · [VPC Network Peering overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing your company’s networking infrastructure on Google Cloud. The design must connect three distinct VPC networks for development, testing, and production to two on-premises data centers, while keeping them isolated from one another. Each data center connects to Google Cloud through Cloud VPN.  
  
Additionally, the design must include a user-published security service hosted in another Google Cloud organization and available for private consumption. You need to create a scalable, centrally managed solution.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use VPC Network Peering to create a full mesh between the development, testing, and production VPCs and the Cloud VPN network.
Create a Network Connectivity Center hub, and configure each of the three VPCs and the two Cloud VPN spokes. Use Private Service Connect to access the third-party service.
Create a Shared VPC, and migrate the resources from the development, testing, and production VPCs into service projects.

Use Network Connectivity Center to establish a full-mesh topology between the three VPCs. Use VPC Network Peering to connect to the Cloud VPN and Private Service Connect to access the third-party service.

questions.explanation:
Network Connectivity Center provides a centrally managed hub-and-spoke model that connects multiple VPC networks and hybrid spokes, including HA VPN tunnels, at scale. It can provide site-to-cloud connectivity while preserving the desired VPC segmentation through hub connectivity configuration. Private Service Connect enables private consumption of a published service hosted in a separate VPC network and organization, using internal IP connectivity.

**Learn more:** [Network Connectivity Center overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/overview) · [Private Service Connect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/private-service-connect)

questions.domain: Implementing a VPC network
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You converted an auto mode VPC network into custom mode. Since that conversion, some Cloud Deployment Manager templates no longer work.  
  
You want to fix the issue.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Apply an additional IAM role to the Google API's service account to allow custom mode networks.
Update the VPC firewall to allow the Cloud Deployment Manager to access the custom mode networks.
Explicitly reference the custom mode networks in the Cloud Armor whitelist.
Explicitly reference the custom mode networks in the Deployment Manager templates.

questions.explanation:
After an auto mode VPC network is converted to custom mode, API calls and deployment definitions that implicitly referenced automatically created subnets must be changed to reference the required network or subnet explicitly. Deployment Manager templates therefore need explicit references to the custom mode network resources.

**Learn more:** [Create and manage VPC networks](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/create-modify-vpc-networks) · [Using references in Cloud Deployment Manager](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deployment-manager/docs/configuration/use-references)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization, TerramEarth, is launching a global application for managing credit card payments. Some client VMs in the same VPC as the application must access it privately. Because of compliance requirements, internal clients cannot use the application's global external IP address.  
  
Currently, Cloud DNS resolves `myglobalapp.terramearth.com` to the public IP address through a public zone. Clients must be able to reach `myglobalapp.example.com` without using its external IP address. You need to configure Cloud DNS to meet this requirement while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a sub-domain named internal.terramearth.com. Add the new DNS entry (myglobalapp.internal.terramearth.com) to the sub-domain pointing to the internal IP address from the application VM.
Configure a query logic script inside Cloud DNS to check the source IP address from the VPC, and respond with a modified DNS record to include the internal IP address from the application VM.
Configure a private zone for the application record (myglobalapp.terramearth.com) and point to the internal IP address of the application VM. Bind this zone to the VPC.

Promote the ephemeral IP address from the application VM to static, add this static ip address to each internal client's host file, and change the myglobalapp.terramearth.com DNS record to this new static IP address.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud DNS managed private zone bound to the VPC can provide an internal-IP record for the application name to VMs in that VPC, while the public zone continues serving the public IP to external clients. This provides split-horizon DNS and avoids use of the global external IP by internal clients.

**Learn more:** [Cloud DNS zones overview](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones/zones-overview)

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has 10 separate Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks, with one VPC in each project and all projects located in a single Google Cloud region. The security team requires every VPC network to have private connectivity to the primary on-premises location through a Partner Interconnect connection in that same region. To optimize cost and operations, this connectivity must be shared across all projects. All traffic among different projects, on-premises locations, and the internet must be inspectable by the same third-party appliances.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure the third-party appliances with multiple interfaces and specific Partner Interconnect VLAN attachments per project. Create the relevant routes on the third-party appliances and VPC networks.

Configure the third-party appliances with multiple interfaces, with each interface connected to a separate VPC network. Create separate VPC networks for on-premises and internet connectivity. Create the relevant routes on the third-party appliances and VPC networks.

Consolidate all existing projects’ subnetworks into a single VPCreate separate VPC networks for on-premises and internet connectivity. Configure the third-party appliances with multiple interfaces, with each interface connected to a separate VPC network. Create the relevant routes on the third-party appliances and VPC networks.

Configure the third-party appliances with multiple interfaces. Create a hub VPC network for all projects, and create separate VPC networks for on-premises and internet connectivity. Create the relevant routes on the third-party appliances and VPC networks. Use VPC Network Peering to connect all projects’ VPC networks to the hub VPC. Export custom routes from the hub VPC and import on all projects’ VPC networks.

questions.explanation:
A multi-NIC third-party network virtual appliance can provide the required centralized inspection path when it has an interface in each workload VPC and dedicated interfaces toward separate on-premises and internet connectivity VPCs. Routes in the VPC networks and appliances can direct every required flow through those appliances while sharing the centralized Partner Interconnect connectivity. VPC Network Peering is non-transitive, so peering workload VPCs to a hub alone does not supply the required inspected transit path.

**Learn more:** [Best practices and reference architectures for VPC design](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/best-practices-vpc-design) · [Partner Interconnect overview](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/partner-overview)

You are setting up hybrid connectivity between your company’s data center and Google Cloud. You have already deployed redundant Dedicated Interconnect connections and are now deploying VLAN attachments in `us-central1`. You want an active/passive design, with `interconnect-1` active and `interconnect-2` serving as the passive backup. You must deploy a Cloud Router to enable BGP connectivity. Following Google-recommended practices, what should you do?

options.text: 1. Configure the primary interconnect-1 BGP session on the Cloud Router with priority 0 and ASN 65101.2. Configure the secondary interconnect-2 BGP session on the Cloud Router with priority 200 and ASN 65102.3. Configure the on-premises ASN as 65000.

1. Configure the primary interconnect-1 BGP session on the Cloud Router with priority 0.2. Configure the secondary interconnect-2 BGP session on the Cloud Router with priority 200.3. Configure both Google-side BGP ASNs as 65100.4. Configure the on-premises ASN as 65000.

1. Configure the primary and secondary interconnects of the BGP sessions on the Cloud Router with priority 100 and ASN 16550.2. Configure the on-premises ASN as 65001 for primary interconnect-1.3. Configure the on-premises ASN as 65002 for secondary interconnect-2.

1. Configure the primary and secondary interconnects of the BGP sessions on the Cloud Router with priority 100 and ASN 4200000001.2. Configure the on-premises ASN as 4200000010.3. Disable the BGP session on the on-premises router for the secondary interconnect-2.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Router uses the same ASN for all of its BGP sessions. Active/passive Dedicated Interconnect forwarding is configured by assigning a lower advertised route priority to the active path and a higher priority to the backup path; priorities 0 and 200 establish that preference. Both sessions peer with the same on-premises ASN.

**Learn more:** [Establish BGP sessions | Cloud Router](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/configuring-bgp) · [Configure on-premises routers | Cloud Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/configuring-onprem-routers)
