You want to establish an IPsec tunnel between your on-premises network and a VPC using Cloud VPN. You need to limit reachability through the tunnel to particular local subnets, and you do not have a device that can use Border Gateway Protocol (BGP).  
  
Which routing option should you select?

options.text: Dynamic routing using Cloud Router
Route-based routing using default traffic selectors
Policy-based routing using a custom local traffic selector
Policy-based routing using the default local traffic selector

questions.explanation:
Cloud VPN policy-based routing uses static routing and lets you configure the local traffic selector to the specific VPC subnet CIDR ranges that should be included in the tunnel. Dynamic routing requires BGP, while route-based VPN always uses the default local traffic selector (`0.0.0.0/0`).

**Learn more:** [Networks and tunnel routing | Cloud VPN](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/choosing-networks-routing) · [Create a Classic VPN gateway using static routing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/how-to/creating-static-vpns?hl=en)

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity

options.text: Create an HA VPN gateway and associate the gateway with your two VLAN attachments. Use the existing Cloud Router for HA VPN, the peer VPN gateway resources, and the HA VPN tunnels.
Create an HA VPN gateway and associate the gateway with your two VLAN attachments. Create a new Cloud Router for HA VPN, the peer VPN gateway resources, and the HA VPN tunnels.
Enable MACsec on the VLAN attachments.
Enable MACsec on Partner Cloud Interconnect.

questions.explanation:
HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect requires an HA VPN gateway associated with the encrypted VLAN attachments and a separate Cloud Router dedicated to the BGP sessions for the HA VPN tunnels. The Cloud Router that manages the encrypted VLAN attachments in the Cloud Interconnect tier cannot be used for the HA VPN tier. MACsec is not required for an HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect deployment.

**Learn more:** [Configure HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/configure-ha-vpn-interconnect)

Your company has acquired a new division. The new division's network team needs complete control of its networking infrastructure. You must extend your existing Google Cloud network infrastructure, which consists of a single VPC, so workloads from all divisions can communicate with one another. You want to avoid additional costs and avoid granting unnecessary permissions to the new division's networking team. What should you do?

options.text: • Create a new project for the new division's network team.• Create a new VPC within the new project.• Establish a VPC peering between your existing VPC and the new division’s VPC.• Create a new subnet dedicated to the new division's workloads.• Grant roles/compute.networkUser on the new project to the new division’s network team group.

• Create a new project for the new division's network team.• Create a new VPC within the new project.• Establish a VPC peering between your existing VPC and the new division’s VPC.• Grant roles/compute.networkAdmin on the newly created project to the new division's network team group.

• Ensure that the project hosting the existing network infrastructure is enabled as a host project.• Create a new subnet dedicated to the new division's workloads in the existing VPC.• Grant roles/compute.networkUser on the newly created subnet to the new division’s network team group.

• Create a new project for the new division's network team.• Create a new VPC within the new project.• Establish a VPN connection between your existing VPC and the new division's VPC.• Grant roles/compute.networkAdmin on the newly created project to the new division's network team group.

questions.explanation:
"Complete control of its networking infrastructure" requires the new division to own and administer its own VPC, so you create a separate project and VPC and grant roles/compute.networkAdmin on that project only, which is least privilege and gives no rights over your existing infrastructure. VPC peering connects the two VPCs privately at no additional cost, avoiding the VPN gateway/egress charges of option D. Shared VPC (C) grants only roles/compute.networkUser on a subnet, letting the team use but not fully control the network, so it fails the "complete control" requirement; option A likewise grants only networkUser and is insufficient.

**Learn more:** [VPC Network Peering](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/using-vpc-peering) · [IAM roles for networking](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/job-functions/networking)

Your company’s security team prefers managed services whenever feasible. You must build a dashboard that shows the number of deny hits against configured firewall rules without adding operational overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Firewall Rules Logging. Use Firewall Insights to display the number of hits.
Configure Firewall Rules Logging. View the logs in Cloud Logging, and create a custom dashboard in Cloud Monitoring to display the number of hits.

Configure a firewall appliance from the Google Cloud Marketplace. Route all traffic through this appliance, and apply the firewall rules at this layer. Use the firewall appliance to display the number of hits.

Configure Packet Mirroring on the VPC. Apply a filter with an IP address list of the Denied Firewall rules. Configure an intrusion detection system (IDS) appliance as the receiver to display the number of hits.

questions.explanation:
Firewall Insights derives firewall usage information from Firewall Rules Logging and provides hit-count visibility for traffic allowed or denied by firewall rules, including deny rules with hits. As a managed service, it avoids operating a firewall or IDS appliance and avoids maintaining a custom monitoring solution.

**Learn more:** [View and understand Firewall Insights](https://cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/firewall-insights/how-to/view-understand-insights) · [View Firewall Insights metrics](https://cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/firewall-insights/how-to/view-metrics)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company’s on-premises network connects to a VPC through a Cloud VPN tunnel. A static `0.0.0.0/0` route using the VPN tunnel as its next hop is defined in the VPC. All internet-bound traffic currently goes through the on-premises network.  
  
Cloud NAT is configured to translate the primary IP addresses of Compute Engine instances in one region. Traffic from those instances should now reach the internet directly through their VPC rather than through the on-premises network. However, traffic from the virtual machines (VMs) is not being address-translated as expected. What should you do?

options.text: Lower the TCP Established Connection Idle Timeout for the NAT gateway.

Add firewall rules that allow ingress and egress of the external NAT IP address, have a target tag that is on the Compute Engine instances, and have a priority value higher than the priority value of the default route to the VPN gateway.

Add a default static route to the VPC with the default internet gateway as the next hop, the network tag associated with the Compute Engine instances, and a higher priority than the priority of the default route to the VPN tunnel.
Increase the default min-ports-per-vm setting for the Cloud NAT gateway.

questions.explanation:
Public Cloud NAT can translate internet-bound traffic only when the selected VPC route uses the default internet gateway as its next hop. A `0.0.0.0/0` route whose next hop is a Cloud VPN tunnel sends the traffic to the VPN and cannot be used by Public NAT. A higher-precedence, tagged default route to the default internet gateway applies to the Compute Engine instances and enables Cloud NAT for their egress traffic.

**Learn more:** [Cloud NAT product interactions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/nat-product-interactions) · [Public NAT](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/public-nat?hl=en)

You need to update firewall rules in a shared VPC, but you have been assigned only Network Admin permissions and cannot change the firewall rules.  
  
Your organization requires the least privilege necessary. Which level of permissions should you request?

options.text: Security Admin privileges from the Shared VPC Admin.
Service Project Admin privileges from the Shared VPC Admin.
Shared VPC Admin privileges from the Organization Admin.
Organization Admin privileges from the Organization Admin.

questions.explanation:
Compute Security Admin is the least-privileged predefined role that can create and manage firewall rules in a Shared VPC network. A Shared VPC Admin can grant this role for the host project, whereas Network Admin, Service Project Admin, and Organization Admin are not the least-privilege choice for firewall-rule management.\
\
**Learn more:** [Shared VPC overview](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc)

questions.question:
You need to update firewall rules in a shared VPC, but you have been assigned only Network Admin permissions and cannot change the firewall rules.  
  
Your organization requires the least privilege necessary. Which level of permissions should you request?

options.text: Configure a VPC Network Peering connection between the two VPCs.
Setup Cloud VPN tunnels between the two VPCs.
Create a Network Connectivity Center hub and register both VPCs as spokes.
Use Private Service Connect endpoints.

questions.explanation:
Network Connectivity Center connects independently managed VPC networks as VPC spokes on a hub, including VPCs in different projects. It provides private inter-VPC connectivity over Google Cloud’s network and reduces the operational complexity of managing individual pairwise VPC Network Peering connections. This supports decentralized VPC ownership while providing the required bidirectional application connectivity.

Your organization has more than 250 autonomous business units that presently operate in a decentralized way. Because of the organization’s maturity, routable private IP address space is limited and cannot accommodate every required workload. You need to build a cloud-first network design that reuses the same IP address space across business-unit workloads where possible. The business units need to communicate with one another and access their on-premises data center. What should you do?

options.text: Create a hub and spoke model that incorporates VPC Network Peering with hybrid connectivity centralized within the hub.

Create a Network Connectivity Center design that incorporates Private NAT to facilitate communication between VPC spokes, and a Routing VPC to exchange dynamic routes from the on-premises environment.

Create a Network Connectivity Center design that incorporates Private Service Connect to provide bidirectional communication between VPC spokes, and a Routing VPC to exchange dynamic routes from the on-premises environment.
Create a hub and spoke design that incorporates a centralized network virtual appliance (NVA) in the hub to perform routing and NAT between spokes.

questions.explanation:
Network Connectivity Center can connect VPC spokes and hybrid spokes at scale, while a routing VPC exchanges dynamic routes with the on-premises environment. Private NAT for Network Connectivity Center performs private-to-private address translation between VPC spokes and between VPC spokes and hybrid spokes, allowing communication when subnet IP address ranges overlap.

**Learn more:** [Private NAT for NCC spokes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/about-private-nat-for-ncc) · [Route exchange with VPC spokes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/dynamic-route-exchange-with-vpc-spokes)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An organization operates an on-premises data center and needs connectivity from that data center to Google Cloud. Bandwidth must be at least 1 Gbps, and traffic must not traverse the internet. What should you do?

options.text: Configure HA VPN by using high availability gateways and tunnels.
Configure Cross-Cloud Interconnect by creating a VLAN attachment, activate the connection, and then submit the pairing key to your service provider.
Configure Dedicated Interconnect by creating a VLAN attachment, activate the connection, and submit the pairing key to your service provider.
Configure Partner Interconnect by creating a VLAN attachment, submit the pairing key to your service provider, and activate the connection.

questions.explanation:
Partner Interconnect provides private connectivity between an on-premises network and a VPC through a supported service provider, so traffic does not traverse the public internet. It supports 1-Gbps VLAN attachments. Provisioning requires creating a VLAN attachment, sharing its generated pairing key with the service provider, and activating the attachment after the provider configures it.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/overview?hl=en) · [Partner Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/partner-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are creating a high-throughput, highly reliable, private network connection for a multinational corporation between its on-premises data center in Frankfurt, located in a Google-supported colocation facility, and its Google Cloud VPC in the `europe-west3` region. You require a connection for large-scale data synchronization and real-time application traffic, with bandwidth of 10 Gbps or greater. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a pair of HA VPN tunnels between the on-premises data center and the Google Cloud VPC.
Order a pair of Dedicated Interconnect circuits at the colocation facility to a Google edge location, then configure a VLAN attachment within your Google Cloud VPC.
Implement a Direct Peering connection from your co-location facility to Google's global network edge.
Engage with a Google Cloud Partner to establish a Partner Interconnect connection for your private network.

questions.explanation:
Dedicated Interconnect provides direct physical connectivity between an on-premises network and Google’s network at a common colocation facility. It supports 10-Gbps circuits and redundancy through a pair of circuits, while VLAN attachments associate the interconnect capacity with the VPC through Cloud Router.

**Learn more:** [Dedicated Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/dedicated-overview) · [Create VLAN attachments for Dedicated Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/creating-vlan-attachments)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have the following routing design. You find that Compute Engine instances in Subnet-2 in the asia-southeast1 region cannot communicate with on-premises compute resources. What should you do?  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783823127998-sptehrsu.png)

options.text: Configure a custom route advertisement on the Cloud Router.
Enable IP forwarding in the asia-southeast1 region.
Change the VPC dynamic routing mode to Global.
Add a second Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) session to the Cloud Router.

questions.explanation:
A VPC using global dynamic routing makes routes learned by a Cloud Router available to resources in all Google Cloud regions. This allows instances in the asia-southeast1 subnet to use the on-premises routes learned through the Cloud Router and VPN tunnel in europe-west1. With regional dynamic routing, those learned routes are available only in the Cloud Router’s region.

**Learn more:** [Networks and tunnel routing | Cloud VPN](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/choosing-networks-routing) · [Set routing and best path selection modes | Cloud Router](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/create-network-set-modes)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are troubleshooting an application in your organization’s Google Cloud network that is not operating as expected. You suspect packets are being lost somewhere. The application intermittently sends a low volume of packets from a Compute Engine VM to a destination on your on-premises network through a pair of Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachments. You validated that the Cloud Next Generation Firewall (Cloud NGFW) rules contain no deny statements blocking egress traffic, and you have no explicit allow rules. Following Google-recommended practices, you need to analyze the flow to determine whether packets are being sent correctly out of the VM and isolate the issue. What should you do?

options.text: Create a packet mirroring policy that is configured with your VM as the source and destined to a collector. Analyze the packet captures.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the subnet that the VM is deployed in with SAMPLE_RATE = 1.0, and run a query in Logs Explorer to analyze the packet flow.
Verify the network/attachment/egress_dropped_packets_count Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachment metric.
Enable Firewall Rules Logging on your firewall rules and review the logs.

questions.explanation:
VPC Flow Logs cannot reliably prove egress for intermittent, low-volume traffic because its primary packet sampling can omit such flows; setting the secondary sampling rate to 1.0 only retains all flow-log entries produced after primary sampling. Packet Mirroring captures traffic from the VM for analysis by a collector, allowing direct verification that the VM is transmitting the packets.

**Learn more:** [VPC Flow Logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/flow-logs) · [Packet Mirroring overview](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/packet-mirroring)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization needs its cloud network environment to inspect and deny traffic through a third-party virtual firewall appliance. It currently operates one standalone appliance that is the next-hop target of a custom static route. A new redundant appliance has recently been deployed for high availability and load sharing.  
  
You need to direct cloud network traffic through these appliances in an active/active configuration while preventing asymmetric routing. You must also deploy this configuration with minimal traffic disruption and according to Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Configure an internal passthrough network load balancer to send traffic to the redundant appliance. Then configure a packet mirroring policy that mirrors all traffic from the pre-existing standalone appliance to the new redundant appliance.

Configure an internal passthrough network load balancer to balance traffic to both appliances. Create a route with this internal load balancer as a next hop at a higher priority than the existing route. Then remove the pre-existing route that directed traffic to the standalone appliance.
Create a route for the redundant appliance at the same priority as the pre-existing standalone appliance.

Create routes for both appliances at the same priority, but higher than the existing standalone appliance's route. Then remove the pre-existing route that directed traffic to the standalone appliance.

questions.explanation:
An internal passthrough Network Load Balancer can serve as the next hop for a static route and distribute traffic across multiple healthy virtual firewall appliances. For a low-disruption migration from an existing next-hop route, Google Cloud recommends creating the replacement route to the load balancer at a higher priority than the existing route, then deleting the old route. Session-based hashing keeps a flow consistently assigned to a backend, supporting symmetric handling by stateful appliances.

**Learn more:** [Set up internal passthrough Network Load Balancer for third-party appliances](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/internal/setting-up-ilb-next-hop) · [Internal passthrough Network Load Balancers as next hops](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/internal/ilb-next-hop-overview)

You recently deployed two network virtual appliances in `us-central1`. These appliances provide connectivity to your on-premises network, `10.0.0.0/8`. You need to configure routing for your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). Your design must meet these requirements:  
  
- All access to your on-premises network must pass through the network virtual appliances.  
- Permit on-premises access if one network virtual appliance fails.  
- Use both network virtual appliances concurrently.  
  
Which method should you use to achieve this?

options.text: Configure two routes for 10.0.0.0/8 with different priorities, each pointing to separate network virtual appliances.
Configure an internal HTTP(S) load balancer with the two network virtual appliances as backends. Configure a route for 10.0.0.0/8 with the internal HTTP(S) load balancer as the next hop.
Configure a network load balancer for the two network virtual appliances. Configure a route for 10.0.0.0/8 with the network load balancer as the next hop.
Configure an internal TCP/UDP load balancer with the two network virtual appliances as backends. Configure a route for 10.0.0.0/8 with the internal load balancer as the next hop.

questions.explanation:
An internal passthrough Network Load Balancer (internal TCP/UDP load balancer) can serve as the next hop for a static VPC route and distribute traffic for the destination prefix to a pool of health-checked third-party virtual appliances. This uses both healthy appliances concurrently and stops sending traffic to an unhealthy appliance, providing single-appliance failover.

**Learn more:** [Set up internal passthrough Network Load Balancer for third-party appliances](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/internal/setting-up-ilb-next-hop) · [Internal passthrough Network Load Balancers as next hops](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/internal/ilb-next-hop-overview)

You are planning a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster deployment for a new application whose compute requirements will vary throughout the day. The application will serve different microservices, each of which might need different machine types and GPU configurations. You need a scalable, efficient approach that lets you manage distinct types of worker nodes independently in the same cluster. What should you do?

options.text: Create multiple node pools within the GKE cluster. Configure each node pool with specific machine types and auto-scaling settings to match the varying compute needs of different microservices.
Provision the GKE cluster with a single default node pool using a general-purpose machine type. Enable the cluster autoscaler to add or remove nodes based on overall CPU utilization.
Create a single default node pool within the GKE cluster, and implement Pod affinity and anti-affinity rules to schedule microservices on specific nodes based on their resource requirements.
Deploy separate GKE clusters for each microservice, each with a single node pool, to isolate compute resources and manage them independently.

questions.explanation:
A GKE Standard node pool contains nodes with a shared configuration, such as machine type and attached GPUs. A cluster can have multiple node pools of different types, and each pool can be independently managed and autoscaled. This supports matching each microservice’s scheduling and capacity requirements without creating separate clusters.

**Learn more:** [About node pools | Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/node-pools) · [Run GPUs in GKE Standard node pools](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/gpus)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has a legacy VPN device that uses IKEv1 and does not support BGP. Connectivity must be established from your on-premises environment to Google Cloud.  
  
You use `172.16.100.0/24`, `172.16.101.0/24`, and `172.16.102.0/24` in the on-premises environment, and `192.168.100.0/24`, `192.168.101.0/24`, and `192.168.102.0/24` in the Google Cloud environment. You have configured a VPN gateway and need to configure a policy-based VPN tunnel. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the tunnel with LOCAL_TS set to 172.16.100.0/22 and REMOTE_TS set to 192.168.100.0/22.
Configure the tunnel with LOCAL_TS set to 192.168.100.0/22 and REMOTE_TS set to 172.16.100.0/22.
Configure the tunnel with LOCAL_TS set to 172.16.100.0/24, 172.16.101.0/24, and 172.16.102.0/24, and REMOTE_TS set to 0.0.0.0/0.

questions.explanation:
For a Google Cloud policy-based VPN tunnel, the local traffic selector represents the Google Cloud VPC ranges and the remote traffic selector represents the peer on-premises ranges. IKEv1 supports only one CIDR for each traffic selector per tunnel, so the three listed /24 networks on each side must be represented by a single /22. `192.168.100.0/22` covers the Google Cloud ranges and `172.16.100.0/22` covers the on-premises ranges.

**Learn more:** [Networks and tunnel routing | Cloud VPN](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/choosing-networks-routing)

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have recently observed a recurring daily spike in network usage in your Google Cloud project. You need to determine the virtual machine (VM) instances and traffic type responsible for the spike in traffic utilization, while minimizing the required cost and management overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Enable VPC Flow Logs and send the output to BigQuery for analysis.
Enable Firewall Rules Logging for all allowed traffic and send the output to BigQuery for analysis.
Configure Packet Mirroring to send all traffic to a VM. Use Wireshark on the VM to identity traffic utilization for each VM in the VPC.
Deploy a third-party network appliance and configure it as the default gateway. Use the third-party network appliance to identify users with high network traffic.

questions.explanation:
VPC Flow Logs provides visibility into traffic flows to and from VM instances and supports analyzing top talkers, traffic changes, network throughput, and traffic characteristics. Exporting the logs to BigQuery enables scalable analysis without deploying packet-capture collectors or a third-party network appliance.

**Learn more:** [VPC Flow Logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/flow-logs) · [Configure VPC Flow Logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/using-flow-logs?hl=en)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have the networking configuration illustrated. Two redundant Dedicated Interconnect connections (`int-Iga1` and `int-Iga2`) terminate on the same Cloud Router. The Interconnect connections terminate on two distinct on-premises routers. You advertise identical prefixes from the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) sessions associated with the Dedicated Interconnect connections.  
  
You must configure one connection as Active for both ingress and egress traffic. If the active Interconnect connection fails, the passive Interconnect connection must automatically begin routing all traffic. Which two actions should you take to meet this requirement? (Choose two.)  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783861972189-i5drtgmk.png)

options.text: Configure the advertised route priority as 200 for the BGP session associated with the active interconnect connection.
Configure the advertised route priority > 10,200 on the active Interconnect connection.
Advertise a lower MED on the active Interconnect connection from the on-premises router.
Advertise a lower MED on the passive Interconnect connection from the on-premises router.
Configure the advertised route priority as 200 for the BGP session associated with the passive Interconnect connection.

questions.explanation:
A higher advertised route priority on the passive BGP session causes Cloud Router to advertise a higher MED to the on-premises network, so on-premises traffic prefers the active connection. Advertising a lower MED from the on-premises router on the active connection makes Cloud Router prefer the active path for traffic from the VPC to on-premises prefixes. Withdrawal of the active BGP routes on failure leaves the passive path to carry traffic.

**Learn more:** [Configure on-premises routers — Cloud Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/configuring-onprem-routers) · [Advertised routes — Cloud Router](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/concepts/advertised-routes)

questions.domain: Configuring, implementing and managing a cloud network security solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has established a resource hierarchy containing a parent folder and subfolders for every department. Each department defines its own project and VPC in its assigned folder and has the required permissions to create Google Cloud firewall rules. Traffic must not be permitted to flow between the VPCs. You need to deny all traffic from every source, including other VPCs, while delegating only intra-VPC firewall rules to the respective departments. What should you do?

options.text: Create a VPC firewall rule in each VPC to block traffic from any source, with priority 0.
Create a VPC firewall rule in each VPC to block traffic from any source, with priority 1000.

Create two hierarchical firewall policies per department's folder with two rules in each: a high-priority rule that matches traffic from the private CIDRs assigned to the respective VPC and sets the action to allow, and another lower-priority rule that blocks traffic from any other source.

Create two hierarchical firewall policies per department's folder with two rules in each: a high-priority rule that matches traffic from the private CIDRs assigned to the respective VPC and sets the action to goto_next, and another lower-priority rule that blocks traffic from any other source.

questions.explanation:
A hierarchical firewall policy at each department folder can centrally deny traffic that does not originate from that department’s VPC private CIDRs. A higher-priority rule for the department’s private CIDRs must use `goto_next`, which passes matching intra-VPC traffic to lower-level VPC firewall rules that the department manages. A lower-priority deny rule then blocks every other source, including traffic from other VPCs. An `allow` action would be terminal and would prevent the VPC firewall rules from being evaluated.

**Learn more:** [Hierarchical firewall policies](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies) · [Firewall policy rule components](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies-rule-details)

questions.domain: Configuring, implementing and managing a cloud network security solution
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company uses VPC firewall rules and blocks all egress traffic. You need to permit some VMs to reach external websites based on their fully qualified domain name (FQDN). You apply the new configuration, but the traffic remains denied. You need to modify the setup so the new configuration takes effect. What should you do?

options.text: Raise the priority of the network firewall policy rules.
Lower the priority of the network firewall policy rules.
Update the default policy and rule evaluation order to BEFORE_CLASSIC_FIREWALL.
Update the default policy and rule evaluation order to AFTER_CLASSIC_FIREWALL.

questions.explanation:
`BEFORE_CLASSIC_FIREWALL` evaluates global and regional network firewall policy rules before classic VPC firewall rules. This lets a matching FQDN-based egress allow rule take effect before the existing classic VPC deny-all egress rule is evaluated.

**Learn more:** [Evaluation order for firewall policies and rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies-rule-eval-order)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization runs multiple VMs on Google Cloud in a VPC. The VMs need connectivity to specific Google APIs. You need to enable Private Google Access so the VMs can connect to Cloud Storage. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Private Google Access on the project, remove the default route that points to the default internet gateway, and enable the Cloud Storage API.
Enable Private Google Access on the VM, remove the default route that points to the default internet gateway, and enable the Cloud Storage API.
Enable Private Google Access on the VPC, create a default route that points to the default internet gateway, and enable the Cloud Storage API.
Enable Private Google Access on the subnet, create a default route that points to the default internet gateway, and enable the Cloud Storage API.

questions.explanation:
Private Google Access is enabled on the subnet used by a VM’s network interface. The VPC must also have a route for Google API traffic whose next hop is the default internet gateway; a default route pointing to that gateway satisfies this requirement. Enabling the Cloud Storage API permits use of the Cloud Storage API service endpoint.

**Learn more:** [Configure Private Google Access](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access)

questions.question:
You created an auto-mode VPC network named Retail. You want to create a VPC network named Distribution and peer it with the Retail VPC.  
  
How should you configure the Distribution VPC?

options.text: Create the Distribution VPC in auto mode. Peer both the VPCs via network peering.
Create the Distribution VPC in custom mode. Use the CIDR range 10.0.0.0/9. Create the necessary subnets, and then peer them via network peering.
Create the Distribution VPC in custom mode. Use the CIDR range 10.128.0.0/9. Create the necessary subnets, and then peer them via network peering.
Rename the default VPC as \

questions.explanation: An auto-mode VPC uses subnet IP ranges within 10.128.0.0/9. VPC Network Peering requires non-overlapping subnet IP ranges, so Distribution must be a custom-mode VPC with a distinct range such as 10.0.0.0/9 before its subnets are created and the networks are peered.

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question:
You created an auto-mode VPC network named Retail. You want to create a VPC network named Distribution and peer it with the Retail VPC.  
  
How should you configure the Distribution VPC?

options.text: Enable VPC Flow Logs on the SDWAN_ONE compute instance and the compute instances of the databases. Investigate the rtt_msec metadata in the VPC Flow Logs.
SSH into the SDWAN_ONE compute instance and analyze the situation using the troubleshooting commands provided within the SDWAN_ONE operating system.
Use Network Intelligence Center to run a connectivity test between the SDWAN_ONE compute instance and the public IP address of the SDWAN hub that is located in the CITY_A branch.

Review the Performance Dashboard in Network Intelligence Center. Analyze packet loss and latency between the SDWAN_ONE compute instance and the databases’ compute instances. Analyze latency over the internet between CITY_A and the SDWAN_ONE compute instance.

questions.explanation:
Network Intelligence Center Performance Dashboard requires no setup and is intended to help distinguish application problems from underlying Google Cloud network performance issues. It exposes packet-loss and latency metrics for VM-to-VM traffic, including the SDWAN hub-to-database path, and latency metrics between VM regions and internet endpoint locations, which can reveal latency associated with CITY_A traffic reaching SDWAN_ONE.

**Learn more:** [Performance Dashboard metrics and views](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/performance-dashboard/concepts/metrics-views?hl=en) · [Performance Dashboard overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/performance-dashboard/concepts/overview)

You plan to use Terraform to deploy your company's Google Cloud infrastructure. The design must satisfy these requirements:  
  
- Each Google Cloud project must correspond to an internal project on which your team will work.  
- When an internal project is complete, its infrastructure must be deleted.  
- Each internal project must have its own Google Cloud project owner to manage its Google Cloud resources.  
- You have 10–100 projects deployed at any one time.  
  
While writing the Terraform code, you must ensure that deployment is simple, the code is reusable, and management is centralized.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a single project and single VPC for each internal project.
Create a single Shared VPC and attach each Google Cloud project as a service project.
Create a single project and additional VPCs for each internal project.D.O Create a Shared VPC and service project for each internal project.

questions.explanation:
A Shared VPC uses a host project to centrally manage networks, subnets, routes, and firewall rules while multiple service projects consume that network. Each internal workload can therefore reside in a separate service project with its own project owner and independently removable resources, while Terraform can reuse a common project-and-service-project pattern. Google Cloud documents that Shared VPC supports delegated administration for service-project administrators while retaining centralized network control.

**Learn more:** [Shared VPC | Virtual Private Cloud | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc) · [Delete and restore projects | Resource Manager | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/delete-restore-projects)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization runs two applications in separate Google Cloud VPC networks (`vpc-a` and `vpc-b`) across different projects. You must establish a secure, private, encrypted connection between these VPCs to enable inter-VPC communication. The solution must provide high availability and use dynamic routing. What should you do?

options.text: Configure VPC Network Peering between the two networks, and adjust firewall rules on both sides to allow the required traffic flow between specific subnets.
In vpc-a, deploy an internal Application Load Balancer for your application. Use Private Service Connect to publish this service in vpc-a and create a PSC consumer endpoint in vpc-b.
In each VPdeploy a Classic VPN gateway and use a pre-shared key for authentication. Configure static routes to direct traffic to the other VPC.
In each VPC. deploy an HA VPN gateway and a Cloud Router. Create two VPN tunnels on each gateway, and configure BGP sessions for dynamic routing.

questions.explanation:
HA VPN provides encrypted IPsec connectivity and high availability through redundant VPN tunnels. Cloud Router establishes BGP sessions to exchange routes dynamically between the VPC networks. Google Cloud requires dynamic (BGP) routing for HA VPN tunnels and recommends HA VPN with BGP for high availability.

**Learn more:** [HA VPN topologies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/topologies) · [Cloud VPN best practices](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/best-practices)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a hybrid network that connects your on-premises data center to a Google Cloud VPC by using Cloud Interconnect. You created a Cloud DNS private managed zone, `corp.gcp.internal`, for the VPC. Applications running on Compute Engine VMs are automatically registered in this zone.  
  
Your on-premises users and servers must resolve DNS names in the `corp.gcp.internal` zone, but their requests are currently failing. You need to allow your on-premises DNS servers to forward these specific requests securely to Google Cloud.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: • In Cloud DNS, create an inbound server policy and apply it to your VPC.• Configure your on-premises DNS server to conditionally forward requests for the corp.gcp.internal zone to one of the policy’s allocated IP addresses.• Advertise all VPC subnets from the Cloud Router to your on-premises network.

• In Cloud DNS, create an outbound server policy and apply it to your VPC.• Configure your on-premises DNS server to conditionally forward requests for the corp.gcp.internal zone to an IP address within 35.199.192.0/19, the Cloud DNS proxy range.• Advertise the 35.199.192.0/19 range as a custom advertisement on the Cloud Router to your on-premises network.

• In Cloud DNS, create an inbound server policy and apply it to your VPC.• Configure your on-premises DNS server to conditionally forward requests for the corp.gcp.internal zone to an IP address within 35.199.192.0/19, the Cloud DNS proxy range.• Advertise the 35.199.192.0/19 range as a custom advertisement on the Cloud Router.

• In Cloud DNS, create an outbound server policy and apply it to your VPC.• Configure your on-premises DNS server to conditionally forward requests for the corp.gcp.internal zone to one of the policy’s allocated IP addresses.• Advertise all VPC subnets from the Cloud Router to your on-premises network.

questions.explanation:
Cloud DNS inbound forwarding lets on-premises DNS resolvers send queries for records in a VPC private zone to the inbound server policy’s allocated internal entry-point addresses. These addresses are drawn from VPC subnet ranges, so advertising the VPC subnets over the Cloud Interconnect provides the required route. The `35.199.192.0/19` range is associated with Cloud DNS queries sent outward to alternative name servers, not with destinations for inbound DNS forwarding.

**Learn more:** [DNS server policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/server-policies-overview) · [Configure DNS server policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/policies)

options.text: Turn on Private Google Access at the subnet level.
Turn on Private Google Access at the VPC level.
Turn on Private Services Access at the VPC level.
Create a set of custom static routes to send traffic to the external IP addresses of Google APIs and services via the default internet gateway.
Create a set of custom static routes to send traffic to the internal IP addresses of Google APIs and services via the default internet gateway.

questions.explanation:
Private Google Access must be enabled on the subnet used by VM instances without external IP addresses so they can reach Google APIs and services. When the default `0.0.0.0/0` route points to a firewall instead of the default internet gateway, more-specific static routes for the external IP ranges used by Google APIs and services must use the default internet gateway; their greater prefix specificity bypasses the firewall route.

**Learn more:** [Configure Private Google Access](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access)

You have configured a service on Google Cloud that connects to an on-premises service through a Dedicated Interconnect. Users have reported recent connectivity problems. You need to determine whether traffic is being dropped due to firewall rules or a routing decision. What should you do?

options.text: Use the Network Intelligence Center Connectivity Tests to test the connectivity between the VPC and the on-premises network.
Use Network Intelligence Center Network Topology to check the traffic flow, and replay the traffic from the time period when the connectivity issue occurred.
Configure VPC Flow Logs. Review the logs by filtering on the source and destination.
Configure a Compute Engine instance on the same VPC as the service running on Google Cloud to run a traceroute targeted at the on-premises service.

questions.explanation:
Network Intelligence Center Connectivity Tests simulates the packet forwarding path between the VPC and the on-premises network over Cloud Interconnect. It evaluates the applicable VPC firewall rules and route selection, and reports where the simulated traffic is dropped.

**Learn more:** [Connectivity Tests overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/connectivity-tests/concepts/overview) · [Test connectivity to and from non-Google Cloud networks](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/connectivity-tests/concepts/test-between-networks)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is launching a new video game that will be globally available to all users through Cloud CDN. During the early-release phase, you discovered that an incorrect binary version was uploaded from Cloud Storage and cached in Cloud CDN. Thousands of users downloaded the incorrect version. Your marketing department has informed users that this was the wrong version of the game and has asked all users to download the updated version using the same URL.  
  
You need to ensure that users download the updated version of the game. What should you do?

options.text: Create a security policy to block all Cloud CON requests, review the logs, and filter which users are attempting to download the wrong game binary.
Create a new URL path for the updated game binary. Allow the cache to expire automatically through HTTP headers.
Upload the updated game binary to Cloud Storage. Invalidate the wrong game binary from the Cloud CDN cache.
Disable Cloud CDN. Reconfigure the load balancer with the updated game binary. Enable Cloud CDN.

questions.explanation:
After the corrected binary is uploaded to the Cloud Storage origin, invalidating the corresponding Cloud CDN cache entry removes the incorrect cached content before its normal expiration. The next request to the same URL retrieves the updated binary from the origin and repopulates the cache with that version.

**Learn more:** [Cache invalidation overview | Cloud CDN | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/cache-invalidation-overview?hl=en) · [Invalidate cached content | Cloud CDN | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/invalidating-cached-content)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is modernizing its infrastructure by expanding its services. You are concerned about your network’s long-term scalability because of IPv4 address exhaustion. You need to design and deploy a new Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster that enables Pods and Services to communicate over IPv6 while preserving IPv4 connectivity for backward compatibility with existing systems.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a new standard GKE cluster, and enable an IPv6-only address range for Pods.
Create a new GKE cluster, and enable an IPv6-only node pool.
Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway within your VPC to translate traffic between your existing IPv4-only GKE cluster and external IPv6 clients.
Create a new dual-stack subnet within your VPC, and then create a new GKE cluster within that subnet and specify dual-stack networking mode.

questions.explanation:
GKE dual-stack networking assigns both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses to Pods and nodes, and supports dual-stack Services, allowing IPv6 communication while continuing to support IPv4-only workloads and clients. A new GKE dual-stack cluster can be created on a dual-stack VPC subnet.

**Learn more:** [Create a VPC-native cluster — GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/alias-ips) · [VPC-native clusters — IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack networking](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/alias-ips)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],The company architecture has two distinct VPCs, `dev-vpc` and `prod-vpc`, each in a separate project. Both VPCs connect to the on-premises data center through their own dedicated Cloud VPN tunnels and Cloud Routers. The on-premises network contains a legacy DNS server at `192.168.1.10` that is authoritative for the `corp.local` zone.  
  
You must allow Compute Engine instances in both VPCs to resolve hostnames in the `corp.local` zone while adhering to Google-recommended practices for a scalable, manageable hub-and-spoke DNS design.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: • Create a Cloud DNS forwarding zone in the prod-vpc for the corp.local zone that forwards to 192.168.1.10.• Create a Cloud DNS peering zone in the dev-vpc for corp.local that peers with the prod-vpc.• Add a custom BGP advertisement on the prod-vpc’s Cloud Router for the 35.199.192.0/19 range.
• Create a Cloud DNS forwarding zone in both VPCs for the corp.local zone that forwards to 192.168.1.10.• Add a custom BGP advertisement on the prod-vpc’s Cloud Router for the 35.199.192.0/19 range.

• Create a Cloud DNS forwarding zone in the prod-vpc for the corp.local zone that forwards to 192.168.1.10.• Create a Cloud DNS peering zone in the dev-vpc for corp.local that peers with the prod-vpc.• Use the default BGP advertisements on the prod-vpc’s Cloud Router.

• Create a Cloud DNS forwarding zone in both VPCs for the corp.local zone that forwards to 192.168.1.10.• Add a custom BGP advertisement on their respective Cloud Routers for the 35.199.192.0/19 range.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud DNS peering zone lets the consumer VPC resolve a namespace according to the producer VPC’s resolution order, including a forwarding zone in that producer VPC. This supports a hub-and-spoke DNS design with one forwarding zone in `prod-vpc` and a peering zone in `dev-vpc`. Because `192.168.1.10` is an on-premises forwarding target reached through Cloud VPN, its DNS responses must have a return route to Cloud DNS source range `35.199.192.0/19` through the same VPC. You are setting up a secure, resilient connection between your company’s on-premises data center and a Google Cloud VPC. You have two distinct physical VPN gateways in the on-premises data center for redundancy. You must ensure the design has no single point of failure and use dynamic routing to exchange prefixes. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy an HA VPN gateway and establish connection to one of the interfaces on-premises with multiple tunnels.
Deploy a single Classic VPN gateway in Google Cloud and create two tunnels, both pointing to the same primary on-premises VPN gateway to increase bandwidth.
Deploy an HA VPN gateway and connect its two interfaces to the two on-premises gateways. Use Cloud Router to establish a BGP session over each tunnel.
Deploy two Classic VPN gateways, each connected to a separate on-premises gateway. Configure matching static routes with different priorities on both sides to handle failover.

questions.explanation:
An HA VPN gateway provides two Google Cloud interfaces. Connecting each interface to a separate on-premises VPN gateway removes the gateway-level single point of failure, and Cloud Router establishes BGP sessions over the VPN tunnels to exchange routes dynamically. Google Cloud documents this topology as using one tunnel per HA VPN interface to the corresponding interface of the redundant peer gateways.

**Learn more:** [Create an HA VPN gateway to a peer VPN gateway](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/how-to/creating-ha-vpn) · [HA VPN topologies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/topologies)

Your organization runs Compute Engine instances in `us-east1`, `us-west2`, and `us-central1`. It also has an existing Cloud Interconnect physical connection on the East Coast of the United States, with one VLAN attachment and a Cloud Router in `us-east1`.  
  
You need a highly available design that preserves access to all other Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) subnets if a region fails, using the most cost-effective approach. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Configure your VPC routing in regional mode.2. Add an additional Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachment in the us-east1 region, and configure a Cloud Router in us-east1.
1. Configure your VPC routing in global mode.2. Add an additional Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachment in the us-east1 region, and configure a Cloud Router in us-east1.
1. Configure your VPC routing in global mode.2. Add an additional Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachment in the us-west2 region, and configure a Cloud Router in us-west2.
1. Configure your VPC routing in regional mode.2. Add additional Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachments in the us-west2 and us-central1 regions, and configure Cloud Routers in us-west2 and us-central1.

questions.explanation:
Global dynamic routing makes Cloud Router advertise and learn routes across all regions in the VPC, allowing an Interconnect VLAN attachment in one region to provide connectivity to subnets in other regions. A second VLAN attachment and Cloud Router in `us-west2` provide a failover path independent of `us-east1`; placing both attachments in `us-east1` would not protect against loss of that region. One additional attachment is the least-cost option that provides this regional resilience.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Interconnect pricing and global dynamic routing](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/pricing) · [Cloud Interconnect key terms](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/concepts/key-terms)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has a critical project that requires a highly secure connectivity tunnel connected to the on-premises network. A Google Cloud network availability of 99.99% must be maintained. The on-premises network has one device with two interfaces, each having its own external IP address. You need to configure the appropriate Cloud HA VPN to meet the project requirements. What should you do?

options.text: Configure an HA VPN gateway with two VPN tunnel interfaces that connect to the on-premises device interface 0 and interface 1. Peer each tunnel to each external IP address. Set the REDUNDANCY_TYPE to TWO_IPS_REDUNDANCY.

Configure an HA VPN gateway with one VPN tunnel and two IP addresses that connect to the on-premises device interface 0. Use Cloud Router BGP MED and AS_PATH attributes to define redundancy with the on-premises device.

Configure an HA VPN gateways with two VPN tunnel interfaces that connect to the on-premises device interface 0 and interface 1. Peer each tunnel to each external IP address. Set the REDUNDANCY_TYPE to SINGLE_IP_INTERNALLY_REDUNDANT.

Configure an HA VPN gateway with one VPN tunnel and two interfaces that connect to the on-premises device interface 0 and interface 1. Peer each tunnel to each external IP address. Set the REDUNDANCY_TYPE to TWO_IPS_REDUNDANCY.

questions.explanation:
For one peer VPN gateway with two separate external IP addresses, HA VPN requires two tunnels—one from each HA VPN gateway interface to the corresponding peer interface—to meet the 99.99% availability SLA. Google Cloud represents this peer configuration with the `TWO_IPS_REDUNDANCY` redundancy type.

**Learn more:** [HA VPN topologies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/topologies) · [Create an HA VPN gateway to a peer VPN gateway](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/how-to/creating-ha-vpn?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to deploy Google Cloud Armor web application firewall (WAF) policies that use preconfigured WAF rules. You want all Google Cloud Armor logs sent to Cloud Logging with the greatest possible level of detail. You have enabled Cloud Load Balancing logs for every backend service to which Cloud Armor WAF policies are applied. What should you do?

options.text: Set the sample rate of the Cloud Load Balancing logs to 0.5.
Set the Google Cloud Armor logging option to VERBOSE.
Enable Google Cloud Armor logging for all the backend services where Cloud Armor WAF policies are applied. Set the Google Cloud Armor logging option to VERBOSE.
Set the sample rate of the Cloud Load Balancing logs to 1.0.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Armor request logs are included in Cloud Load Balancing logs, and enabled backend-service logging provides their delivery to Cloud Logging. Setting a security policy’s Cloud Armor logging level to `VERBOSE` adds the most detailed fields available for requests that match preconfigured WAF rules.

**Learn more:** [Verbose logging | Google Cloud Armor](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/verbose-logging?hl=en) · [Per-request logging | Google Cloud Armor](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/request-logging?hl=en)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a multinational enterprise that is migrating to GCP.  
  
The cloud requirements are:  
  
- An on-premises data center in the United States, located in Oregon and New York, with Dedicated Interconnects connected to Cloud regions `us-west1` (primary HQ) and `us-east4` (backup)  
- Multiple regional offices in Europe and APAC  
- Regional data processing required in `europe-west1` and `australia-southeast1`  
- A centralized Network Administration Team  
  
Your security and compliance team requires a virtual inline security appliance to perform L7 inspection for URL filtering. You want to deploy the appliance in `us-west1`.  
  
What should you do?
questions.explanation:
A multi-NIC virtual appliance can act as an inline gateway between different VPC networks when each NIC is attached to a subnet in a separate VPC. Shared VPC places the networks, subnets, routes, and firewall controls in the host project, supporting centralized network administration. Deploying the two-NIC appliance in the host project and routing traffic through it provides the required centralized L7 inspection path.

**Learn more:** [Multiple network interfaces](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/multiple-interfaces-concepts) · [Shared VPC overview](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc)

You are designing a new application whose backends are internally exposed on port 800. The application will be externally exposed through both IPv4 and IPv6 via TCP on port 700. You want to ensure high availability for this application. What should you do?

options.text: Create a network load balancer that used backend services containing one instance group with two instances.
Create a network load balancer that uses a target pool backend with two instances.
Create a TCP proxy that uses a zonal network endpoint group containing one instance.
Create a TCP proxy that uses backend services containing an instance group with two instances.

questions.explanation:
A TCP proxy Network Load Balancer terminates incoming TCP connections and establishes new connections to the backend instances, so it can accept traffic on port 700 and send it to the instance group’s configured backend port 800. Instance-group backends use named-port mappings, and two instances provide backend redundancy. By contrast, passthrough Network Load Balancers preserve the destination port, so they cannot perform this port change. TCP proxy load balancing supports IPv4 and IPv6 client traffic.

**Learn more:** [External proxy Network Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/tcp) · [Passthrough Network Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/passthrough-network-load-balancer)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s existing network deployment consists of a single VPC connected to a single data center through a Dedicated Interconnect connection. The Dedicated Interconnect topology has a 99.9% SLA. There is one VLAN attachment for each of the two Dedicated Interconnect links. All VLAN attachments use only IPv4 addresses. Only IPv4 routes are exchanged by BGP between the data center and the VPC.  
  
You need to create a solution that exchanges IPv6 routes between the data center and the VPC. You must use a procedure requiring the least setup effort and minimizing cost. Adding new BGP peers to the on-premises router configuration is impossible; only the existing BGP peers can be modified.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Modify the stack type of the existing VLAN attachments from IPv4 only to dual stack. Add a pair of new IPv6-only interfaces to the cloud router. Add the new IPv6 BGP peers to the cloud router corresponding to on-premises routers.
Enable BFD on the cloud router where the BGP sessions between your cloud router and the on-premises router are configured.
Delete the existing VLAN attachments. Create two new dual stack VLAN attachments. Enable multiprotocol BGP (MP-BGP) on all the BGP sessions between your cloud router and the on-premises router.
Modify the stack type of the existing VLAN attachments from IPv4 only to dual stack. Enable multiprotocol BGP (MP-BGP) on all the BGP sessions between your cloud router and the on-premises router.

questions.explanation:
A Dedicated Interconnect VLAN attachment must be dual stack to support IPv6 traffic. On a dual-stack attachment, MP-BGP can enable IPv6 route exchange over the existing IPv4 BGP session. Changing the existing attachments to dual stack and modifying their existing BGP sessions avoids creating additional peers or recreating VLAN attachments.

**Learn more:** [Modify VLAN attachments | Cloud Interconnect | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/modifying-vlan-attachments) · [Create VLAN attachments | Cloud Interconnect | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/creating-vlan-attachments?hl=en)

questions.question: Your company is planning to migrate to Google Kubernetes Engine. The application team has stated that they require a minimum of 60 Pods per node and a maximum of 100 Pods per node. Which Pod-per-node CIDR range should you use?
questions.explanation:
GKE maps a maximum of 65–128 Pods per node to a /24 CIDR block, providing 256 IP addresses. This maintains the required address buffer while supporting a maximum of 100 Pods per node.\
\
**Learn more:** [Configure maximum Pods per node | GKE networking](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/flexible-pod-cidr?hl=en)

questions.domain: Configuring, implementing and managing a cloud network security solution
questions.question: Your company is planning to migrate to Google Kubernetes Engine. The application team has stated that they require a minimum of 60 Pods per node and a maximum of 100 Pods per node. Which Pod-per-node CIDR range should you use?

options.text: Assign members of the networking team the compute.networkUser role.
Assign members of the networking team the compute.networkAdmin role.
Assign members of the networking team a custom role with only the compute.networks.* and the compute.firewalls.list permissions.
Assign members of the networking team the compute.networkViewer role, and add the compute.networks.use permission.

questions.explanation:
A custom role with `compute.networks.*` lets the networking team manage networking resources, while `compute.firewalls.list` allows it to view firewall rules without granting any firewall creation, update, or deletion permission. The predefined Compute Network Admin role includes broader firewall-management access, which violates separation of duties.

**Learn more:** [Compute Engine IAM roles and permissions](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/access/iam)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are connecting your company’s on-premises SD-WAN fabric to Google Cloud so application VPC traffic can reach the on-premises network. The SD-WAN appliance is already deployed as a virtual machine in a central hub VPC. You want to reduce operational complexity by using the SD-WAN virtual appliance for policy enforcement and dynamic route exchange. What should you do?

options.text: Place the SD-WAN appliance that is in the hub VPC in a backend service behind an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer. Create a custom route in the spoke VPC that uses the load balancer as the next hop.
Establish a direct HA VPN connection from the application VPCs to the on-premises data center, and configure BGP to exchange dynamic routes directly.
Create a Network Connectivity Center hub in the hub VPC, and register the SD-WAN virtual machine as a router appliance hybrid spoke. Add the application networks to the hub as VPC spokes.
Peer the central hub and application VPCs. Create a static route in the application VPCs for the on-premises CIDR range with the next-hop set to the internal IP address of the SD-WAN appliance.

questions.explanation:
A Network Connectivity Center hub can connect application VPCs as VPC spokes to a Router appliance hybrid spoke backed by the SD-WAN VM. The Router appliance feature supports BGP-based dynamic route exchange with Cloud Router, while the appliance remains the traffic-policy enforcement point. [Router appliance overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/ra-overview) [Route exchange with VPC spokes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/dynamic-route-exchange-with-vpc-spokes)

**Learn more:** [Router appliance overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/ra-overview) · [Route exchange with VPC spokes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/dynamic-route-exchange-with-vpc-spokes)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An application in your organization runs on a VPC-native GKE Standard cluster that has public IP addresses. You must configure access to the remote address range `35.100.0.0/16` through Cloud NAT rather than through the GKE nodes’ external IP addresses. SNAT is enabled on the cluster and must be configured. What should you do?

options.text: Configure nonMasqueradeCIDRs in the ip-masq-agent ConfigMap. Include the 35.100.0.0/16 range in the list.
Configure nonMasqueradeCIDRs in the ip-masq-agent ConfigMap. Remove the 35.100.0.0/16 range from the list.
Configure Cloud NAT and create an exclusion rule for any SNAT address translation.
Configure Cloud NAT with nonMasqueradeCIDRs, and enable SNAT with the same configuration to allow traffic to 35.100.0.0/16.

questions.explanation:
`nonMasqueradeCIDRs` defines destination ranges for which GKE preserves the source Pod IP instead of performing node-level SNAT. Including `35.100.0.0/16` allows traffic to that range to retain its Pod source IP and be translated by Cloud NAT, rather than being translated to a node address first.

**Learn more:** [Configuring an IP masquerade agent in Standard clusters](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/ip-masquerade-agent) · [IP masquerade agent](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ip-masquerade-agent)

questions.domain: Designing and planning a Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has about 100 teams that must manage their own environments. A central team needs to manage the network. You need to design a landing zone that gives each team separate projects and ensures that the solution can scale. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Policy-based Routing for each team.
Configure a Shared VPC, and create a VPC network in the host project.
Configure VPC Network Peering, and peer one of the VPC's to the service project.
Configure a Shared VPC, and create a VPC network in the service project.

questions.explanation:
Shared VPC centralizes management of network resources such as subnets, routes, and firewall rules in a host project, while separate service projects allow teams to manage their own workloads. The Shared VPC network is defined in the host project and made available to attached service projects, which supports a scalable separation of network and workload responsibilities.

**Learn more:** [Shared VPC overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc) · [Best practices and reference architectures for VPC design](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/best-practices-vpc-design)

questions.domain: Configuring, implementing and managing a cloud network security solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A hub-and-spoke architecture has been deployed in a Google Cloud environment, using VPC Network Peering to connect the spokes to the hub. For security, a private Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster with a private control-plane endpoint was deployed in one spoke project. Authorized networks were configured as the subnet range in which the GKE nodes are deployed.  
  
When attempting to access the GKE control plane from another spoke project, access fails. You need to permit access to the GKE control plane from the other spoke projects. What should you do?

options.text: Add a firewall rule that allows port 443 from the other spoke projects.
Enable Private Google Access on the subnet where the GKE nodes are deployed.
Configure the authorized networks to be the subnet ranges of the other spoke projects.
Deploy a proxy in the spoke project where the GKE nodes are deployed and connect to the control plane through the proxy.

questions.explanation:
A GKE cluster that uses VPC Network Peering cannot have its private control plane accessed from another peered network. Authorized networks control which source CIDRs are permitted, but they do not make the Google-managed control-plane network reachable through transitive VPC peering. A proxy in the cluster’s spoke can reach the private endpoint directly and relay control-plane traffic from the other spokes.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for GKE networking](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/best-practices/networking)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a connection from your single on-premises data center to a VPC in Google Cloud by using an IPsec VPN connection. The connection must provide a minimum SLA of 99.99%. There is one VPN termination device in your on-premises data center, and it can be configured with only one public IP address. Your design must also require the least setup effort. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create two HA VPN gateways.2. Create one tunnel on interface 0 of one gateway and create one tunnel on interface 1 of the other gateway.3. Terminate each of the two tunnels on the single public IP address that is configured on the VPN termination device located in your on-premises data center.

1. Create one Classic VPN gateway and one HA VPN gateway.2. Create one tunnel on the interface of the Classic VPN gateway and one tunnel on interface 1 of the HA VPN gateway.3. Terminate each of the two tunnels on the single public IP address that is configured on the VPN termination device located in your on-premises data center.

1. Replace the existing on-premises VPN termination device with a new device that is configured with two different public IP addresses.2. Create one HA VPN gateway.3. Create one tunnel for each of the two HA VPN gateway interfaces.4. Terminate each of the two tunnels on one of the two public IP addresses that is configured on the new VPN termination device located in your on-premises data center.

1. Create one HA VPN gateway.2. Create one tunnel for each of the two HA VPN gateway interfaces.3. Terminate each of the two tunnels on the single public IP address that is configured on the VPN termination device located in your on-premises data center.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud HA VPN supports a 99.99% availability SLA when a tunnel is configured on each of the two interfaces of one HA VPN gateway. For an on-premises peer VPN gateway with one external IP address, both tunnels can terminate on that same address. This satisfies the availability requirement without replacing the existing VPN device or deploying an additional HA VPN gateway.

**Learn more:** [HA VPN topologies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/topologies) · [Create an HA VPN gateway to a peer VPN gateway](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/how-to/creating-ha-vpn?hl=en)

Your organization wants to deploy HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect to provide encryption in transit across the Cloud Interconnect connections. You have created a Cloud Router and two encrypted VLAN attachments with 5 Gbps capacity and a BGP configuration. The BGP sessions are operational. You need to finish deploying HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect. What should you do?

options.text: Create an HA VPN gateway and associate the gateway with your two encrypted VLAN attachments. Configure the HA VPN Cloud Router, peer VPN gateway resources, and HA VPN tunnels. Use the same encrypted Cloud Router used for the Cloud Interconnect tier.
Enable MACsec on Partner Interconnect.
Enable MACsec for Cloud Interconnect on the VLAN attachments.
Create an HA VPN gateway and associate the gateway with your two encrypted VLAN attachments. Create a new dedicated HA VPN Cloud Router, peer VPN gateway resources, and HA VPN tunnels.

questions.explanation:
HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect has separate Cloud Interconnect and HA VPN tiers, and each tier requires its own Cloud Router. The Cloud Router used by the encrypted VLAN attachments is reserved for the Cloud Interconnect tier and cannot be used for HA VPN. An HA VPN gateway must be associated with the encrypted VLAN attachments, and a new dedicated HA VPN Cloud Router must manage the HA VPN tunnel BGP sessions.

**Learn more:** [Configure HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/configure-ha-vpn-interconnect) · [HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/ha-vpn-interconnect)
