questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a university that is moving to GCP.  
  
The cloud requirements are:  
  
- On-premises connectivity at 10 Gbps  
- Lowest-latency access to the cloud  
- A centralized Networking Administration Team  
  
New departments are requesting on-premises connectivity to their projects. You want to deploy the most cost-effective interconnect solution for connecting the campus to Google Cloud.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Shared VPC, and deploy the VLAN attachments and Interconnect in the host project.
Use Shared VPC, and deploy the VLAN attachments in the service projects. Connect the VLAN attachment to the Shared VPC's host project.
Use standalone projects, and deploy the VLAN attachments in the individual projects. Connect the VLAN attachment to the standalone projects' Interconnects.
Use standalone projects and deploy the VLAN attachments and Interconnects in each of the individual projects.

questions.explanation:
Shared VPC provides centralized network administration while allowing departmental service projects to use a common VPC and Cloud Interconnect connectivity. VLAN attachments for a Shared VPC network must be configured in the host project, and Shared VPC is more cost-efficient than creating separate VLAN attachments for standalone projects and networks.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for Cloud Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/best-practices) · [Options for connecting to multiple VPC networks](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/enabling-multiple-networks-access-same-attachment)

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are planning a large application deployment in Google Cloud that includes connectivity to on-premises environments. The application needs direct connectivity between workloads in every region and on-premises locations without address translation, but all RFC 1918 ranges are already used at the on-premises locations. What should you do?

options.text: Use multiple VPC networks with a transit network using VPC Network Peering.
Use overlapping RFC 1918 ranges with multiple isolated VPC networks.
Use overlapping RFC 1918 ranges with multiple isolated VPC networks and Cloud NAT.
Use non-RFC 1918 ranges with a single global VPC.

questions.explanation:
A single global VPC provides routing between its regional subnets. Using a non-RFC 1918 range that is valid for Google Cloud private use supplies non-overlapping, routable address space for on-premises connectivity without NAT. Overlapping RFC 1918 ranges prevent the required direct end-to-end routing, and Cloud NAT violates the no-address-translation requirement.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud VPC subnets](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/subnets) · [Google Cloud VPC overview](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/overview)

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are trying to establish an HA VPN to your on-premises network, but the VPN connection does not establish successfully. You have full administrative control of the Google Cloud networking environment and of the on-premises firewalls acting as the VPN devices. The Google Cloud console displays **"Negotiation failure"** and **"BGP is down"**. You check Cloud Logging with a query for `resource.type="vpn_gateway"` and `resource.labels.gateway_id="TUNNEL_ID_NUMBER"`. Logs Explorer shows frequent log entries:  
  
```text  
log name: …/logs/cloud.googleapis.com%2Fipsec_events"  
type: "vpn_gateway"  
textPayload: "received NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN notify, no CHILD_SA built"  
```  
  
You need to troubleshoot the VPN failure and take corrective action based on the Cloud Logging entries. What should you do?

options.text: Update the Google Cloud BGP session configuration to match the BGP peer ASN on the on-premises side.
Compare and review the Phase 2 settings on the on-premises firewall. Make sure the settings match one of the supported cipher suites for HA VPN.
Create a new Cloud VPN gateway in a region closer to the peer VPN gateway.
Compare the Phase 1 settings and recreate the Cloud VPN tunnel by choosing a different IKE version and pre-shared key.

questions.explanation:
`NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN` indicates that Cloud VPN and the peer VPN gateway could not agree on a cipher proposal. Because the log also states that no Child Security Association (Child SA) was built, the mismatch is in IPsec Phase 2. The on-premises firewall’s Phase 2 settings must include a cipher suite supported by HA VPN.

**Learn more:** [Cloud VPN troubleshooting](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/support/troubleshooting?hl=en) · [Cloud VPN best practices](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/best-practices)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your global media company provides premium video content to a worldwide audience. You configured an external Application Load Balancer with an internet network endpoint group (NEG) that points to your on-premises video storage. Cloud CDN is enabled on this backend service, and you use signed URLs to ensure that only authorized users can access the video files.  
  
A new, updated version of a popular video was recently uploaded to the on-premises origin server, replacing the old file. You must make sure that all subsequent user requests immediately retrieve the new version of the video while preserving content security.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Rotate the Cloud CDN signed URL keys for the backend service.
Modify the backend service’s Cloud CDN policy to use origin headers for caching (USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS), and configure the origin to serve the video with a Cache-Control: no-store header.
Temporarily disable signed URLs on the backend service, wait for the cache to expire, and then re-enable signed URLs.
Invalidate the cache for the specific video file path, and ensure your application generates new signed URLs for users.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud CDN invalidation for the specific video path removes the existing cached object, causing subsequent requests to fetch and cache the replacement from the origin. Signed URLs can remain enabled to enforce authorized access; signing new URLs maintains that access-control workflow. Cloud CDN documentation states that invalidation removes cached content before normal expiration and refills it from the backend on the next request. It also states that responses for signed requests are cached regardless of the backend's Cache-Control header.

**Learn more:** [Invalidate cached content | Cloud CDN | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/invalidating-cached-content) · [Use signed URLs | Cloud CDN | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/using-signed-urls)

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],The company’s current network architecture includes two VPCs connected by a dual-NIC instance that functions as a bump-in-the-wire firewall between the two VPCs. Flows between subnet pairs across the two VPCs have been working correctly. Suddenly, you receive an alert that none of the flows between the two VPCs are working. You need to troubleshoot the issue. What should you do? (Choose two.)

Use Cloud Logging to verify that there were no modifications to the VPC firewall rules or policies that were applied to the two network interfaces of the dual-NIC instance.

questions.explanation:
A multi-NIC firewall or router VM requires IP forwarding to pass traffic that is not addressed to the VM itself. Firewall rules and policies are evaluated per network interface, so a modification affecting either interface can block the routed traffic; Cloud Audit Logs records administrative configuration changes and can be reviewed in Cloud Logging.

questions.explanation:
A /28 primary node range supplies 12 usable addresses after the four addresses reserved by Google Cloud, supporting up to 10 nodes. At a maximum of 8 Pods per node, GKE assigns a /28 (16-address) Pod range to each node; 10 nodes require 160 addresses, so a /24 Pod secondary range is the smallest listed range that is sufficient. A /22 Service secondary range supplies 1,024 Service addresses, matching the maximum required capacity.

**Learn more:** [Configure maximum Pods per node | GKE networking](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/flexible-pod-cidr?hl=en) · [VPC-native clusters | GKE networking](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/alias-ips?hl=en)

You are configuring an HA VPN connection between your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) and an on-premises network. The VPN gateway is named VPN_GATEWAY_1. You must restrict VPN tunnels created in the project so they can connect only to your on-premises VPN public IP address, `203.0.113.1/32`. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a firewall rule accepting 203.0.113.1/32, and set a target tag equal to VPN_GATEWAY_1.
Configure the Resource Manager constraint constraints/compute.restrictVpnPeerIPs to use an allowList consisting of only the 203.0.113.1/32 address.
Configure a Google Cloud Armor security policy, and create a policy rule to allow 203.0.113.1/32.
Configure an access control list on the peer VPN gateway to deny all traffic except 203.0.113.1/32, and attach it to the primary external interface.

questions.explanation:
The Resource Manager organization-policy constraint `constraints/compute.restrictVpnPeerIPs` defines the valid peer IP addresses for Cloud VPN tunnels. It applies to HA VPN and can restrict all tunnels in the project to an allowlist containing only the specified on-premises peer address.

**Learn more:** [Restrict IP addresses for peer VPN gateways](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/how-to/restrict-peer-ip-addresses)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application running in a managed instance group. Your development team released an updated instance template containing a new feature that was not extensively tested. You want to minimize the effect on users if the new template contains a bug.  
  
How should you update the instances?

options.text: Manually patch some of the instances, and then perform a rolling restart on the instance group.
Using the new instance template, perform a rolling update across all instances in the instance group. Verify the new feature once the rollout completes.
Deploy a new instance group and canary the updated template in that group. Verify the new feature in the new canary instance group, and then update the original instance group.

Perform a canary update by starting a rolling update and specifying a target size for your instances to receive the new template. Verify the new feature on the canary instances, and then roll forward to the rest of the instances.

questions.explanation:
A managed instance group canary update deploys the new instance template to a specified target size while the remaining instances continue using the existing template. After the canary instances are verified, the updated template can be rolled forward to the rest of the group, limiting the impact of an untested feature.

**Learn more:** [Automatically apply VM configuration updates in a MIG](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/rolling-out-updates-to-managed-instance-groups) · [gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/instance-groups/managed/rolling-action/start-update)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You administer a multi-tenant Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster in which several teams deploy applications to a shared namespace.  
  
- One team has deployed a two-tier application consisting of a frontend deployment and a backend deployment, identified by the labels `app:frontend` and `app:backend`, respectively.  
- Another team operates an analytics service, labeled `app:analytics`, in that same namespace.  
  
You must enforce a security rule under which only Pods in the frontend deployment can connect to the backend Pods over TCP port 8080. You must also block all other traffic to the backend Pods, including traffic from the analytics Pods, while minimizing operational overhead.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a VPC firewall rule with a high priority to deny ingress traffic on port 8080 for all GKE nodes.
Install Istio on the cluster, and configure an AuthorizationPolicy to only allow requests from the frontend’s service account to the backend service.
Create a NetworkPolicy that selects the Pods with the app:backend label and includes an ingress rule that denies traffic from Pods with the app:analytics label.
Create a NetworkPolicy that selects Pods with the app:backend label and includes an ingress rule that only allows traffic on TCP port 8080 from Pods with the app:frontend label.

questions.explanation:
A Kubernetes `NetworkPolicy` can target the backend Pods with `podSelector: app:backend` and enforce ingress isolation. Its sole ingress rule should permit only Pods labeled `app:frontend` on TCP port 8080. Because ingress to selected Pods is allowed only when it matches an allowed rule, analytics Pods and every other source or destination port are blocked.

**Learn more:** [Learn GKE networking architecture](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/learn/learn-gke-net-architecture) · [Configure network policies for applications](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/tutorials/network-policy)

You recently deployed Compute Engine instances in the us-west1 and us-east1 regions in a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) using the default routing configuration. Your company security policy requires that virtual machines (VMs) not have public IP addresses assigned to them. You need to let the instances retrieve updates from the internet while blocking external access. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud NAT gateway and Cloud Router in both us-west1 and us-east1.
Create a single global Cloud NAT gateway and global Cloud Router in the VPC.
Change the instances’ network interface external IP address from None to Ephemeral.
Create a firewall rule that allows egress to destination 0.0.0.0/0.

questions.explanation:
Public Cloud NAT lets Compute Engine VMs without external IP addresses initiate internet connections, such as downloading updates, while allowing only established response traffic and no unsolicited inbound connections. A Cloud NAT gateway and its Cloud Router are regional resources, so separate configurations are required for the subnets in us-west1 and us-east1.

**Learn more:** [Cloud NAT overview](https://cloud.google.com/nat/docs/overview) · [Troubleshoot Cloud NAT configuration](https://cloud.google.com/nat/docs/troubleshooting)

You are configuring HA VPN to connect your organization’s on-premises environment to its Google Cloud network. Your on-premises environment is nearest to the `us-west1` Google Cloud region. You have Google Cloud resources in `us-west2` that require throughput of 300,000 packets per second (PPS) and approximately 4 Gbps of bandwidth. You need predictable bandwidth management while maintaining a 99.99% SLA at minimal cost. What should you do?

options.text: Create an HA VPN gateway with two tunnels. Configure BGP on both tunnels with tunnel 0 configured with a base routing priority metric of 100 and tunnel 1 with a base routing priority metric of 200. Configure the on-premises router with the corresponding multi-exit discriminator (MED) value.

Create two HA VPN gateways, each with two tunnels. Configure BGP on each of the gateways' tunnels with tunnel 0 configured with a base routing priority metric of 100 and tunnel 1 with a base routing priority metric of 100. Configure the on-premises router with the same corresponding multi-exit discriminator (MED) value.

Create an HA VPN gateway with two tunnels. Configure BGP on both tunnels with tunnel 0 configured with a base routing priority metric of 100 and tunnel 1 with a base routing priority metric of 100. Configure the on-premises router with the corresponding multi-exit discriminator (MED) value.

Create an HA VPN gateway with four tunnels. Configure BGP on four tunnels with tunnel 0 configured with a base routing priority metric of 100, tunnel 1 with a base routing priority metric of 200, tunnel 2 with a base routing priority of 300, and tunnel 3 with a base routing priority of 400. Configure the on-premises router with the corresponding multi-exit discriminator (MED) value.

questions.explanation:
An HA VPN tunnel supports up to 250,000 PPS for combined ingress and egress. A 300,000-PPS requirement therefore needs two redundant tunnel pairs—four tunnels total—to provide the needed capacity while retaining failover capability. For multiple HA VPN gateways, active-active routing is recommended; equal base priorities and equal corresponding MED values allow traffic to be distributed across the active tunnels. Each gateway has tunnels on both interfaces, satisfying the 99.99% HA VPN availability configuration.

**Learn more:** [HA VPN topologies to increase bandwidth](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/topologies-increase-bandwidth) · [HA VPN topologies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/topologies)

You are diagnosing connectivity problems between Google Cloud and a public SaaS provider. Connectivity between the two environments uses the public internet. Your users report intermittent connection errors when connecting with TCP; however, ICMP testing shows no failures. Users say that the errors happen at about the same time each day. You want to troubleshoot and collect information using Google Cloud tools that are most likely to reveal what is happening within Google Cloud. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Connectivity Test. Review the results for configuration issues in the VPC routing table.
Enable and review Cloud Logging for Cloud Armor. Look for logs with errors that match the destination IP address of the public SaaS provider.
Enable and review Cloud Logging on your Cloud NAT Gateway. Look for logs with errors that match the destination IP address of the public SaaS provider.
Enable the Firewall Insights API. Set the Deny rule insights observation period to one day. Review Insight results to assure there are no firewall rules denying traffic.

questions.explanation:
Cloud NAT logging records NAT connections and errors for TCP and UDP traffic. An error log is generated when an outbound packet is dropped because no NAT port is available, making it the appropriate way to investigate recurring TCP failures that can be caused by predictable periods of NAT port exhaustion. Filtering those logs for the SaaS provider's destination IP correlates the NAT failures with the affected service. [Cloud NAT logs and metrics](https://cloud.google.com/nat/docs/monitoring)

**Learn more:** [Cloud NAT logs and metrics](https://cloud.google.com/nat/docs/monitoring) · [Cloud NAT troubleshooting](https://cloud.google.com/nat/docs/troubleshooting)

You want to configure two Cloud Routers so that one maintains an active Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) session while the other acts as standby.  
  
Which BGP attribute should be used on the on-premises router?

options.text: AS-Path
Community
Local Preference
Multi-exit Discriminator

questions.explanation:
Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED) communicates route priority between BGP peers. Configuring the preferred path with a lower MED and the standby path with a higher MED produces active/passive forwarding. Cloud Router advertises route priority as MED, and Google Cloud guidance for active/passive forwarding calls for higher MED values on both the Cloud Router and on-premises sides.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Interconnect: Configure on-premises routers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/configuring-onprem-routers) · [Cloud Router: Advertised routes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/concepts/advertised-routes)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team has deployed two applications in GKE that are exposed through an external Application Load Balancer. Queries sent to `www.mountkirkgames.com/sales` and `www.mountkirkgames.com/get-an-analysis` display the correct pages. However, you have received complaints that `www.mountkirkgames.com` returns a 404 error. You need to fix this error. What should you do?

options.text: Review the Service YAML file. Add a new path rule for the * character that directs to the base service. Reapply the YAML.
Review the Ingress YAML file. Add a new path rule for the * character that directs to the base service. Reapply the YAML.
Review the Ingress YAML file. Define the default backend. Reapply the YAML.
Review the Service YAML file. Define a default backend. Reapply the YAML.

questions.explanation:
GKE Ingress sends requests that do not match a rule path to `spec.defaultBackend`. Without a custom default backend, GKE uses a default backend that returns HTTP 404. Defining the default backend in the Ingress manifest routes the root URL to the intended base service.

**Learn more:** [About GKE Ingress routing and security](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ingress-routing-security)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are creating an instance group and must create a new health check for HTTP(S) load balancing.  
  
Which two methods can you use to do this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a new health check using the gcloud command line tool.
Create a new health check using the VPC Network section in the GCP Console.
Create a new health check, or select an existing one, when you complete the load balancer's backend configuration in the GCP Console.
Create a new legacy health check using the gcloud command line tool.
Create a new legacy health check using the Health checks section in the GCP Console.

questions.explanation:
HTTP(S) load balancing uses non-legacy health checks. Google Cloud supports creating these health checks with `gcloud compute health-checks create`, including HTTP and HTTPS variants, or creating/selecting one during backend configuration in the Google Cloud console. The VPC Network area does not create health checks, and legacy health checks are not the applicable type.

**Learn more:** [Use health checks | Cloud Load Balancing](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/health-checks) · [gcloud compute health-checks create](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/health-checks/create)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company operates a single Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network in Google Cloud that is accessible from its on-premises network through Cloud Interconnect. You must configure access only to Google APIs and services supported by VPC Service Controls by using hybrid connectivity with a service level agreement (SLA) in place. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the existing Cloud Routers to advertise the Google API's public virtual IP addresses.
Use Private Google Access for on-premises hosts with restricted.googleapis.com virtual IP addresses.
Configure the existing Cloud Routers to advertise a default route, and use Cloud NAT to translate traffic from your on-premises network.
Add Direct Peering links, and use them for connectivity to Google APIs that use public virtual IP addresses.

questions.explanation:
Private Google Access for on-premises hosts supports access to Google APIs and services through a Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachment. The `restricted.googleapis.com` virtual IP restricts access to APIs and services supported by VPC Service Controls, preventing access to unsupported services and helping mitigate data-exfiltration risk.

**Learn more:** [Private Google Access with VPC Service Controls](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/private-connectivity?hl=en) · [Configure Private Google Access for on-premises hosts](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access-hybrid)

You have two Google Cloud projects in a perimeter that prevents data exfiltration. You must move a third project into the perimeter, but the move might adversely affect the existing environment. You need to validate the change's impact. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Firewall Rules Logging inside the third project.
Modify the existing VPC Service Controls policy to include the new project in dry run mode.
Monitor the Resource Manager audit logs inside the perimeter.
Enable VPC Flow Logs inside the third project, and monitor the logs for negative impact.

questions.explanation:
VPC Service Controls dry-run mode evaluates the proposed perimeter configuration and logs policy violations without denying requests or altering the enforced perimeter. It is specifically intended to determine the impact of changes to existing service perimeters, including adding or moving projects.

**Learn more:** [Dry run mode for service perimeters](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/dry-run-mode)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Recently, your networking team enabled Cloud CDN for an external-facing service exposed through an external Application Load Balancer. The application team has already specified, within the responses, which content should be cached. When testing the load balancer, you saw no performance change after enabling Cloud CDN. You need to resolve the issue. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the CACHE_ALL_STATIC caching mode on Cloud CDN to ensure Cloud CDN caches all static content as well as content defined by the backends.
Configure the FORCE_CACHE_ALL caching mode on Cloud CDN to ensure all appropriate content is cached.
Configure the USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS caching mode on Cloud CDN to ensure Cloud CDN caches content depending on responses to requests from the backends.
Configure the CACHE_ALL_STATIC caching mode on Cloud CDN to ensure Cloud CDN cache content depending on responses to requests from the backends.

questions.explanation:
The `USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS` cache mode caches successful backend responses only when they contain valid caching directives, such as `Cache-Control` or `Expires`, and uses those directives to determine cache freshness. It therefore applies the application-defined caching policy without forcibly caching content that the origin has not identified as cacheable.

**Learn more:** [Change cache modes | Cloud CDN | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/using-cache-modes?hl=en) · [Caching overview | Cloud CDN | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/caching)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have successfully provisioned one Dedicated Interconnect. Its physical connection is in a colocation facility nearest to `us-west2`. Seventy-five percent of your workloads run in `us-east4`, while the other twenty-five percent run in `us-central1`. All workloads share the same network-traffic profile.  
  
You need to minimize data-transfer costs when deploying VLAN attachments. What should you do?

options.text: Keep the existing Dedicated interconnect. Deploy a VLAN attachment to a Cloud Router in us-west2, and use VPC global routing to access workloads in us-east4 and us-central1.
Keep the existing Dedicated Interconnect. Deploy a VLAN attachment to a Cloud Router in us-east4, and deploy another VLAN attachment to a Cloud Router in us-central1.
Order a new Dedicated Interconnect for a colocation facility closest to us-east4, and use VPC global routing to access workloads in us-central1.
Order a new Dedicated Interconnect for a colocation facility closest to us-central1, and use VPC global routing to access workloads in us-east4.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Interconnect discounted transfer pricing applies when traffic originates in the same region as the VLAN attachment. Accessing a workload through an attachment in another region incurs standard cross-region transfer charges. VLAN attachments in both `us-east4` and `us-central1` therefore keep each workload group local to its attachment and avoid those cross-region charges.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Interconnect pricing](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/pricing) · [Cloud Interconnect key terms](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/terminology)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company maintains separate Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks in one region for two departments: Sales and Finance. The Sales department's VPC network already connects to on-premises locations through HA VPN, and you have verified that the subnet ranges do not overlap. You plan to peer the two VPC networks so they can use the same HA tunnels for on-premises connectivity, while supplying internet connectivity to the Google Cloud workloads through Cloud NAT. Internet traffic from the on-premises locations must not traverse Google Cloud. You need to propagate all routes between the Finance department and the on-premises locations. What should you do?

options.text: Peer the two VPCs, and use the default configuration for the Cloud Routers.
Peer the two VPCs, and use Cloud Router’s custom route advertisements to announce the peered VPC network ranges to the on-premises locations.

Peer the two VPCs. Configure VPC Network Peering to export custom routes from Sales and import custom routes on Finance's VPC network. Use Cloud Router’s custom route advertisements to announce a default route to the on-premises locations.

Peer the two VPCs. Configure VPC Network Peering to export custom routes from Sales and import custom routes on Finance's VPC network. Use Cloud Router’s custom route advertisements to announce the peered VPC network ranges to the on-premises locations.

questions.explanation:
VPC Network Peering requires explicit export of custom routes from the VPC containing the HA VPN-learned dynamic routes and explicit import of those routes by the peered VPC. This lets Finance reach on-premises prefixes through Sales. Cloud Router's default advertisement mode does not advertise subnet routes learned through VPC peering, so the Sales Cloud Router must use custom advertisements that include Finance's VPC subnet ranges to establish the on-premises-to-Finance return path. Advertising only these VPC ranges, rather than a default route, prevents on-premises internet traffic from being routed through Google Cloud.

**Learn more:** [VPC Network Peering documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering) · [Cloud VPN route order and advertisements](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/order-of-routes)

You use a 10-Gbps direct peering connection to Google along with the `gsutil` tool to upload files from on-premises servers to Cloud Storage buckets. The on-premises servers are 100 milliseconds from the Google peering point. You find that uploads are not using the full 10-Gbps bandwidth available.  
  
You want to optimize utilization of the connection's bandwidth. What should you do on the on-premises servers?

options.text: Tune TCP parameters on the on-premises servers.
Compress files using utilities like tar to reduce the size of data being sent.
Remove the -m flag from the gsutil command to enable single-threaded transfers.
Use the perfdiag parameter in your gsutil command to enable faster performance: gsutil perfdiag gs://[BUCKET NAME].

questions.explanation:
A high-bandwidth, high-latency TCP path requires sufficiently large TCP send and receive buffers, plus suitable TCP congestion-control settings, to keep data in flight equal to the bandwidth-delay product. At 10 Gbps and 100 ms RTT, that is approximately 125 MB; undersized TCP settings can prevent `gsutil` uploads from saturating the available link. Direct Peering is designed to exchange high-throughput traffic between an on-premises network and Google’s edge network.

**Learn more:** [Direct Peering overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/direct-peering)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You configured Cloud VPN with dynamic routing using Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). You added a custom route to advertise a network reachable through the VPN tunnel. However, on-premises clients still cannot access the network through that tunnel. You need to review Cloud Logging logs to confirm that the appropriate routers are advertised over the VPN tunnel. Which Cloud Logging filter should you use to examine the logs?

options.text: resource.type= “gce_router”
resource.type= “gce_network_region”
resource.type= “vpn_tunnel”
resource.type= “vpn_gateway”

questions.explanation:
Cloud Router records BGP and route-announcement events in Cloud Logging. Advertised-prefix route events use the `gce_router` monitored resource, so filtering on `resource.type="gce_router"` accesses the logs that show prefixes advertised to BGP peers.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company uses Network Connectivity Center (NCC) to enable communication among multiple spoke VPCs. A development team reports that application instances in `app-dev-spoke-vpc` cannot connect to a new database service in `db-dev-spoke-vpc`.  
  
You need to diagnose the problem with an observability tool and identify its root cause. What should you do?

options.text: Use Firewall Insights to analyze the firewall rule configuration and modify the appropriate rule.
Check each firewall rule in both the app-dev-spoke-vpc and db-dev-spokevpc.
Verify that the application instances in app-dev-spoke-vpc connected to Network Connectivity Center are assigned external IP addresses to reach the database service.
Use Network Intelligence Center’s Connectivity Tests to perform a reachability analysis between an instance in app-dev-spoke-vpc and the database service in db-dev-spoke-vpc.

questions.explanation:
Network Intelligence Center’s Connectivity Tests performs end-to-end reachability analysis between specified network endpoints. Its configuration analysis simulates the forwarding path and evaluates relevant configurations, including routes and firewall rules, so it can identify the point that prevents traffic from reaching the database service. NCC-connected spoke VPC communication does not require external IP addresses.

**Learn more:** [Measuring reachability — Connectivity Tests](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/connectivity-tests/concepts/reachability) · [Common test scenarios — Connectivity Tests](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/connectivity-tests/concepts/common-use-cases)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization depends on a critical Dedicated Interconnect connection for its hybrid cloud strategy. You must proactively monitor the health and network connectivity of this connection to maintain its reliability. You want an alert when an optical transceiver's light level falls below the recommended operating power, or when traffic across the connection suddenly stops. What should you do?

options.text: Create an alerting policy in Cloud Monitoring that triggers if the total byte count sent over the VLAN attachment drops to zero.
Configure a periodic connectivity test in the Network Intelligence Center to ping an on-premises host and alert based on its success rate.
Create alerting policies in Cloud Monitoring based on the metrics for both the optical power level of the physical link and the BGP session state of the VLAN attachment.
Build a log-based alert in Cloud Logging that parses Cloud Router logs to detect when BGP keepalive messages are no longer received.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring receives Dedicated Interconnect metrics for physical circuits and VLAN attachments. The physical-link receive-power metric detects low optical light levels, and the BGP session-state metric identifies a lost Layer 3 session on the VLAN attachment, providing direct alerting for both required connection-health conditions.

**Learn more:** [Monitor connections | Cloud Interconnect](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/monitoring) · [Google Cloud metrics: I through O](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/api/metrics_gcp_i_o)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A 20-Gbps Dedicated Interconnect connection has been provisioned with a 10-Gbps VLAN attachment. You have recently observed a steady rise in ingress traffic on the Interconnect connection from the on-premises data center. You need to ensure that end users can achieve the full 20-Gbps throughput as soon as possible.  
  
Which two methods can accomplish this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Configure an additional VLAN attachment of 10 Gbps in another region. Configure the on-premises router to advertise routes with the same multi-exit discriminator (MED).
Configure an additional VLAN attachment of 10 Gbps in the same region. Configure the on-premises router to advertise routes with the same multi-exit discriminator (MED).
From the Google Cloud Console, modify the bandwidth of the VLAN attachment to 20 Gbps.
From the Google Cloud Console, request a new Dedicated Interconnect connection of 20 Gbps, and configure a VLAN attachment of 10 Gbps.
Configure Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) on the on-premises router to use the 20-Gbps Dedicated Interconnect connection.

questions.explanation:
A VLAN attachment’s configured capacity limits its bandwidth, so increasing the existing attachment to 20 Gbps lets it use the available 20-Gbps Dedicated Interconnect capacity. Alternatively, create a second 10-Gbps VLAN attachment in the same region and advertise routes with equal MED values; Google Cloud can then use ECMP to distribute traffic across the attachments.

**Learn more:** [Create VLAN attachments for Dedicated Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/creating-vlan-attachments?hl=en) · [Modify VLAN attachments](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/modifying-vlan-attachments)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has just acquired Altostrat, an existing GCP customer. Both companies have separate GCP organizations and use custom DNS solutions. Each organization will keep its existing domains and host names until a complete transition and architectural review is finished in one year.  
  
The following assumptions apply to both GCP environments:  
  
- Each organization has enabled complete connectivity among all its projects by using Shared VPC.  
- Both organizations use only the `10.0.0.0/8` address space for their instances, except for bastion hosts used to access instances and load balancers serving web traffic.  
- No prefix overlaps exist between the two organizations.  
- Both organizations already have firewall rules allowing all inbound and outbound traffic from the `10.0.0.0/8` address space.  
- Neither organization has Interconnects to its on-premises environment.  
  
You need to integrate the networking and DNS infrastructure of both organizations as rapidly as possible with minimal downtime.  
  
Which two steps should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Provision Cloud Interconnect to connect both organizations together.
Set up some variant of DNS forwarding and zone transfers in each organization.
Connect VPCs in both organizations using Cloud VPN together with Cloud Router.
Use Cloud DNS to create A records of all VMs and resources across all projects in both organizations.
Create a third organization with a new host project, and attach all projects from your company and Altostrat to it using shared VPC.

questions.explanation:
Cloud VPN with Cloud Router provides dynamic BGP route exchange between the VPC networks, and the non-overlapping address ranges plus existing `10.0.0.0/8` firewall allowances make that connectivity immediately usable. DNS forwarding or zone transfers preserves resolution of each organization’s existing DNS domains and host names during the transition, without requiring all records to be recreated. Cloud DNS supports outbound DNS forwarding through forwarding zones, and Cloud Router manages dynamic routing for Cloud VPN connections.

**Learn more:** [Cloud VPN: Networks and tunnel routing](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/choosing-networks-routing) · [Cloud DNS zones overview](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones/zones-overview)

You have enabled HTTP(S) load balancing for your application, and its developers report that HTTP(S) requests are not being distributed correctly among your Compute Engine Virtual Machine instances. You want to obtain data on how the requests are being distributed.  
  
Which two methods can accomplish this? (Choose two.)

options.text: On the Load Balancer details page of the GCP Console, click on the Monitoring tab, select your backend service, and look at the graphs.
In Stackdriver Error Reporting, look for any unacknowledged errors for the Cloud Load Balancers service.
In Stackdriver Monitoring, select Resources > Metrics Explorer and search for https/request_bytes_count metric.

The `loadbalancing.googleapis.com/https/backend_request_count` metric measures requests sent from the load balancer to its backends and can be charted in a custom dashboard to compare backend request distribution.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has deployed Vertex AI online prediction in its Google Cloud environment in the `us-central1` region. Online prediction is available through private services access by using the IP CIDR range `172.16.53.0/24`.  
  
You need to configure access to Vertex AI without affecting existing routes. You want the VLAN attachments in the `us-west1` region to be primary. The interconnect VLAN attachments in the `us-west2` region must be used only as backup. What should you do?

options.text: Create a custom route advertisement on VLAN attachments in the us-west1 region for prefix 172.16.53.0/24. Create a custom route advertisement on VLAN attachments in the us-west2 region for prefix 172.16.53.0/24.

Create a custom learned route on VLAN attachments in the us-west1 region for prefix 172.16.53.0/24, and set the route priority on the BGP session as 100. Create a custom route advertisement on VLAN attachments in the us-west2 region for prefix 172.16.53.0/24, and set the route priority on the BGP session as 200.

Create a custom route advertisement on VLAN attachments in the us-west1 region for prefix 172.16.53.0/24, and set the route priority on the BGP session as 100. Create a custom route advertisement on VLAN attachments in the us-west2 region for prefix 172.16.53.0/24, and set the route priority on the BGP session as 200.

Create a custom route advertisement on VLAN attachments in the us-west1 region for prefix 172.16.53.0/24, and create a BGP route-policy to set the multi-exit discriminator (MED) to 100. Create a custom route advertisement on VLAN attachments in the us-west2 region for prefix 172.16.53.0/24, and create a BGP route-policy to set the multi-exit discriminator (MED) to 200.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Router custom route advertisements selectively advertise the private services access prefix to on-premises BGP peers. The BGP advertised route priority is used as the MED for that session; a lower MED is preferred. Advertising `172.16.53.0/24` with priority 100 through `us-west1` and priority 200 through `us-west2` therefore selects `us-west1` as the primary path and preserves `us-west2` as the backup, without changing the other routes advertised by the sessions.

**Learn more:** [Advertised routes | Cloud Router | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/concepts/advertised-routes) · [Create VLAN attachments | Cloud Interconnect | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/creating-vlan-attachments)

You are configuring a Google Cloud environment to connect with your on-premises network. The configuration must be able to reach Cloud Storage APIs and your Google Kubernetes Engine nodes over the private Cloud Interconnect network. You have already configured a Cloud Router with your Interconnect VLAN attachments. You now need to configure the appropriate router advertisements on the Cloud Router. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the route advertisement to the default setting.
On the on-premises router, configure a static route for the storage API virtual IP address which points to the Cloud Router's link-local IP address.
Configure the route advertisement to the custom setting, and manually add prefix 199.36.153.8/30 to the list of advertisements. Leave all other options as their default settings.
Configure the route advertisement to the custom setting, and manually add prefix 199.36.153.8/30 to the list of advertisements. Advertise all visible subnets to the Cloud Router.

questions.explanation:
Private Google Access for on-premises hosts uses the `private.googleapis.com` virtual IP range `199.36.153.8/30`, which Cloud Router must advertise through a custom route advertisement. Custom advertisement mode does not retain default VPC subnet advertisements unless `ALL_SUBNETS` is enabled; advertising all visible subnets preserves reachability to the VPC subnet containing the GKE nodes.

**Learn more:** [Configure Private Google Access for on-premises hosts](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access-hybrid)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An organization uses a hub-and-spoke architecture with VPC Network Peering, with hybrid connectivity centralized in the hub. The Cloud Router in the hub VPC advertises subnet routes, but the on-premises router does not seem to receive any subnet routes from the VPC spokes. You need to resolve the issue. What should you do?

options.text: Create custom routes at the Cloud Router in the spokes to advertise the subnets of the VPC spokes.
Create custom routes at the Cloud Router in the hub to advertise the subnets of the VPC spokes.
Create a BGP route policy at the Cloud Router, and ensure the subnets of the VPC spokes are being announced towards the on-premises environment.
Create custom learned routes at the Cloud Router in the hub to advertise the subnets of the VPC spokes.

questions.explanation:
In default advertisement mode, Cloud Router advertises only subnets belonging to its own VPC and excludes routes learned through VPC Network Peering. Configuring custom route advertisements on the Cloud Router in the hub to include the spoke VPC subnet ranges causes those ranges to be advertised to the on-premises BGP peer.

**Learn more:** [Advertise custom address ranges | Cloud Router | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/advertising-custom-ip)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to configure the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) session for a VPN tunnel that was just created between two Google Cloud VPCs, 10.1.0.0/16 and 172.16.0.0/16. You have a Cloud Router (router-1) in the 10.1.0.0/16 network and another Cloud Router (router-2) in the 172.16.0.0/16 network. Which configuration should be used for the BGP session?

options.text: ![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785598630915-862079j1.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785598635843-58g47vw9.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785598639934-zgeo6btl.png)
![](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1785598643638-is36oev7.png)

questions.explanation:
A Cloud VPN BGP session uses two distinct, reciprocal IPv4 link-local peering addresses in the 169.254.0.0/16 range. Each Cloud Router must use its own address as the BGP IP and the other router’s address as the peer IP; its peer ASN must be the remote router’s ASN. The 169.254.20.1/169.254.20.2 pairing with reciprocal ASNs 65001 and 65002 meets those requirements.

**Learn more:** [Establish BGP sessions — Cloud Router](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/configuring-bgp) · [Create HA VPN gateways to connect VPC networks](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/how-to/creating-ha-vpn2)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An application is hosted on a Compute Engine virtual machine instance and cannot communicate with a resource outside its subnet. When reviewing the flow and firewall logs, no denied traffic appears.  
  
During troubleshooting, you discover:  
  
- Flow logs are enabled on the VPC subnet, and every firewall rule is configured to log.  
- The subnetwork logs are not excluded from Stackdriver.  
- The instance hosting the application can communicate beyond the subnet.  
- Other instances in the subnet can communicate beyond the subnet.  
- The external resource initiates the communication.  
  
What is the most likely reason for the missing log lines?

options.text: The traffic is matching the expected ingress rule.
The traffic is matching the expected egress rule.
The traffic is not matching the expected ingress rule.
The traffic is not matching the expected egress rule.

questions.explanation:
Traffic initiated by the external resource is ingress traffic to the VM. When it does not match the intended ingress rule, it can be blocked by ingress firewall processing. VPC Flow Logs sample ingress packets only after ingress firewall evaluation, so denied ingress packets are not logged; firewall-rule logging also does not support the implied deny-ingress rule.

**Learn more:** [VPC Flow Logs](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/flow-logs) · [VPC firewall rules logging overview](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/vpc-firewall-rules-logging-overview)

You have established a Partner Interconnect connection to extend connectivity from your on-premises data center to Google Cloud. You must configure a Cloud Router and create a VLAN attachment to connect to resources within your VPC. You need to set an Autonomous System number (ASN) for use with the associated Cloud Router and create the VLAN attachment.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use a 4-byte private ASN 4200000000-4294967294.
Use a 2-byte private ASN 64512-65535.
Use a public Google ASN 15169.
Use a public Google ASN 16550.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Router that manages BGP sessions for Partner Interconnect VLAN attachments must be configured with Google-owned public ASN 16550. Private ASNs are used for other Cloud Router connectivity types, but Partner Interconnect specifically requires ASN 16550.

**Learn more:** [Create a Cloud Router to connect a VPC network to a peer network](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/create-router-vpc-network) · [Establish BGP sessions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/configuring-bgp)

You are developing a new application and need to access Cloud SQL from VPC instances that do not have public IP addresses.  
  
Which two actions should you perform? (Choose two.)

options.text: Activate the Service Networking API in your project.
Activate the Cloud Datastore API in your project.
Create a private connection to a service producer.
Create a custom static route to allow the traffic to reach the Cloud SQL API.
Enable Private Google Access.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL private-IP connectivity uses Private Services Access, which creates a private connection between the consumer VPC and the Cloud SQL service-producer VPC. Creating and managing this connection requires enabling the Service Networking API. [Cloud SQL private IP documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/private-ip)\
\
**Learn more:** [Learn about using private IP — Cloud SQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/private-ip)

You need to centralize Identity and Access Management permissions and email distribution for the WebServices Team as efficiently as possible.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a Google Group for the WebServices Team.
Create a G Suite Domain for the WebServices Team.
Create a new Cloud Identity Domain for the WebServices Team.
Create a new Custom Role for all members of the WebServices Team.

questions.explanation:
A Google Group has a group email address for email distribution and can be assigned IAM roles. Its members inherit the IAM roles granted to the group, which centralizes access management and membership administration.\
\
**Learn more:** [Create and manage Google groups in the Google Cloud console](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/groups-in-cloud-console) · [Groups API overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/identity/docs/groups)

questions.question:
You need to centralize Identity and Access Management permissions and email distribution for the WebServices Team as efficiently as possible.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Customize the operating system DNS configuration files to target the on-premises DNS servers.
Keep the different VPC networks from both departments isolated with different on-premises links, and separate Cloud DNS private zones and Cloud DNS forwarding zones.
Peer Department A's and Department B's VPC networks to have all on-premises connectivity via a single VPC network. Use separate Cloud DNS private zones and Cloud DNS forwarding zones.

Configure a Cloud DNS Peering zone in Department A's VPC network pointing to Department B's VPC and a Cloud DNS outbound forwarding zone in Department B's VPC network. Use separate on-premises links in each VPC network.

questions.explanation:
Cloud DNS supports outbound forwarding to shared on-premises DNS servers across multiple VPC networks by placing the forwarding zone in one designated VPC and creating a DNS peering zone in each other VPC that targets it. DNS peering preserves VPC network isolation while eliminating the need to maintain separate forwarding-zone configurations. Separate on-premises links can remain attached to each VPC for isolated connectivity.

**Learn more:** [Special configurations — Cloud DNS](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/special-configurations) · [Best practices for Cloud DNS](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/best-practices)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are preparing to deploy an internal HTTP(S) load balancer for web server virtual machine (VM) instances. Which two prerequisite tasks must be completed before you create the load balancer? (Choose two.)

options.text: Choose a region.
Create firewall rules for health checks.
Reserve a static IP address for the load balancer.
Determine the subnet mask for a proxy-only subnet.
Determine the subnet mask for Serverless VPC Access.

questions.explanation:
An internal Application Load Balancer needs a proxy-only subnet for its Envoy proxies, and the subnet’s address range must be determined when creating that subnet. Health-check probes must be allowed to reach the backend VM instances through an ingress firewall rule; otherwise, the load balancer cannot establish backend health. A reserved static IP address is optional, and Serverless VPC Access does not apply to VM instance backends.

**Learn more:** [Set up a regional internal Application Load Balancer with VM instance group backends](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/l7-internal/setting-up-l7-internal) · [Proxy-only subnets for Envoy-based load balancers](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/proxy-only-subnets)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have recently assumed responsibility for managing identity and access management for your organization. You have several projects and want to use scripting and automation wherever possible. You want to grant the Editor role to a member of a project.  
  
Which two methods can you use to do this? (Choose two.)

options.text: GetIamPolicy() via REST API
setIamPolicy() via REST API
gcloud pubsub add-iam-policy-binding Sprojectname --member user:Susername --role roles/editor
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding Sprojectname --member user:Susername --role roles/editor
Enter an email address in the Add members field, and select the desired role from the drop-down menu in the GCP Console.

questions.explanation:
A project-level Editor-role binding can be granted by updating the project’s IAM allow policy with the Resource Manager REST `setIamPolicy()` method, or by using `gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding` with the project, member, and `roles/editor`. `getIamPolicy()` only retrieves the policy and does not change access.

**Learn more:** [gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/projects/add-iam-policy-binding) · [Method: projects.setIamPolicy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/resource-manager/reference/rest/v3/projects/setIamPolicy)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must enable Private Google Access for use by certain subnets in your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). Your security team configured the VPC to route all internet-bound traffic back to the on-premises data center for inspection before it exits to the internet, and it is also implementing VPC Service Controls in the environment for API-level security control. The subnets have already been enabled for Private Google Access.  
  
What configuration changes should you make to enable Private Google Access while meeting your security team’s requirements?

options.text: 1. Create a private DNS zone with a CNAME record for *.googleapis.com to restricted.googleapis.com, with an A record pointing to Google's restricted API address range.2. Create a custom route that points Google's restricted API address range to the default internet gateway as the next hop.

1. Create a private DNS zone with a CNAME record for *.googleapis.com to restricted.googleapis.com, with an A record pointing to Google's restricted API address range.2. Change the custom route that points the default route (0/0) to the default internet gateway as the next hop.

1. Create a private DNS zone with a CNAME record for *.googleapis.com to private.googleapis.com, with an A record painting to Google's private AP address range.2. Change the custom route that points the default route (0/0) to the default internet gateway as the next hop.

1. Create a private DNS zone with a CNAME record for *.googleapis.com to private.googleapis.com, with an A record pointing to Google's private API address range.2. Create a custom route that points Google's private API address range to the default internet gateway as the next hop.

questions.explanation:
`restricted.googleapis.com` is the restricted virtual IP endpoint for Google APIs and services supported by VPC Service Controls. It resolves to `199.36.153.4/30`. When the VPC’s default route sends `0.0.0.0/0` traffic to an on-premises next hop, a more-specific custom route for that restricted API range must use the default internet gateway. Despite that next-hop name, this API traffic remains on Google’s network.

**Learn more:** [Private Google Access with VPC Service Controls](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/private-connectivity?hl=en) · [Configure Private Google Access](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access)

Your company operates a single on-premises data center that must connect to a VPC in Google Cloud. The overall bandwidth requirement is 10 Gbps. The connection needs redundancy and a minimum 99.9% SLA. Because the workloads are sensitive, implement the solution with the lowest possible latency.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Order a 10Gbps Partner Interconnect VLAN attachment. Create a Cloud Router in your Google Cloud VPC.

Order two 10Gbps Dedicated Interconnect connections in a single metropolitan area (metro). Distribute the connections across different edge availability domains. Create a Cloud Router and two 10Gbps VLAN attachments.

Create one HA VPN gateway. Create two tunnels-one tunnel for each of the two interfaces of the HA VPN gateway. Terminate each of the two tunnels on the single public IP address that is configured on the VPN termination device that is located on-premises.

Create one HA VPN gateway. Create two tunnels-one tunnel for each of the two interfaces of the HA VPN gateway. Terminate each of the two tunnels on different public IPs addresses that are configured on the VPN termination device that is located on-premises.

questions.explanation:
A 99.9% Dedicated Interconnect topology requires at least two Dedicated Interconnect connections in one metro, distributed across different edge availability domains. VLAN attachments connected through Cloud Router provide the VPC connectivity. Dedicated Interconnect is the direct private connectivity option and offers lower latency than VPN-based connectivity; a single Partner Interconnect VLAN attachment has no SLA.

**Learn more:** [Establish 99.9% availability for Dedicated Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/tutorials/dedicated-creating-999-availability?hl=en) · [Dedicated Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/dedicated-overview)

You are deploying an application on a fleet of Compute Engine virtual machines (VMs) that must process sensitive financial data while communicating with the Cloud Storage API. The VMs currently use internal IP addresses. You need to enable this communication by using the most secure available method. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Keep the VMs configured with only internal IP addresses. On the subnet, enable Private Google Access and configure the necessary private DNS records for private.googleapis.com.
Create a Cloud DNS private zone for googleapis.com that resolves to the restricted.googleapis.com IP addresses, and associate the private zone with the VMs' VPC network.
Modify the VMs to each have an external IP address. Create a restrictive egress firewall rule that only allows outbound traffic to the public IP ranges for Google APIs.
Create a Cloud NAT gateway, and configure it for the subnet housing the VMs. Remove the 0.0.0.0/0 route to the default internet gateway.
Create a regional Private Service Connect endpoint in your VPC that targets the Cloud Storage service. Configure the application on the VMs to send API requests to this endpoint.

questions.explanation:
Private Google Access lets VMs that have only internal IP addresses access Google APIs. For sensitive data, routing `googleapis.com` through the `restricted.googleapis.com` VIP restricts access to APIs and services supported by VPC Service Controls, which adds mitigation against data exfiltration. This configuration requires a private DNS zone and records for the restricted VIP. A global Google APIs Private Service Connect endpoint is configured against an API bundle; it is not a regional endpoint that directly targets the global Cloud Storage API.

**Learn more:** [Configure Private Google Access](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access) · [About accessing Google APIs through endpoints](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/about-accessing-google-apis-endpoints)

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently deployed Cloud VPN to connect your on-premises data center with Google Cloud. You must monitor this VPN's usage and configure alerts if traffic surpasses the maximum permitted level. You need to quickly determine whether to add additional links or migrate to a Dedicated Interconnect. What should you do?

options.text: In the Network Intelligence Canter, check for the number of packet drops on the VPN.
In the Google Cloud Console, use Monitoring Query Language to create a custom alert for bandwidth utilization.
In the Monitoring section of the Google Cloud Console, use the Dashboard section to select a default dashboard for VPN usage.
In the VPN section of the Google Cloud Console, select the VPN under hybrid connectivity, and then select monitoring to display utilization on the dashboard.

questions.explanation:
Cloud VPN capacity planning requires alerting on tunnel bandwidth utilization, using the sent and received traffic metrics against the tunnel's supported throughput. This gives timely notice of capacity pressure and supports a decision to add connectivity or move to Dedicated Interconnect. Packet-drop views and dashboards provide observability but do not by themselves create the required bandwidth alert. Current Google Cloud documentation recommends PromQL-based alert policies for Cloud VPN tunnel bandwidth.

**Learn more:** [View logs and metrics | Cloud VPN](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/how-to/viewing-logs-metrics) · [Cloud VPN overview](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],The organization’s existing architecture includes one Shared VPC host project (`SH_HOST_PRJ`) containing a single VPC (`SH_VPC`), plus two Shared VPC service projects (`SP_ONE_PRJ` and `SP_TWO_PRJ`) that contain no VPCs. Each Shared VPC service project is owned by a separate team: `TEAM_ONE` manages `SP_ONE_PRJ`, and `TEAM_TWO` manages `SP_TWO_PRJ`.  
  
Design a solution that lets each team create its own DNS private zones and DNS records only in its respective Shared VPC service project. Workloads in `SP_ONE_PRJ` must resolve every DNS private zone defined in `SP_TWO_PRJ`, and vice versa. The design must require the least setup effort. What should you do?

options.text: 1. TEAM_ONE uses cross-project binding and creates Cloud DNS private zones and DNS records in SP_ONE_PRJ, and binds the zones to the Shared VPC host project (SH_HOST_PRJ).2. TEAM_TWO creates Cloud DNS private zones and DNS records in SP_TWO_PRJ, and uses cross-project binding to connect the zones to the Shared VPC host project (SH_HOST_PRJ).

1. TEAM_ONE uses cross-project binding and creates Cloud DNS private zones and DNS records in SP_ONE_PRJ, and binds the zones to the VPC (SH_VPC) in the Shared VPC host project (SH_HOST_PRJ).2. TEAM_TWO creates DNS private zones and DNS records in SP_TWO_PRJ and uses cross-project binding to connect the zones to the VPC (SH_VPC) in the Shared VPC host project (SH_HOST_PRJ).

1. TEAM_ONE creates a new VPC (SP_ONE_VPC) in the Shared VPC service projects (SP_ONE_PRJ). TEAM_ONE creates Cloud DNS private zones and DNS records in SP_ONE_PRJ, and binds the zones to the new VPC (SP_ONE_VPC). TEAM_ONE creates a Cloud DNS peering relationship between SP_ONE_VPC and the VPC (SH_VPC) in the Shared VPC host project (SH_HOST_PRJ).2. TEAM_TWO completes the same actions for the SP_TWO_PRJ project.

1. TEAM_ONE creates a new VPC (SP_ONE_VPC) in the Shared VPC service projects (SP_ONE_PRJ). TEAM_ONE creates Cloud DNS private zones and DNS records in SP_ONE_PRJ, and binds the zones to the new VPC (SP_ONE_VPC). TEAM_ONE creates a VPC Network Peering relationship between SP_ONE_VPC and the VPC (SH_VPC) in the Shared VPC host project (SH_HOST_PRJ).2. TEAM_TWO completes the same actions for the SP_TWO_PRJ project.

questions.explanation:
Cloud DNS cross-project binding lets a team create and manage a private zone in its own service project while authorizing a VPC network owned by another project to query that zone. Binding each team’s zones to `SH_VPC` makes the zones visible to all workloads using that Shared VPC, including workloads in both service projects, without creating additional VPCs or peering relationships.

**Learn more:** [Create a zone with cross-project binding | Cloud DNS](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones/cross-project-binding) · [Shared VPC | Virtual Private Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc)

You are configuring an Application Load Balancer. The backend is located in your on-premises data center and connected through Dedicated Interconnect. You must ensure that the load balancer can reference these on-premises resources. Traffic must not traverse the internet at all. What should you do?

options.text: Configure an internet network endpoint group (NEG) as a backend service as part of the load balancer. Ensure firewalls are opened for the proxy-only subnet.
Configure a zonal network endpoint group (NEG) as a backend service as part of the load balancer. Ensure firewalls are opened for the client source IPs.
Configure a hybrid network endpoint group (NEG) as a backend service as part of the load balancer. Ensure firewalls are opened for the proxy-only subnet.
Configure a Private Service Connect network endpoint group (NEG) as a backend service as part of the load balancer. Ensure firewalls are opened for the client source IPs.

questions.explanation:
Hybrid connectivity NEGs are designed for non-Google Cloud IP:port endpoints reachable through Cloud Interconnect, Cloud VPN, or router appliances. Envoy-based Application Load Balancers send proxied traffic to hybrid NEG endpoints from the regional proxy-only subnet, so the on-premises firewall must allow that source range.

**Learn more:** [Hybrid connectivity network endpoint groups overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/negs/hybrid-neg-concepts)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for designing a new connectivity solution that lets your organization’s enterprise network access and use Google Workspace. You already have a Shared VPC with Compute Engine instances in `us-west1`. At present, Google Workspace is accessed through your service provider’s internet access. You want to establish a direct connection between your network and Google. What should you do?

options.text: Order a Dedicated Interconnect connection in the same metropolitan area. Create a VLAN attachment, a Cloud Router in us-west1, and a Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) session between your Cloud Router and your router.
Order a Direct Peering connection in the same metropolitan area. Configure a Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) session between Google and your router.
Configure HA VPN in us-west1. Configure a Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) session between your Cloud Router and your on-premises data center.
Order a Carrier Peering connection in the same metropolitan area. Configure a Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) session between Google and your router.

questions.explanation:
Direct Peering establishes a direct peering connection between a business network and Google’s edge network. It is an appropriate option for direct access to Google Workspace, and it uses a BGP session between Google and the customer’s router. Cloud Interconnect products support private connectivity to VPC resources but do not provide access to Google Workspace.

**Learn more:** [Direct Peering overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/direct-peering) · [Choosing a Network Connectivity product](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/how-to/choose-product)
