questions.question:
You want to use Cloud Interconnect to link your on-premises network to a GCP VPC. You cannot connect with Google at one of its point-of-presence (POP) locations, and your on-premises router cannot run a Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) configuration.  
  
Which connectivity model should you use?

options.text: Direct Peering
Dedicated Interconnect
Partner Interconnect with a layer 2 partner
Partner Interconnect with a layer 3 partner

questions.explanation:
Partner Interconnect is intended for locations that cannot reach a Dedicated Interconnect colocation facility. With a Layer 3 partner, the service provider establishes the BGP session with Cloud Router, so no BGP configuration is required on the local on-premises router.\
\
**Learn more:** [Partner Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/partner-overview)

questions.domain: Designing and planning a Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network
questions.question:
You want to use Cloud Interconnect to link your on-premises network to a GCP VPC. You cannot connect with Google at one of its point-of-presence (POP) locations, and your on-premises router cannot run a Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) configuration.  
  
Which connectivity model should you use?

options.text: Create a subnet of size /28 with 2 secondary ranges of: /24 for Pods and /24 for Services. Create a VPC-native cluster and specify those ranges. When the Services are ready to be deployed, resize the subnets.
Use gcloud container clusters create [CLUSTER_NAME]--enable-ip-alias to create a VPC-native Cluster.
Create a subnet of size /25 with 2 secondary ranges of: /17 for Pods and /21 for Services. Create a VPC-native cluster and specify those ranges.
Use gcloud container clusters create [CLUSTER_NAME] to create a VPC-native Cluster.

questions.explanation:
For a VPC-native GKE cluster configured for 200 Pods per node, each node receives a /24 Pod CIDR. Supporting 100 nodes therefore requires 25,600 Pod addresses, making /17 the smallest adequate Pod secondary range. A /21 Service secondary range supports 2,048 Services, enough for 1,500, and a /25 primary subnet supports up to 124 nodes. This capacity meets the planned growth with the smallest listed ranges that do so.

**Learn more:** [VPC-native clusters | GKE networking](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/alias-ips) · [Configure maximum Pods per node | GKE networking](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/flexible-pod-cidr)

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You create a private Google Kubernetes Engine cluster and want to use `kubectl` to retrieve pod status. On one of your instances, you find that the master is not responding even though the cluster is running.  
  
What should you do to resolve the issue?

options.text: Assign a public IP address to the instance.
Create a route to reach the Master, pointing to the default internet gateway.
Create the appropriate firewall policy in the VPC to allow traffic from Master node IP address to the instance.
Create the appropriate master authorized network entries to allow the instance to communicate to the master.

questions.explanation:
A private GKE control plane uses an internal endpoint. To allow `kubectl` from an instance that is outside the cluster subnet’s automatically permitted ranges, add the instance IP address or subnet CIDR to the cluster’s master authorized networks. This authorizes the instance to reach the control-plane API endpoint.

**Learn more:** [Creating a private cluster](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/legacy/network-isolation)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company runs a web application, `app.example.com`, on a Compute Engine instance in a Google Cloud VPC. You must configure DNS so employees within the VPC resolve `app.example.com` to its private IP address, while external internet users resolve the same hostname to a public IP address managed by a global external HTTPS Application Load Balancer. The solution must follow Google-recommended practices.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use a Cloud DNS forwarding zone to send all queries for app.example.com from your VPC to an on-premises DNS server that holds the private record.
Create a single public Cloud DNS zone for app.example.com. Add two ‘A’ records with the same hostname: one for the public IP and one for the private IP, relying on DNS round-robin.
Use Cloud DNS split horizon to create two Cloud DNS zones for app.example.com: a public zone for the public IP and a VPC-authorized private zone for the private IP.
Create a private Cloud DNS zone for app.example.com, and use a Cloud NAT gateway to translate the private IP to a public IP for external users.

questions.explanation:
Cloud DNS split-horizon DNS provides different record sets for the same domain based on where the query originates. A public zone supplies the load balancer’s public IP to internet clients, and a private zone authorized for the VPC supplies the Compute Engine instance’s private IP to internal clients. Cloud DNS resolves an authorized private zone before the corresponding public zone for VPC queries.

**Learn more:** [DNS zones overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones/zones-overview) · [General DNS overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/dns-overview)

questions.domain: Designing and planning a Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing an IP addressing scheme for new private Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters. Because your enterprise has exhausted its RFC 1918 address space, you plan to use privately used public IP space for the new clusters. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do after designing the IP scheme?

options.text: Create the minimum usable RFC 1918 primary and secondary subnet IP ranges for the clusters. Re-use the secondary address range for the pods across multiple private GKE clusters.
Create the minimum usable RFC 1918 primary and secondary subnet IP ranges for the clusters, Re-use the secondary address range for the services across multiple private GKE clusters.
Create privately used public IP primary and secondary subnet ranges for the clusters. Create a private GKE cluster with the following options selected: --enable-ip-alias and --enable-private-nodes.

Create privately used public IP primary and secondary subnet ranges for the clusters. Create a private GKE cluster with the following options selected: --disable-default-snat, --enable-ip-alias, and --enable-private-nodes.

questions.explanation:
For a private GKE cluster using privately reused public IP address ranges, default SNAT must be disabled. The `--disable-default-snat` option requires a VPC-native configuration using `--enable-ip-alias` and private nodes enabled with `--enable-private-nodes`; this prevents Kubernetes traffic using non-RFC 1918 addresses from being incorrectly source-NATed.

**Learn more:** [gcloud container clusters create reference](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/container/clusters/create) · [Troubleshoot IP address management in VPC clusters](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/troubleshooting/vpc-clusters)

questions.domain: Designing and planning a Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team is designing the network architecture for a new global web application on Google Cloud. The application's frontend will deliver HTTPS traffic to external users worldwide, while its backend will comprise game servers that communicate over custom TCP. You must provide low-latency access and high availability for the application while supporting global distribution and resilience.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure a global external Application Load Balancer for the HTTPS frontend and a cross-regional internal TCP proxy Network Load Balancer for the TCP game servers.

Configure a global external Application Load Balancer for the HTTPS frontend and an internal Network Load Balancer (Passthrough) for the game servers to handle direct client connections to backend instances globally.
Implement a regional external Application Load Balancer for the HTTPS frontend and multiple regional internal Network Load Balancers (Passthrough) for the TCP game servers across all regions.
Implement a regional internal Application Load Balancer for the HTTPS frontend and a regional internal TCP proxy Network Load Balancer for the game servers, and replicate this in each region.

questions.explanation:
A global external Application Load Balancer distributes HTTPS traffic through Google’s globally distributed frontend infrastructure, enabling low-latency access for external users. A cross-region internal TCP proxy Network Load Balancer is an internal Layer 4 TCP load balancer with a global forwarding rule, global access, and support for backends in multiple regions, which provides resilient cross-region connectivity for the game-server tier.

**Learn more:** [Application Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/application-load-balancer) · [Internal proxy Network Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/tcp/internal-proxy)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has a web-based application that will be migrated from an on-premises environment to Google Cloud. You need to configure Cloud CDN for the application migration. The application previously used another CDN provider and is configured to return `Cache-Control` headers. You want to preserve this configuration. What should you do?

options.text: Don’t configure Cloud CDN at all since the backend is already configured for caching.
Use the automatic caching mechanism in Cloud CDN by configuring CACHE_ALL_STATIC cache mode.
Migrate the website to a Cloud Storage bucket, and use its built-in caching.
Configure USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS to honor the cache headers delivered by the origin.

questions.explanation:
Cloud CDN's `USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS` cache mode uses valid `Cache-Control` (or `Expires`) directives returned by the origin to determine cacheability and freshness. This preserves the application's existing origin-controlled caching configuration.

**Learn more:** [Change cache modes | Cloud CDN | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/using-cache-modes?hl=en) · [Caching overview | Cloud CDN | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/caching)

questions.domain: Implementing a VPC network

options.text: Create a GKE cluster with a primary IP address range for Pods that is separate from the Node's primary IP range.
Create a routes-based GKE cluster, and rely on the automatically generated custom static routes in the VPC for Pod IP address connectivity.
Enable VPC-native traffic routing by creating a cluster that uses alias IP ranges for its Pods and Services.
Implement a public GKE cluster so that the Pods can communicate to the databases through public or private IP addresses.

questions.explanation:
A VPC-native GKE cluster uses alias IP ranges, with Pod IP addresses allocated from a VPC subnet secondary range. Those Pod addresses are directly routable within the VPC, allowing private connectivity to internal services and database resources.

**Learn more:** [VPC-native clusters](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/alias-ips) · [Understand IP addressing in GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-ip-addressing)

You are designing a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster for a highly sensitive application that handles confidential financial data in one shared VPC. Your developers must securely access the Kubernetes API endpoint from their corporate network, which connects to Google Cloud through Cloud VPN. You need to provide the strongest network security and ensure that the GKE control plane is not exposed to the internet. What should you do?

options.text: Create a GKE cluster with a public endpoint. Implement VPC Service Controls to prevent any unauthorized access to the Kubernetes API from the internet.

Deploy a private GKE cluster with the public endpoint disabled. Enable Private Service Connect to the control plane, allowing access only from within the VPC network or on-premises networks through Cloud VPN.
Deploy a private GKE cluster with a public endpoint disabled. Use an internal TCP/UDP load balancer with identity proxy as a backend to connect to the Kubernetes API within the VPC network.
Create a public GKE cluster, and configure authorized networks on the control plane to restrict access to the corporate network's external IP address.

questions.explanation:
A private GKE cluster with the public control-plane endpoint disabled prevents Kubernetes API access from the internet. Its private control-plane endpoint can be accessed from the VPC and from an on-premises network connected through Cloud VPN. Private Service Connect supplies private connectivity to the GKE control plane without sending management traffic over the public internet.

**Learn more:** [About Private Service Connect in GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/private-service-connect) · [Creating a private GKE cluster](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/legacy/network-isolation)

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are completing the final steps of a migration in which resources were moved from on-premises to Google Cloud. While reviewing the deployed architecture, you notice DNS resolution fails when queries are sent to the on-premises environment. You log in to a Compute Engine instance, attempt to resolve an on-premises hostname, and the query fails. DNS queries are not reaching the on-premises DNS server. You must use managed services to reconfigure Cloud DNS and resolve this DNS issue. What should you do?

options.text: Ensure that the operating systems of the Compute Engine instances are configured to send DNS queries to the on-premises DNS servers directly.

Validate that there is network connectivity to the on-premises environment and that the Compute Engine instances can reach other on-premises resources. If errors persist, remove the VPC Network Peerings and recreate the peerings after validating the routes.

Validate that the Compute Engine instances are using the Metadata Service IP address as their resolver. Configure an outbound forwarding zone for the on-premises domain pointing to the on-premises DNS server. Configure Cloud Router to advertise the Cloud DNS proxy range to the on-premises network.

Review the existing Cloud DNS zones, and validate that there is a route in the VPC directing traffic destined to the IP address of the DNS servers. Recreate the existing DNS forwarding zones for . to forward all queries to the on-premises DNS servers.

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine instances must use the metadata server resolver so their requests follow the VPC DNS resolution order and can use Cloud DNS resources. An outbound Cloud DNS forwarding zone forwards the on-premises domain’s queries to the on-premises DNS server. For an on-premises forwarding target reached through dynamic Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect, Cloud Router must advertise the Cloud DNS proxy source range, `35.199.192.0/19`, so replies can return to Cloud DNS.

**Learn more:** [Create a forwarding zone | Cloud DNS](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones/forwarding-zones) · [DNS server policies | Cloud DNS](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/server-policies-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a solution to examine all traffic between your company’s production-vpc and development-vpc for threat detection and compliance logging. The company will deploy a fleet of third-party Cloud Next Generation Firewall (NGFW) appliances that provide intrusion prevention system (IPS) capabilities. You must prevent attacks by blocking malicious traffic in real time before it reaches its destination, without introducing significant latency or a single point of failure for inter-VPC communication.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: • Deploy the third-party NGFW appliances as multi-NIC VMs, with an NIC in each VPC.• Create custom static routes in each VPC that direct traffic destined for the other VPC to an internal TCP/UDP load balancer that uses the NGFW appliances as its backends.

• Use Packet Mirroring to send traffic to the third-party NGFW appliances.• When a threat is detected, have the appliances use the Google Cloud Armor API to insert a rule blocking the malicious source.
• Use Packet Mirroring to create a copy of all inter-VPC traffic.• Forward it to an internal Application Load Balancer that distributes the traffic to the NGFW appliance fleet for analysis.
• Configure a Cloud NAT gateway to handle routing between the two VPCs, and enable NAT logging.• Use a script to parse the logs, and send them to the NGFW appliances.

questions.explanation:
Inline inspection and real-time blocking require routing inter-VPC flows through the NGFW appliances. Multi-NIC virtual appliances can connect to both VPC networks, and custom static routes can use an internal passthrough TCP/UDP load balancer as the next hop. The load balancer distributes traffic across health-checked firewall backends, supporting a highly available, scaled-out inspection path. Packet Mirroring and log analysis are out-of-band mechanisms, so they cannot block a malicious flow before it reaches its destination.

**Learn more:** [Set up internal passthrough Network Load Balancer for third-party appliances](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/internal/setting-up-ilb-next-hop) · [Internal passthrough Network Load Balancers as next hops](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/internal/ilb-next-hop-overview)

You operate a rapidly growing ecommerce application on a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. The cluster currently has one node pool, `default-pool`, configured with `e2-standard-4` machine types and a `/24` CIDR range for its nodes.  
  
You recently found application pods stuck in a “pending” state and determined that `default-pool` had reached its maximum size because the subnet’s node IP address space was exhausted. You must immediately add compute capacity to the cluster to handle the increased load and support future node scalability.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure a new primary range (that is, a new subnet) within the cluster’s VPC. Create a new node pool using this new primary range.
Add a new secondary IP address range to the existing subnet, and configure the default-pool to use it for new nodes.
Edit the default-pool to use a larger machine type, such as e2-standard-8, to provide more resources per node.
Increase the maxPodsPerNode setting on the existing default-pool to allow more pods to be scheduled.

questions.explanation:
GKE allocates each worker node’s internal IP address from the primary IP address range of the subnet associated with its node pool. An additional subnet provides a new primary node-IP range, so a new node pool can scale without relying on the exhausted `/24`. Secondary IP ranges are for Pod and Service addressing, not node addresses; changing machine size or pod density does not resolve node-IP exhaustion.

**Learn more:** [Understand IP addressing in GKE](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-ip-addressing) · [Add subnets to clusters](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/multi-subnet-cluster)

Your organization recently exposed a set of services using a global external Application Load Balancer. After performing tests, you found that responses intermittently returned HTTP 4xx or 5xx error codes. You have already enabled and reviewed the health check logs. You need to identify the error. What should you do?

options.text: Access a VM in the VPC through SSH to access the backend VM directly. If the request is successful from the VM, increase the quantity of backends.
Delete the load balancer and backend services. Create a new Passthrough Network Load Balancer. Configure a failover group of VMs for the backend.
Validate the health of the backend service. Enable logging for the backend service and identify the error response in Cloud Logging. Review the statusDetails log field.
Validate the health of the backend service. Disable any Cloud Armor policies on the backend service, and identify any error response in Cloud Logging. Review the statusDetails log field.

questions.explanation:
For a global external Application Load Balancer, Cloud Logging entries and the `statusDetails` field distinguish responses generated by the load balancer from those returned by a backend. A value such as `response_sent_by_backend` shows that the backend generated the HTTP response, while other `statusDetails` values identify proxy or backend-selection failures. Backend-service logging therefore supplies the diagnostic evidence needed after health-check logs have been reviewed.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot issues with external Application Load Balancers](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/https/troubleshooting-ext-https-lbs) · [Global external Application Load Balancer logging and monitoring](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/https/https-logging-monitoring)

You manage a complex collection of VPC firewall rules across multiple projects. Over time, many rules have been added, resulting in unintended behavior or security gaps when higher-priority rules shadow other rules. You need a systematic method to identify these inefficient or ineffective firewall rules.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Review Cloud Logging entries for firewall rules to see which rules are being triggered.
Use VPC Flow Logs to trace network traffic and determine which firewall rules were applied to specific connections.
Create and run Connectivity Tests to see which paths are blocked or allowed.
Use Firewall Insights within the Network Intelligence Center to analyze rule usage and identify unused rules.

questions.explanation:
Firewall Insights in Network Intelligence Center analyzes VPC firewall-rule configuration and usage to identify shadowed rules, rules with no hits, and unused rule attributes. Shadowed-rule insights detect rules that share relevant attributes with rules of higher or equal priority, enabling systematic cleanup of ineffective or unnecessary rules.

**Learn more:** [Firewall Insights overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/firewall-insights/concepts/overview) · [Firewall Insights categories and states](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/firewall-insights/concepts/insights-categories-states?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You provisioned a Cloud Interconnect connection with a VLAN attachment and configured Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) between your on-premises router and Cloud Router. After deployment and testing, you find that the BGP session between the on-premises router and Cloud Router is not established. Which two actions should you take to fix the issue? (Choose two.)

options.text: From the Google Cloud console, run gcloud compute routers get-status to verify the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) learned.
Verify that you have configured the on-premises router's subinterface with a subnet mask of /31.
Verify that you have configured the on-premises router's eBGP multihop with a minimum hop length of 4.
Verify that you have configured the on-premises router's BGP security parameters to use MD5 authentication.
From the Google Cloud console, run gcloud compute interconnects get-diagnostics to verify the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) learned.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Interconnect BGP troubleshooting requires eBGP multihop on the on-premises router and validation of the underlying interconnect’s ARP state. The `gcloud compute interconnects get-diagnostics` command provides interconnect diagnostics, including ARP information. A /31 mask is not the VLAN attachment addressing configuration described by Google Cloud, MD5 authentication is optional, and `gcloud compute routers get-status` does not verify ARP learned on the interconnect.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshooting Cloud Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/support/troubleshooting) · [Get diagnostics for Dedicated Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/getting-diagnostics)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manually deployed a proof-of-concept application by placing instances in one Compute Engine zone. You are now moving the application into production, so you must improve application availability and make sure that it can autoscale.  
  
How should you provision the instances?

options.text: Create a single managed instance group, specify the desired region, and select Multiple zones for the location.
Create a managed instance group for each region, select Single zone for the location, and manually distribute instances across the zones in that region.
Create an unmanaged instance group in a single zone, and then create an HTTP load balancer for the instance group.
Create an unmanaged instance group for each zone, and manually distribute the instances across the desired zones.

questions.explanation:
A regional managed instance group deploys and manages VM instances across multiple zones in a region, protecting the workload from a zonal failure. Managed instance groups support autoscaling, which automatically adds or removes VMs in response to load.

**Learn more:** [About regional managed instance groups](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/regional-migs) · [Autoscaling groups of instances](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/autoscaler)

questions.domain: Designing and planning a Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your VPC uses regional dynamic routing mode. You have deployed VMs and VLAN attachments in the `europe-west2` region, along with regional internal Application Load Balancers in `us-east1`. You need to ensure that the VMs in `europe-west2` can connect to the regional internal Application Load Balancers in `us-east1`. What should you do?

options.text: Create the backend in us-east1, create multiple forwarding rules in each region, and then enable regional access.
Create the backend service in europe-west2, create the forwarding rule in us-east1, and then enable regional access.
Create the backend service in us-east1, create the forwarding rule in europe-west2, and then enable global access.
Create the backend service in us-east1, create the forwarding rule in us-east1, and then enable global access.

questions.explanation:
A regional internal Application Load Balancer uses regional backend resources and a regional forwarding rule in the load balancer's region; its backends must be in that same region. Enabling global access on the regional forwarding rule permits clients in other regions of the VPC to reach the load balancer. With regional dynamic routing, the relevant regional routes are exchanged for the `europe-west2` VLAN attachment and VMs.

**Learn more:** [Internal Application Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/l7-internal)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has just launched a new, critical revenue-generating web application. The application was deployed for scalability by using managed instance groups, autoscaling, and a Network Load Balancer as the frontend. One day, you observe severe bursty traffic that causes autoscaling to reach the maximum number of instances, and application users cannot complete transactions. After investigating, you believe this is a DDoS attack. You want to rapidly restore user access and enable successful transactions while minimizing cost.  
  
Which two steps should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use Cloud Armor to blacklist the attacker's IP addresses.
Increase the maximum autoscaling backend to accommodate the severe bursty traffic.
Create a global HTTP(s) load balancer and move your application backend to this load balancer.
Shut down the entire application in GCP for a few hours. The attack will stop when the application is offline.
SSH into the backend compute engine instances, and view the auth logs and syslogs to further understand the nature of the attack.

questions.explanation:
A global HTTP(S) load balancer enables Cloud Armor policies to filter requests at Google’s network edge. Cloud Armor can deny traffic from identified attacker IP addresses before it consumes backend capacity, preserving instances for legitimate transactions and avoiding the ongoing cost of scaling the backend merely to absorb malicious traffic.

**Learn more:** [Security policy overview | Google Cloud Armor](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/security-policy-overview) · [Faster web performance and improved web protection for load balancing | Cloud Load Balancing](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/tutorials/faster-performance-improved-protection)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are in the initial planning phase of a migration to GCP. You want to test the functionality of your hybrid-cloud design before implementing it in production. The design includes services running on a Compute Engine virtual machine instance that must communicate with on-premises servers by using private IP addresses. The on-premises servers are connected to the internet, but no Cloud Interconnect connections have been established yet. You want to select the lowest-cost way to enable connectivity between your instance and the on-premises servers and finish the test within 24 hours.  
  
Which connectivity method should you select?

options.text: Cloud VPN
50-Mbps Partner VLAN attachment
Dedicated Interconnect with a single VLAN attachment
Dedicated Interconnect, but don't provision any VLAN attachments

questions.explanation:
Cloud VPN securely extends an on-premises peer network to a VPC through a site-to-site IPsec VPN connection over the internet, allowing routed communication between private networks. It can be configured using the existing internet-connected on-premises VPN endpoint. Partner Interconnect depends on prior connectivity with a supported service provider and provider-side provisioning, while Dedicated Interconnect requires an ordered physical connection; Dedicated Interconnect VLAN attachments are what determine which VPC networks can reach the on-premises network.

**Learn more:** [Cloud VPN overview | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/overview) · [Partner Interconnect overview | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/partner-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company operates `shop.example.com`, a global e-commerce application deployed in three Google Cloud regions: `us-central1`, `europe-west1`, and `asia-east1`. Each regional deployment is served by a regional external Application Load Balancer. You need to configure Cloud DNS to send users to the regional load balancer nearest to their geographic location, minimizing latency. What should you do?

options.text: Create a record set for shop.example.com using a Cloud DNS geolocation route policy that maps traffic originating from source geographies to the corresponding regional load balancer.
Configure a failover routing policy where the primary backend is dynamically set to the region with the lowest latency, with the other regions serving as hot standbys.
Use a weighted round-robin (WRR) policy to specify different weights per regional load balancer, assigning higher weights to the regional load balancers.
Create a single “A

questions.explanation:
A Cloud DNS geolocation routing policy maps traffic from source geographies to specific DNS targets. Mapping each relevant source geography to the IP address of its corresponding regional external Application Load Balancer provides geography-based traffic steering; weighted routing and ordinary multi-value A records do not select targets by client location.

**Learn more:** [Cloud DNS routing policies and health checks](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/routing-policies-overview) · [Configure DNS routing policies and health checks](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/configure-routing-policies?hl=en)

You are designing a critical multi-tier application on Google Cloud that needs high availability across multiple regions. The application includes a web frontend in a managed instance group (MIG), an API backend, and a Cloud SQL database. You must ensure the application can seamlessly fail over to a secondary region when the primary region becomes unavailable, while minimizing downtime and data loss.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the web frontend MIG in a single region, and configure a Cloud DNS failover policy pointing to a load balancer in another region.
Implement a strategy by deploying identical application components in two separate regions and using a global external HTTPS load balancer with multiple backend services.

Implement a disaster recovery strategy by deploying identical application components in two separate regions. Configure global external HTTPS load balancers in both regions, and use Cloud DNS to distribute traffic between them based on latency.
Configure cross-regional VPC Network Peering between the primary and secondary regions to allow for direct traffic flow during a failover event.

questions.explanation:
Deploying matching application components in two regions provides regional redundancy. A global external HTTPS load balancer can use backend services with backends in multiple regions and automatically direct traffic away from an unhealthy region to healthy backends in another region, providing cross-region failover through one global entry point.

**Learn more:** [Application Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/application-load-balancer) · [Cloud Load Balancing overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/load-balancing-overview)

questions.question:
You choose to configure Cloud NAT. After you complete the configuration, you discover that one of your instances is not using Cloud NAT for outbound NAT.  
  
What is the most likely cause of this issue?

options.text: The instance has been configured with multiple interfaces.
An external IP address has been configured on the instance.
You have created static routes that use RFC1918 ranges.
The instance is accessible by a load balancer external IP address.

questions.explanation:
An instance network interface that has an external IP address uses automatic one-to-one NAT for outbound traffic from its primary internal IP address. That behavior takes precedence over Public Cloud NAT, so Cloud NAT is not used for that traffic.\
\
**Learn more:** [Cloud NAT troubleshooting](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/troubleshooting) · [Public NAT specifications](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/public-nat)

questions.question:
You choose to configure Cloud NAT. After you complete the configuration, you discover that one of your instances is not using Cloud NAT for outbound NAT.  
  
What is the most likely cause of this issue?
questions.explanation:
For a non-BGP-capable peer, use Classic VPN with static routing. A route-based VPN sets both local and remote traffic selectors to `0.0.0.0/0` and uses static routes for reachable prefixes. Because the selectors do not need modification as subnets are added, network growth can be handled by updating routes without recreating the VPN tunnel, avoiding the downtime and operational burden associated with changing policy-based traffic selectors.

**Learn more:** [Networks and tunnel routing | Cloud VPN](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/choosing-networks-routing) · [Create a Classic VPN connection to a remote site](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/tutorials/configure-vpn-between-onprem-cloud)

questions.domain: Designing and planning a Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization must address a shortage of private IP addresses. You need to create new GKE clusters and restrict the Pods secondary range size to no larger than `/22`.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a secondary range for pods with a size of /22. Create a secondary range for services manually. Reference these ranges during the GKE cluster creation.
Specify a new /22 IP range for pods during the GKE cluster creation. Let GKE automatically create the secondary range in your existing primary subnet range.
Deploy GKE Autopilot instead of GKE Standard.
Configure the pods per node value to the minimum to automatically use smaller subnet ranges for pods during the GKE cluster creation.

questions.explanation:
VPC-native GKE clusters allocate Pod and Service addresses from separate subnet secondary ranges. Creating a `/22` secondary range for Pods and a separate secondary range for Services, then specifying those ranges when the cluster is created, directly controls the Pod CIDR size. A secondary range must not overlap the subnet’s primary IP range.

**Learn more:** [Create a VPC-native cluster](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/alias-ips) · [Configure maximum Pods per node](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/flexible-pod-cidr)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A storage bucket contains two objects. Cloud CDN is enabled for the bucket, and both objects have been cached successfully. You now need to ensure that one of the two objects is no longer cached and is always served to the internet directly from the origin.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Ensure that the object you don't want to be cached anymore is not shared publicly.
Create a new storage bucket, and move the object you don't want to be checked anymore inside it. Then edit the bucket setting and enable the private attribute.
Add an appropriate lifecycle rule on the storage bucket containing the two objects.
Add a Cache-Control entry with value private to the metadata of the object you don't want to be cached anymore. Invalidate all the previously cached copies.

questions.explanation:
Cloud CDN does not cache a response whose `Cache-Control` directive is `private` (provided the backend is not configured with `FORCE_CACHE_ALL`, which overrides origin cache directives). Updating the object metadata changes its response header for future origin responses, and invalidating the existing cached copies removes the already-cached entries so subsequent requests are served from the origin rather than Cloud CDN.

**Learn more:** [Cloud CDN caching overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/caching) · [Invalidate cached content](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/invalidating-cached-content)

questions.domain: Implementing a VPC network
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization’s security policy requires all internet-bound traffic to return to the on-premises data center through HA VPN tunnels before it exits to the internet, while permitting virtual machines (VMs) to use private Google APIs through private virtual IP addresses `199.36.153.4/30`.  
  
You need to configure routes that enable these traffic flows. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a custom route 0.0.0.0/0 with a priority of 500 whose next hop is the default internet gateway. Configure another custom route 199.36.153.4/30 with priority of 1000 whose next hop is the VPN tunnel back to the on-premises data center.

Configure a custom route 0.0.0.0/0 with a priority of 1000 whose next hop is the internet gateway. Configure another custom route 199.36.153.4/30 with a priority of 500 whose next hop is the VPN tunnel back to the on-premises data center.
Announce a 0.0.0.0/0 route from your on-premises router with a MED of 1000. Configure a custom route 199.36.153.4/30 with a priority of 1000 whose next hop is the default internet gateway.

Announce a 0.0.0.0/0 route from your on-premises router with a MED of 500. Configure another custom route 199.36.153.4/30 with a priority of 1000 whose next hop is the VPN tunnel back to the on-premises data center.

questions.explanation:
A `0.0.0.0/0` route advertised from the on-premises router sends general internet-bound traffic through the HA VPN. A custom route for `199.36.153.4/30` with the default internet gateway as next hop is required for the restricted Google APIs VIP range. Because `/30` is more specific than `/0`, traffic to those private Google API addresses uses the gateway route while all other internet-bound traffic uses the VPN-learned default route.

**Learn more:** [Configure Private Google Access](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access) · [Order of routes for Cloud VPN](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/order-of-routes)

questions.domain: Configuring, implementing and managing a cloud network security solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has deployed a mission-critical application that is expected to become a new revenue source. During planning and deployment, you recently implemented a security profile using the default set of threat signatures supplied by Cloud Next Generation Firewall (Cloud NGFW). This application is the only application running in this project.  
  
You need to strengthen the application's security posture so that threats are logged and the associated packets are dropped. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a new default threat signature with Deny All to all severity options. Review the logs to understand the impact.
Set up a Linux VM as the frontend gateway for the application. Create iptables rules to drop all packets, excluding the application port.
For all severity options (critical, high, medium, low and informational) in the security profile, change the default override action to Deny.

Configure Cloud Scheduler to run a task that checks the Cloud NGFW logs to verify the threats. Configure the task to create a security profile with each signature ID set to override the default action.

questions.explanation:
Cloud NGFW threat-prevention security profiles can override the default action for each threat severity. Applying the `DENY` override to critical, high, medium, low, and informational threats causes matching packets to be dropped and produces a threat-log entry; the logged action appears as `DROP`.

**Learn more:** [Threat logs | Cloud Next Generation Firewall](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/threat_logs) · [Create and manage threat prevention security profiles | Cloud Next Generation Firewall](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/configure-security-profiles)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You administer a large, VPC-native Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster that is exhausting IP addresses in its primary Pod CIDR range, `10.100.0.0/16`. You have identified an available, non-contiguous CIDR block, `10.200.0.0/16`, for new Pods. You need to expand the cluster's Pod address space using this new range.  
  
You must also ensure that traffic from Pods, irrespective of the CIDR range to which they belong, has its source address translated to the node's IP address when communicating with an on-premises legacy monitoring system at `192.168.10.0/24`, while minimizing operational overhead.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a new node pool, and assign the 10.200.0.0/16 range as a secondary IP range to the underlying subnet.

• Create a new secondary IP address range in the cluster’s subnet with the range 10.200.0.0/16.• Update the GKE cluster to use this new secondary range for Pods.• Ensure the ip-masq-agent ConfigMap’s nonMasqueradeCIDRs list does not include 192.168.10.0/24.

• Create a new secondary IP address range in the cluster’s subnet with the range 10.200.0.0/16.• Update the GKE cluster to use this new secondary range for Pods.• Modify the ip-masq-agent ConfigMap to add 192.168.10.0/24 to the nonMasqueradeCIDRs list.
Create a new GKE cluster with the new Pod range, and use VPC Network Peering to connect it to the old cluster.

questions.explanation:
A VPC-native GKE cluster can use an additional non-contiguous secondary IPv4 range in its existing subnet as an additional Pod range. In an `ip-masq-agent` configuration, `nonMasqueradeCIDRs` specifies destination ranges for which Pod source addresses are preserved. Omitting `192.168.10.0/24` ensures traffic to that on-premises range is SNATed to the underlying node IP address. [Adding Pod IPv4 address ranges](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/multi-pod-cidr) and [Configuring an IP masquerade agent in Standard clusters](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/ip-masquerade-agent) document these behaviors.

**Learn more:** [Adding Pod IPv4 address ranges](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/multi-pod-cidr) · [Configuring an IP masquerade agent in Standard clusters](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/ip-masquerade-agent)

You are designing the network architecture for a hybrid environment in which applications in Google Cloud and on-premises services must resolve one another’s DNS records. You need a scalable, managed solution that provides seamless, bidirectional DNS resolution between your Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) and your on-premises network. You want to avoid manual DNS-record synchronization and follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: • Implement Cloud DNS private zones for your Google Cloud resources.• Configure an inbound server policy in your VPC for on-premises resolution.• Create a Cloud DNS forwarding zone to resolve on-premises domain names.

• Establish Cloud DNS private zones within your Google Cloud project for all Google Cloud resources.• Configure all on-premises DNS servers to conditionally forward queries for Google Cloud domains to these private.• zones through an inbound server policy on your VPC.

• Deploy a pair of custom DNS virtual machines in two Google Cloud regions of your VPC.• Configure the pair to replicate DNS records with on-premises DNS servers.• Update DHCP options for all cloud and on-premises instances.
• Configure a Cloud DNS public zone, and import all on-premises DNS records into it.• Update all on-premises clients to use this Cloud DNS public zone as their primary DNS server.

questions.explanation:
Cloud DNS private zones provide authoritative private DNS records for resources in the VPC. An inbound DNS server policy lets on-premises resolvers query Cloud DNS through managed inbound forwarding entry points, while a Cloud DNS forwarding zone forwards queries for on-premises domains to the on-premises DNS servers. Together, these managed services provide bidirectional hybrid DNS resolution without synchronizing records or operating custom DNS virtual machines.

**Learn more:** [DNS server policies](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/server-policies-overview) · [Create a forwarding zone](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones/forwarding-zones)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing the VPC network for a large enterprise with numerous development teams. You need to centralize management of shared network resources while allowing each development team to provision and manage its own virtual machines and other compute resources within its respective project. You must also ensure that all applications can communicate securely within the corporate environment.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Designate a host project to contain a Shared VPC network, and then attach each development team’s project as a service project to share this network.
Configure Cloud VPN tunnels from each development project’s VPC to a central network project that acts as a hub.
Implement a single large VPC for all development teams in one project and grant them specific IAM roles to manage resources within it.
Create individual VPCs in each development project and establish VPC Network Peering connections between all of them.

questions.explanation:
Shared VPC centralizes ownership and administration of networks, subnets, routes, and firewall rules in a host project while attached service projects retain the ability to create and manage eligible compute resources that use the shared subnets. Workloads in service projects attached to the same Shared VPC can communicate over internal IP addresses, subject to applicable firewall rules.

**Learn more:** [Shared VPC](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc) · [Provision Shared VPC](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/provisioning-shared-vpc)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your on-premises data center has 2 routers, each connected to your Google Cloud environment by a VPN. All applications work correctly; however, all traffic traverses one VPN rather than being load-balanced across the 2 connections as intended.  
  
During troubleshooting, you discover:  
  
- Each on-premises router is configured with a distinct ASN.  
- Each on-premises router has the same routes and priorities configured.  
- Both on-premises routers have a VPN connected to one Cloud Router.  
- BGP sessions are established between both on-premises routers and the Cloud Router.  
- Only 1 on-premises router's routes is being added to the routing table.  
  
What is the most likely cause of this issue?

options.text: The on-premises routers are configured with the same routes.
A firewall is blocking the traffic across the second VPN connection.
You do not have a load balancer to load-balance the network traffic.
The ASNs being used on the on-premises routers are different.

questions.explanation:
For active-active Cloud VPN routing, equivalent routes with identical MED values/priorities are needed for equal-cost multipath (ECMP). Using different ASNs on the two on-premises BGP peers causes Cloud Router’s BGP best-path processing to distinguish the paths by neighbor ASN, so they are not installed as the intended equal-cost routes. Google Cloud documents that active-active HA VPN uses identical route metrics to enable ECMP and that Cloud Router’s route processing considers neighbor ASN values when comparing MEDs.

**Learn more:** [HA VPN topologies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/topologies) · [Learned routes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/concepts/learned-routes?hl=en)

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a hybrid-cloud environment for your organization. Your Google Cloud environment connects to your on-premises network through Cloud HA VPN and Cloud Router. Cloud Router is configured with its default settings. Your on-premises DNS server is at `192.168.20.88` and protected by a firewall, and your Compute Engine resources are in `10.204.0.0/24`.  
  
Your Compute Engine resources must resolve on-premises private hostnames in the `corp.altostrat.com` domain while continuing to resolve Google Cloud hostnames. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create a private forwarding zone in Cloud DNS for ‘corp.altostrat.com’ called corp-altostrat-com that points to 192.168.20.88.2. Configure your on-premises firewall to accept traffic from 10.204.0.0/24.3. Set a custom route advertisement on the Cloud Router for 10.204.0.0/24

1. Create a private forwarding zone in Cloud DNS for ‘corp.altostrat.com’ called corp-altostrat-com that points to 192.168 20.88.2. Configure your on-premises firewall to accept traffic from 35.199.192.0/193. Set a custom route advertisement on the Cloud Router for 35.199.192.0/19.

1. Create a private forwarding zone in Cloud DNS for ‘corp .altostrat.com’ called corp-altostrat-com that points to 192.168.20.88.2. Configure your on-premises firewall to accept traffic from 10.204.0.0/24.3. Modify the /etc/resolv conf file on your Compute Engine instances to point to 192.168.20 88

1. Create a private zone in Cloud DNS for ‘corp altostrat.com’ called corp-altostrat-com.2. Configure DNS Server Policies and create a policy with Alternate DNS servers to 192.168.20.88.3. Configure your on-premises firewall to accept traffic from 35.199.192.0/19.4. Set a custom route advertisement on the Cloud Router for 35.199.192.0/19.

questions.explanation:
For an on-premises DNS server used as a Cloud DNS forwarding target over Cloud VPN, Cloud DNS sends DNS requests from `35.199.192.0/19`. The on-premises firewall must permit DNS traffic from that range, and the on-premises network needs a return route for the same range. With dynamically routed Cloud VPN, that return route is supplied by configuring a custom `35.199.192.0/19` advertisement on the Cloud Router BGP session. A private forwarding zone for `corp.altostrat.com` forwards only that private namespace to the on-premises DNS server while other names continue through normal Google Cloud resolution.

**Learn more:** [Create a forwarding zone | Cloud DNS](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones/forwarding-zones) · [Best practices for Cloud DNS](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/best-practices)

options.text: Open the Cloud Shell SSH into the instance using gcloud compute ssh.
Set the custom metadata enable-oslogin to TRUE, and SSH into the instance using a third-party tool like putty or ssh.
Generate a new SSH key pair. Verify the format of the private key and add it to the instance. SSH into the instance using a third-party tool like putty or ssh.
Generate a new SSH key pair. Verify the format of the public key and add it to the project. SSH into the instance using a third-party tool like putty or ssh.

questions.explanation:
With OS Login disabled, Compute Engine uses metadata-managed SSH keys. When `gcloud compute ssh` cannot store its public key in project metadata because `block-project-ssh-keys` is `TRUE`, it stores the public key in the target instance's metadata, enabling access. SSH authentication uses a public key on the instance; a private key must remain on the client.

**Learn more:** [About SSH connections](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/ssh) · [Add SSH keys to VMs](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/connect/add-ssh-keys)

An organization has a Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) with subnets in us-east1, us-west4, and europe-west4 that use the default VPC configuration. Employees at a branch office in Europe must access resources in the VPC by using HA VPN. The HA VPN associated with the organization's Google Cloud VPC is configured with a Cloud Router deployed in europe-west4.  
  
You need to ensure that branch-office users can quickly and easily access every resource in the VPC. What should you do?

options.text: Create custom advertised routes for each subnet.
Configure each subnet’s VPN connections to use Cloud VPN to connect to the branch office.
Configure the VPC dynamic routing mode to Global.
Set the advertised routes to Global for the Cloud Router.

questions.explanation:
In global dynamic routing mode, Cloud Router advertises the VPC subnet routes from all regions to its BGP peer. Therefore, the HA VPN connection through the Cloud Router in europe-west4 provides the branch office with routes to resources in europe-west4, us-east1, and us-west4 without manually advertising each subnet.

**Learn more:** [Advertised routes | Cloud Router | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/concepts/advertised-routes) · [Networks and tunnel routing | Cloud VPN | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/choosing-networks-routing)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You configured a single IPsec Cloud VPN tunnel from your organization to a customer. The VPN Tunnel Status shows **Established**; however, the BGP Session Status shows **BGP not configured**. Your customer’s BGP settings are:  
  
- Customer BGP address: `169.254.11.1/30`  
- Customer ASN: `64515`  
- Google Cloud BGP address: `169.254.11.2`  
- Google Cloud ASN: `64517`  
- MD5 Authentication: Disabled  
  
You need to configure the local BGP session for this tunnel using the settings supplied by the third-party customer. You have already associated the Cloud Router with the Cloud VPN Tunnel. What should you do?

options.text: Create a BGP session with these settings:• Peer ASN: 64517• Advertise Route Priority (MED): 100• Local BGP IP: 169.254.11.2• Peer BGP IP: 169.254.11.1• MD5 Authentication: Disabled.
Create a BGP session with these settings:• Peer ASN: 64515• Advertise Route Priority (MED): 100• Local BGP IP: 169.254.11.1• Peer BGP IP: 169.254.11.2• MD5 Authentication: Disabled.
Create a BGP session with these settings:• Peer ASN: 64515• Advertise Route Priority (MED): 100• Local BGP IP: 169.254.11.2• Peer BGP IP: 169.254.11.1• MD5 Authentication: Disabled.
Create a BGP session with these settings:• Peer ASN: 64515• Advertise Route Priority (MED): 1000• Local BGP IP: 169.254.11.2• Peer BGP IP: 169.254.11.1• MD5 Authentication: Enabled.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Router BGP peer uses the remote router’s ASN as the peer ASN, the Cloud Router’s assigned address as the local BGP IP, and the customer router’s assigned address as the peer BGP IP. Thus, the session requires peer ASN `64515`, local IP `169.254.11.2`, peer IP `169.254.11.1`, and disabled MD5 authentication. Google Cloud documentation specifies that the Cloud Router peer ASN matches the on-premises router ASN and that the Cloud Router BGP IP is the address assigned to the Cloud Router interface.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot BGP sessions | Cloud Router](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/support/troubleshoot-bgp-sessions) · [Establish BGP sessions | Cloud Router](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/configuring-bgp)

questions.domain: Configuring, implementing and managing a cloud network security solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has a multi-VPC architecture that isolates its production, development, and testing environments. After a recent security mandate, you must ensure that all Compute Engine VMs in multiple production VPCs can access Google APIs, including Cloud Storage and Cloud SQL, without any route pointing to the internet gateway, in compliance with security policies. The solution must also be scalable and simple to manage across all VPCs.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway in each VPC region to provide a secure egress point for traffic destined for Google APIs.
Configure VPC Service Controls, and create a service perimeter that includes all relevant projects and the required Google services on each VPC.
Enable Private Google Access on all subnets where the VMs are located. Create a private zone in Cloud DNS for googleapis.com, with an A record pointing to 199.36.153.8/30.
Create a Private Service Connect endpoint for Google APIs in each of the VPCs. Create a private zone in Cloud DNS for googleapis.com, with an A record pointing to the PSC endpoint created.

questions.explanation:
A Private Service Connect endpoint for Google APIs gives each VPC a private internal endpoint for services such as Cloud Storage and Cloud SQL. Private DNS can resolve the standard `googleapis.com` names to that endpoint, keeping API traffic private and avoiding a route to the default internet gateway. This supports isolated production VPCs while using a consistent endpoint-and-DNS pattern in each VPC.

**Learn more:** [Access Google APIs through endpoints](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-service-connect-apis) · [Configure Private Google Access](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access)

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have the networking configuration illustrated below. Two VLAN attachments, associated with two Dedicated Interconnect connections, terminate on the same Cloud Router (`mycloudrouter`). The Interconnect connections terminate on two different on-premises routers. You advertise the same prefixes through the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) sessions associated with each VLAN attachment.  
  
You observe asymmetric traffic flow between the two Interconnect connections. Which of the following actions should you take to troubleshoot the asymmetric traffic flow?  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783862102499-a8tr1a19.png)

options.text: From the Google Cloud console, navigate to Cloud Logging to view VPC Flow Logs and review the results.
From the Cloud CLI, run gcloud compute –-project PROJECT_ID routers get-status mycloudrouter –-region REGION and review the results.
From the Google Cloud console, navigate to the Hybrid Connectivity, select the Cloud Router, and view BGP sessions.
From the Cloud CLI, run gcloud compute routers describe mycloudrouter –-region REGION and review the results.

questions.explanation:
`gcloud compute routers get-status` exposes Cloud Router runtime status, including BGP-peer status plus advertised, learned, and best routes. Comparing that output for the two VLAN-attachment peers reveals the route and next-hop selection that can cause traffic to use one Dedicated Interconnect path differently from the other. The `describe` command primarily returns the router configuration rather than this operational route-status data.

**Learn more:** [View router details](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/viewing-router-details) · [Troubleshoot BGP routes and route selection](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/support/troubleshoot-bgp-routes)

Your company’s public domain, `example.com.`, is managed through a public Cloud DNS zone. You need to improve security and safeguard users against DNS spoofing and cache-poisoning attacks. What should you do?

options.text: Request DNSSEC be enabled at your domain registrar, and then import the provided key-signing keys (KSKs) into the Cloud DNS zone.
Attach a Google Cloud Armor security policy to the DNS zone to filter malicious queries and protect against DNS protocol-level attacks.
Use Cloud NGFW network policies to allow only specific DNS domains into the VPC.
Enable DNSSEC on the public Cloud DNS zone, and add the provided DS records to your domain registrar.

questions.explanation:
DNSSEC authenticates DNS responses and protects against manipulation and cache poisoning. Enabling DNSSEC on the public Cloud DNS zone causes Cloud DNS to sign the zone and manage DNSSEC keys; publishing the Cloud DNS-provided DS records at the domain registrar establishes the DNSSEC chain of trust from the parent zone.

**Learn more:** [DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/dnssec) · [Activate DNSSEC](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/registrars?hl=en)

You have multiple microservices running in a private subnet within an existing Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). You need to create additional serverless services using Cloud Run and Cloud Functions that can access those microservices. Network traffic between the serverless services and the private microservices is low. However, every serverless service must be able to communicate with any microservice. You want to implement the lowest-cost solution. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy your serverless services to the serverless VPC. Peer the serverless service VPC to the existing VPC. Configure firewall rules to allow traffic between the serverless services and your existing microservices.
Create a serverless VPC access connector for each serverless service. Configure the connectors to allow traffic between the serverless services and your existing microservices.
Deploy your serverless services to the existing VPConfigure firewall rules to allow traffic between the serverless services and your existing microservices.
Create a serverless VPC access connector. Configure the serverless service to use the connector for communication to the microservices.

questions.explanation:
A single Serverless VPC Access connector attached to the existing VPC can route the serverless services’ private-network traffic to the microservices. Connectors can be reused by multiple services, and because connectors incur charges, using one shared connector avoids the unnecessary cost of a separate connector for each service.

**Learn more:** [VPC with connectors | Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/vpc-connectors) · [Send serverless traffic to a VPC network](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/serverless-vpc-access)

You create multiple Compute Engine virtual machine instances to use as TFTP servers.  
  
Which type of load balancer should you use?

options.text: HTTP(S) load balancer
SSL proxy load balancer
TCP proxy load balancer
Network load balancer

questions.explanation:
TFTP communicates over UDP. A Network Load Balancer supports UDP traffic to Compute Engine virtual machine backends; HTTP(S), SSL proxy, and TCP proxy load balancers are not appropriate for UDP-based TFTP traffic.\
\
**Learn more:** [Cloud Load Balancing overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/load-balancing-overview) · [Use UDP with regional external passthrough Network Load Balancers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/network/udp-with-network-load-balancing)

options.text: Update the TTL for the zone.
Set the zone to the TRANSFER state.
Disable DNSSEC at your domain registrar.
Transfer ownership of the domain to a new registrar.

questions.explanation:
The DS records that establish the DNSSEC chain of trust for a delegated domain reside in the parent zone and are managed through the domain registrar. If those records remain active while the Cloud DNS zone is no longer signed, validating resolvers expect valid DNSSEC signatures and fail resolution. Deactivate DNSSEC at the domain registrar to remove the parent-zone DS records.

**Learn more:** [Activate DNSSEC — Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/registrars) · [Manage DNSSEC configuration — Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/dnssec-config)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have several VMs in multiple VPCs in your cloud environment that need access to internet endpoints. Because security policies prohibit public IP addresses on these VMs, you plan to use Cloud NAT for outbound internet connectivity. Each VPC has several subnets in every region. You need to ensure that only particular subnets can access the internet through Cloud NAT. You also want to prevent unintended configuration changes by other administrators and follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a firewall rule in each VPC at priority 500 that targets all instances in the network and denies egress to the internet, 0.0.0.0/0. Create a firewall rule at priority 300 that targets all instances in the network, has a source filter that maps to the allowed subnets, and allows egress to the internet, 0.0.0.0/0. Deploy Cloud NAT, and configure all primary and secondary subnet source ranges.

Create a constraints/compute.restrictCloudNATUsage organizational policy constraint. Attach the constraint to a folder that contains the associated projects. Configure the allowedValues to only contain the subnets that should have internet access. Deploy Cloud NAT and select only the allowed subnets.

Create a firewall rule in each VPC at priority 500 that targets all instances in the network and denies egress to the internet, 0.0.0.0/0. Create a firewall rule at priority 300 that targets all instances in the network, has a source filter that maps to the allowed subnets, and allows egress to the internet, 0.0.0.0/0. Deploy Cloud NAT, and configure a custom source range that includes the allowed subnets.
Deploy Cloud NAT in each VPC, and configure a custom source range that includes the allowed subnets. Configure Cloud NAT rules to only permit the allowed subnets to egress through Cloud NAT.

questions.explanation:
The `constraints/compute.restrictCloudNATUsage` organization-policy constraint defines which subnetworks are allowed to use Cloud NAT. An allowlist applied to the containing folder governs descendant projects, so Cloud NAT configurations that include other subnets are prevented. This gives centralized protection against unintended administrator changes while allowing Cloud NAT to serve the approved subnets.

**Learn more:** [Organization policy constraints for Cloud NAT](https://cloud.google.com/nat/docs/org-policy-constraints) · [Organization Policy constraints reference](https://cloud.google.com/organization-policy/reference/org-policy-constraints)

A media organization hosts its primary news site on Cloud Run. The site is delivered through a global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud CDN enabled to provide fast page-load times for a worldwide audience. A critical correction was recently published to a major news article, but reports indicate that users still see the original, incorrect article version.  
  
The updated content has been confirmed live on the Cloud Run service. You must ensure that all users receive the corrected article immediately, with limited disruption.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Redeploy the Cloud Run service with a new revision.
Update the Time to Live (TTL) for the backend service in the Cloud CDN configuration to 0.
Disable and then re-enable Cloud CDN in the backend service configuration.
Run the gcloud compute url-maps invalidate-cdn-cache command with the path to the updated article.

questions.explanation:
Cloud CDN can invalidate a specific cached object by URL path. Running `gcloud compute url-maps invalidate-cdn-cache` with the updated article’s path instructs Cloud CDN to stop serving that stale cached content, so requests retrieve the corrected version from the origin. [Invalidate cached content | Cloud CDN | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/invalidating-cached-content)

**Learn more:** [Invalidate cached content | Cloud CDN](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/invalidating-cached-content) · [gcloud compute url-maps invalidate-cdn-cache](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/url-maps/invalidate-cdn-cache)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently reviewed user behavior for your primary application, which uses an external global Application Load Balancer, and discovered that erratic spikes in the client request rate were overloading the backend servers.  
  
You need to limit concurrent sessions and return an HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` response to the client while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Armor security policy, and associate the policy with the load balancer. Configure the security policy's settings as follows: action: throttle; conform action: allow; exceed action: deny-429.

Configure the load balancer to accept only the defined amount of requests per client IP address, increase the backend servers to support more traffic, and redirect traffic to a different backend to burst traffic.
Create a Cloud Armor security policy, and apply the predefined Open Worldwide Security Application Project (OWASP) rules to automatically implement the rate limit per client IP address.
Configure a VM with Linux, implement the rate limit through iptables, and use a firewall rule to send an HTTP 429 response to the client application.

questions.explanation:
A Google Cloud Armor security policy with a `throttle` rate-limiting rule protects backend services from erratic client-request spikes. Requests within the configured threshold use the required `allow` conform action, while requests above the threshold can use `deny-429`, which returns HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. Google Cloud documents this configuration for per-client rate limiting.

**Learn more:** [Configure rate limiting | Google Cloud Armor](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/configure-rate-limiting) · [Rate limiting overview | Google Cloud Armor](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/rate-limiting-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has five separate VPCs, in different projects within your Google Cloud organization, that require high-throughput connectivity. An audit of IP address utilization in every VPC found two overlapping subnets used by two VPCs: `240.0.0.0/16` and `240.128.0.0/24`.  
  
You have confirmed that no Class E subnets (`240.0.0.0/4`) need inter-VPC connectivity, but every other subnet in the VPCs requires connectivity. You need to deploy a Google Cloud routing solution that meets these connectivity requirements. What should you do?

options.text: Create a full mesh of VPC Network Peering connections between all five VPCs. Make sure not to import or export subnet routes with public IP addresses. Add Cloud network firewall policy rules to allow traffic.

Create a Network Connectivity Center hub with a mesh topology. Add a VPC spoke for each of the five VPCs and configure an export exclude filter for 240.0.0.0/4. Add Cloud network firewall policy rules to allow traffic.

Create a series of multiple network interface VMs with an interface in each VPPlace the VMs in an instance group. Create an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer in each VPC with the backend of the instance group. Configure custom static routes in each VPC with the next hop of the respective load balancer. Add Cloud network firewall policy rules to allow traffic.
Create a full mesh of VPC Network Peering connections between all five VPCs with an export exclude filter for 240.0.0.0/4 on every side. Add Cloud network firewall policy rules to allow traffic.

questions.explanation:
A Network Connectivity Center hub with mesh topology provides managed any-to-any connectivity among VPC spokes. VPC spokes cannot export conflicting subnet ranges into the same hub, but an export exclude filter can prevent the Class E `240.0.0.0/4` range from being advertised, eliminating the `240.0.0.0/16` and `240.128.0.0/24` conflict while allowing the remaining required ranges to exchange routes. VPC Network Peering rejects overlapping subnet ranges and has no granular control for excluding specific subnet routes.

**Learn more:** [Network Connectivity Center VPC spoke administration overview](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/vpc-spoke-admin) · [Network Connectivity Center spoke filters overview](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/spoke-filters-overview)

Your company runs applications on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), and the team recently created a private Cloud DNS zone, `corp.internal`, for records used by internal services, including a managed database at `db.corp.internal`. You confirmed that a Compute Engine VM in the same VPC as the GKE cluster can resolve `db.corp.internal` successfully. However, from a Pod in the GKE cluster, you can resolve in-cluster services (for example, `kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`), but every attempt to resolve `db.corp.internal` fails.  
  
After inspecting the `coredns` ConfigMap in the `kube-system` namespace, you find that the default `forward` plugin was changed to point directly to a public DNS provider IP address, bypassing the node-local resolver. You must allow Pods in the cluster to resolve records in the existing `corp.internal` private zone and in other zones beneath `.internal`.

options.text: Modify the coredns ConfigMap in the kube-system namespace, and add corp.internal to a stubDomains entry that points to the VPC’s DNS resolver.
Create a Kubernetes service and endpoint of type ExternalName for db.corp.internal.
Enable Cloud DNS for GKE for the GKE cluster.
Modify the coredns ConfigMap in the kube-system namespace. In the Corefile configuration, change the forward plugin to point to /etc/resolv.conf.

questions.explanation:
CoreDNS must forward non-cluster DNS queries through the node’s `/etc/resolv.conf` resolver so that queries use the VPC DNS path. That resolver can resolve Cloud DNS private zones associated with the VPC and Google internal `.internal` names, whereas a public DNS provider cannot resolve those private names.

**Learn more:** [About kube-dns for GKE](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/kube-dns) · [Overview of internal DNS](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/internal-dns?hl=en)
