questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must establish network connectivity among three Virtual Private Cloud networks—Sales, Marketing, and Finance—so users can access resources in all three VPCs. You configure VPC peering between the Sales VPC and the Finance VPC. You also configure VPC peering between the Marketing VPC and the Finance VPC. After completing the configuration, some users cannot connect to resources in the Sales VPC and the Marketing VPC. You want to fix the issue.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure VPC peering in a full mesh.
Alter the routing table to resolve the asymmetric route.
Create network tags to allow connectivity between all three VPCs.
Delete the legacy network and recreate it to allow transitive peering.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud VPC Network Peering provides connectivity only between the two VPC networks in a peering relationship; it does not support transitive routing through a third VPC. A direct Sales–Marketing peering is therefore required, resulting in a full-mesh topology among the three VPCs.

**Learn more:** [VPC Network Peering](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are setting up a hybrid connection between your on-premises data center and Google Cloud. You configured a Cloud DNS private zone and an inbound server policy in your primary VPC so that on-premises hosts can resolve private DNS zones hosted in Google Cloud, such as `vm.gcp.corp.internal`. The inbound server policy has been assigned an IP address, and you configured your on-premises DNS servers to conditionally forward requests for the `gcp.corp.internal` domain to that IP.  
  
From your on-premises network, you can confirm that routes for the inbound forwarding addresses were learned as expected, and that response traffic is properly routed through your on-premises edge firewall to GCP. However, all DNS queries from on-premises clients for this domain time out, and they cannot resolve the addresses of any Google Cloud resources.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a firewall rule on your on-premises firewall to allow traffic on TCP:53 and UDP:53 from the on-premises IP address range to Cloud DNS inbound server policy IP addresses.
Ensure the Cloud DNS API is enabled in the project that contains your primary VPC.
Create a Cloud DNS peering connection between your VPC and the VPC where the private zone is hosted.
Configure the Cloud DNS outbound server policy with the same IP address as the inbound policy.

questions.explanation:
Cloud DNS automatically accepts TCP and UDP traffic on port 53 at inbound forwarder entry points, but the on-premises edge firewall must allow DNS requests to reach those IP addresses. Permit both UDP/53 and TCP/53 from the on-premises DNS/client address range to the Cloud DNS inbound server policy IP addresses.

**Learn more:** [Configure DNS server policies](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/policies)

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An HTTP(S) load balancer has been deployed, but health checks to port 80 on the Compute Engine virtual machine instance are failing and no traffic is being sent to the instances. You need to fix the issue. Which command should you run?

options.text: gcloud compute instances add-access-config instance-1
gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-lb --network load-balancer --allow tcp --destination-ranges 130.211.0.0/22,35.191.0.0/16 --direction EGRESS
gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-lb --network load-balancer --allow tcp --source-ranges 130.211.0.0/22,35.191.0.0/16 --direction INGRESS
gcloud compute health-checks update http health-check --unhealthy-threshold 10

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud load-balancer health checks require an ingress allow firewall rule that permits probe traffic to the backend instances. For an HTTP(S) load balancer, allowing TCP traffic from `130.211.0.0/22` and `35.191.0.0/16` lets the health-check systems reach port 80 on the VMs.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Load Balancing firewall rules](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/firewall-rules)

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are configuring a Dedicated Interconnect connection from your organization’s on-premises data center in Frankfurt, Germany, to the `europe-west3` region, which is also within the Frankfurt metropolitan area. The AI team lead has expressed concern about connectivity to the `europe-west4` region because the team wants to use Google Cloud TPUs for its workloads. You must ensure low-latency network connectivity for the team’s workloads while minimizing costs and operational overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Set up the Dedicated Interconnect connection towards the europe-west4 region instead of the europe-west3 region.
Set up an additional Partner Interconnect connection between your data center and the europe-west4 region.
Set up a remote VLAN attachment to the europe-west4 region on the Dedicated Interconnect connection.
Use Cloud VPN instead of Dedicated Interconnect to send traffic over the internet.

questions.explanation:
A remote VLAN attachment can be created on an existing Dedicated Interconnect connection for a Cloud Router in a different region, enabling private connectivity from the on-premises network to `europe-west4` without provisioning another Interconnect connection. This provides connectivity to TPU-supported `europe-west4` while minimizing additional cost and operational work.

**Learn more:** [Create VLAN attachments for Dedicated Interconnect](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/creating-vlan-attachments) · [Dedicated Interconnect overview](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/dedicated-overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is transitioning to a hybrid cloud environment and must connect two on-premises data centers to Google Cloud. The company has selected **no service level agreement (SLA)** for the Dedicated Interconnect ports.  
  
You configure a single Dedicated Interconnect for each on-premises data center to connect to Google Cloud: one Dedicated Interconnect in `us-east1` and another in `us-west1`. You also configure a Cloud Router for each Dedicated Interconnect in its respective region.  
  
You now need to configure the Interconnect attachments to achieve as much high-availability diversity as possible with this design. What should you do?

options.text: • Build one VLAN attachment from each Dedicated Interconnect corresponding to the Cloud Router in that region.• Enable global routing at the VPC layer.
• Build one VLAN attachment from each Dedicated Interconnect corresponding to the Cloud Router in that region.• Enable regional routing at the VPC layer.

• Build two VLAN attachments from each Dedicated Interconnect: one connecting to the Cloud Router in us-east1, and one connecting to the Cloud Router in us-west1.• Enable regional routing at the VPC layer.

• Build two VLAN attachments from each Dedicated Interconnect: one connecting to the Cloud Router in us-east1, and one connecting to the Cloud Router in us-west1.• Enable global routing at the VPC layer.

questions.explanation:
A VLAN attachment associates a Dedicated Interconnect connection with a Cloud Router. Creating an attachment from each interconnect connection to both regional Cloud Routers provides the greatest available path diversity across the two connections and regions. A VPC network must use global dynamic routing when a VLAN attachment is located in a different Google Cloud region than its Dedicated Interconnect connection.

**Learn more:** [Create VLAN attachments for Dedicated Interconnect](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/creating-vlan-attachments) · [Dedicated Interconnect overview](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/dedicated-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company recently established a Cloud VPN tunnel between its on-premises data center and its Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). You must configure Cloud Functions API access for on-premises servers. The configuration must satisfy these requirements:  
  
- Certain data must remain in the project where it is stored and must not be exfiltrated to other projects.  
- Traffic from data-center servers using RFC 1918 addresses must not traverse the internet to reach Google Cloud APIs.  
- All DNS resolution must occur on-premises.  
- The solution must provide access only to APIs compatible with VPC Service Controls.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create an A record for private.googleapis.com using the 199.36.153.8/30 address range.2. Create a CNAME record for *.googleapis.com that points to the A record.3. Configure your on-premises routers to use the Cloud VPN tunnel as the next hop for the addresses you used in the A record.4. Remove the default internet gateway from the VPC where your Cloud VPN tunnel terminates.

Configure your on-premises routers to use the Cloud VPN tunnel as the next hop for the addresses you used in the A record.4. Configure your on-premises firewalls to allow traffic to the restricted.googleapis.com addresses.

Configure your on-premises routers to use the Cloud VPN tunnel as the next hop for the addresses you used in the A record.4. `restricted.googleapis.com` provides access only to Google APIs and services supported by VPC Service Controls, providing additional mitigation against data exfiltration. It uses the `199.36.153.4/30` VIP range. Mapping `*.googleapis.com` to this endpoint in on-premises DNS and routing that range through the Cloud VPN keeps API traffic off the public internet; the on-premises firewall must allow outbound traffic to the restricted VIP addresses and established return traffic.

You are designing a new connectivity solution between your organization's on-premises data center and its Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network. There is currently no end-to-end connectivity. You must provide a service level agreement (SLA) of 99.99% availability. What should you do?

options.text: Use one Dedicated Interconnect connection in a single metropolitan area. Configure one Cloud Router and enable global routing in the VPC.
Use a Direct Peering connection between your on-premises data center and Google Cloud. Configure Classic VPN with two tunnels and one Cloud Router.
Use two Dedicated Interconnect connections in a single metropolitan area. Configure one Cloud Router and enable global routing in the VPC.

Use HA VPN. Configure one tunnel from each interface of the VPN gateway to connect to the corresponding interfaces on the peer gateway on-premises. Configure one Cloud Router and enable global routing in the VPC.

questions.explanation:
HA VPN provides a 99.99% availability SLA when tunnels are configured on both HA VPN gateway interfaces. For an on-premises peer gateway with corresponding interfaces, one tunnel must connect interface 0 to interface 0 and another must connect interface 1 to interface 1. Cloud Router provides the dynamic BGP routing used by HA VPN; enabling global routing makes learned routes available across the VPC network.

**Learn more:** [HA VPN topologies](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/topologies) · [Cloud VPN Service Level Agreement (SLA)](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/sla)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has deployed 2,000 virtual machines (VMs) in the private subnet of its Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) in the `us-east1` region. Each VM must have at least 128 TCP connections to a public repository so users can download software updates and packages from the internet.  
  
You need to implement a Cloud NAT gateway so the VMs can perform outbound NAT to the internet. Ensure that every VM can connect to the public repository and download software updates and packages simultaneously.  
  
Which two methods can accomplish this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Configure the NAT gateway in manual allocation mode, allocate 2 NAT IP addresses, and update the minimum number of ports per VM to 256.
Create a second Cloud NAT gateway with the default minimum number of ports configured per VM to 64.
Use the default Cloud NAT gateway's NAT proxy to dynamically scale using a single NAT IP address.
Use the default Cloud NAT gateway to automatically scale to the required number of NAT IP addresses, and update the minimum number of ports per VM to 128.
Configure the NAT gateway in manual allocation mode, allocate 4 NAT IP addresses, and update the minimum number of ports per VM to 128.

questions.explanation:
Each Cloud NAT IP address supplies 64,512 TCP source ports. Supporting 2,000 VMs with a minimum allocation of 128 ports each requires 256,000 ports. Four manually allocated NAT IP addresses provide 258,048 ports, satisfying that capacity. With automatic NAT IP address allocation, Cloud NAT automatically obtains the required number of external IP addresses when the minimum ports per VM is increased to 128.

**Learn more:** [IP addresses and ports | Cloud NAT](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/ports-and-addresses)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to design the technical architecture for hybrid connectivity from your data center to Google Cloud, managed by a partner. You want to follow Google-recommended practices for production-level applications. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the partner to install two security appliances in the data center. Configure one VPN connection from each of these devices to Google Cloud, and ensure that the VPN devices on-premises are in separate racks on separate power and cooling systems.

Configure two Partner Interconnect connections in one metropolitan area (metro). Make sure the Interconnect connections are placed in different metro edge availability domains. Configure two VLAN attachments in a single region, and configure regional dynamic routing on the VPC.

Configure two Partner Interconnect connections in one metro and two connections in another metro. Make sure the Interconnect connections are placed in different metro edge availability domains. Configure two VLAN attachments in one region and two VLAN attachments in another region, and configure global dynamic routing on the VPC.

Configure two Partner Interconnect connections in one metro and two connections in another metro. Make sure the Interconnect connections are placed in different metro edge availability domains. Configure two VLAN attachments in one region and two VLAN attachments in another region, and configure regional dynamic routing on the VPC.

questions.explanation:
Google’s recommended 99.99% availability topology for production Partner Interconnect uses four VLAN attachments across two metros, with connections in separate edge availability domains, two Cloud Routers in separate Google Cloud regions, and global dynamic routing enabled on the VPC. This provides redundant paths across both metro and regional failures.

**Learn more:** [Partner Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/partner-overview) · [Establish 99.99% availability for Partner Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/tutorials/partner-creating-9999-availability?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage the static assets for your company’s global website. Users have reported slow loading times when visiting the website. You need to create a scalable solution that improves website load times for users worldwide. You must also reduce the direct-access load on the Cloud Storage bucket where the website’s static assets are stored. What should you do?

options.text: Configure an internal Application HTTPS Load Balancer in front of the Cloud Storage bucket and enable Cloud CDN on the storage bucket.
Deploy a Global external Application HTTPS Load Balancer, configure a backend bucket pointing to your Cloud Storage bucket, and enable Cloud CDN on the backend bucket.
Deploy a Global external Application HTTPS Load Balancer with a Private Service Connect backend pointing to the Cloud Storage API.
Create a new Compute Engine instance, host the static assets on it, frontend the VM with a load balancer and then enable Cloud CDN directly on the backend service of the load balancer.

questions.explanation:
A global external Application HTTPS Load Balancer can use a Cloud Storage bucket as a backend bucket. Enabling Cloud CDN on that backend bucket caches static assets at globally distributed edge locations, improving delivery latency for worldwide users and reducing requests that reach the Cloud Storage origin bucket.

**Learn more:** [Set up a global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud Storage buckets](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/https/setup-global-ext-https-buckets) · [Backend buckets overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/backend-bucket)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are the network administrator accountable for hybrid connectivity in your organization. Your developer team plans to use Cloud SQL in the `us-west1` region in your Shared VPC. You configured a Dedicated Interconnect connection and a Cloud Router in `us-west1`, and connectivity between your Shared VPC and on-premises data center is functioning as expected. You have just created the private services access connection required for Cloud SQL by using the reserved IP address range and default settings. However, your developers cannot access the Cloud SQL instance from on-premises. You want to fix the issue. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Modify the VPC Network Peering connection used for Cloud SQL, and enable the import and export of routes.2. Create a custom route advertisement in your Cloud Router to advertise the Cloud SQL IP address range.
1. Change the VPC routing mode to global.2. Create a custom route advertisement in your Cloud Router to advertise the Cloud SQL IP address range.

1. Create an additional Cloud Router in us-west2.2. Create a new Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) peering connection to your on-premises data center.3. Modify the VPC Network Peering connection used for Cloud SQL, and enable the import and export of routes.
1. Change the VPC routing mode to global.2. Modify the VPC Network Peering connection used for Cloud SQL, and enable the import and export of routes.

questions.explanation:
Private services access is implemented with VPC Network Peering. To support on-premises hosts, the private-services-access peering must export custom routes so the service producer can return traffic to the on-premises network. The prefixes containing the allocated private services access range must also be advertised to the on-premises network; a Cloud Router custom route advertisement provides that route.

**Learn more:** [Configure private services access](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-services-access) · [Configure private services access for Cloud SQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/configure-private-services-access)

options.text: Enable firewall logging, and forward all filtered egress firewall logs to the IDS.
Enable VPC Flow Logs. Create a sink in Cloud Logging to send filtered egress VPC Flow Logs to the IDS.
Create an internal TCP/UDP load balancer for Packet Mirroring, and add a packet mirroring policy filter for egress traffic.
Create an internal HTTP(S) load balancer for Packet Mirroring, and add a packet mirroring policy filter for egress traffic.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Packet Mirroring copies VM packet payloads to collector instances, enabling an IDS to inspect egress traffic. The collector destination must be behind an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer, and a packet-mirroring filter can select egress-only traffic. Firewall logs and VPC Flow Logs provide logging metadata rather than packet payloads, while an internal HTTP(S) load balancer is not a supported Packet Mirroring collector destination.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Packet Mirroring](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/packet-mirroring)

Your organization’s security team has recently identified a high risk of malicious activity originating from some internet-connected VMs. These activities currently go undetected when TLS communication is used. You must make sure that encrypted traffic destined for the internet is inspected. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Cloud Armor TLS inspection policy, and associate the policy with the backend VMs.

Use Cloud NGFW Essentials. Create a firewall rule for egress traffic, and enable VPC Flow Logs with the TLS inspect option. Analyze the output logs content and block the outputs that have malicious activities.
Configure a TLS agent on every VM to intercept TLS traffic before it reaches the internet. Configure Sensitive Data Protection to analyze and allow/deny the content.
Use Cloud NGFW Enterprise. Create a firewall rule for egress traffic with the --tls-inspect flag, and associate the firewall rules with the VMs.

questions.explanation:
Cloud NGFW Enterprise supports TLS interception and decryption for selected traffic. An egress firewall policy rule configured with `--tls-inspect` enables inspection of encrypted TLS traffic, allowing Layer 7 security controls such as intrusion detection and prevention to detect malicious activity before the traffic reaches the internet.

**Learn more:** [TLS inspection overview | Cloud Next Generation Firewall](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/about-tls-inspection) · [Set up TLS inspection | Cloud Next Generation Firewall](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/setup-tls-inspection)

questions.domain: Designing and planning a Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Following a network change window, one of your company’s applications stops functioning. The application uses an on-premises database server that no longer receives traffic from the application. The database server IP address is `10.2.1.25`.  
  
You review the change request and find that the only change was creation of three additional VPC subnets:  
  
- `10.1.0.0/16`  
- `10.2.0.0/16`  
- `10.3.1.0/24/`  
  
The on-premises router advertises `10.0.0.0/8`.  
  
What is the most likely cause of this issue?

options.text: The less specific VPC subnet route is taking priority.
The more specific VPC subnet route is taking priority.
The on-premises router is not advertising a route for the database server.
A cloud firewall rule that blocks traffic to the on-premises database server was created during the change.

questions.explanation:
The address `10.2.1.25` is contained in the newly created `10.2.0.0/16` VPC subnet as well as the on-premises `10.0.0.0/8` route. A subnet route is evaluated before custom dynamic routes in Google Cloud VPC, so the more-specific VPC subnet route captures this traffic rather than forwarding it to the on-premises network.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud VPC routes](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/routes)

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You maintain a Shared VPC in a host project. Several departments in your company have infrastructure in separate service projects attached to the Shared VPC and use Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to manage cloud resources in those projects. VPC Network Peering is also configured between the Shared VPC and a common services VPC that is not part of a service project.  
  
Several users are encountering failed connectivity between certain instances in different Shared VPC service projects and between certain instances and the internet. You need to validate the network configuration to determine whether a misconfiguration is the root cause of the issue. What should you do?

options.text: Review the VPC audit logs in Cloud Logging for the affected instances.
Use Secure Shell (SSH) to connect to the affected Compute Engine instances, and run a series of PING tests to the other affected endpoints and the 8.8.8.8 IPv4 address.
Run Connectivity Tests from Network Intelligence Center to check connectivity between the affected endpoints in your network and the internet.
Enable VPC Flow Logs for all VPCs, and review the logs in Cloud Logging for the affected instances.

questions.explanation:
Network Intelligence Center Connectivity Tests analyzes the expected network path and configuration between endpoints, including Shared VPC and VPC Network Peering environments. It evaluates relevant routing and firewall configuration and supports testing connectivity to internet IP addresses, making it appropriate for identifying configuration-caused reachability failures.

**Learn more:** [Connectivity Tests overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/connectivity-tests/concepts/overview) · [Test connectivity within VPC networks](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-intelligence-center/docs/connectivity-tests/concepts/test-within-vpc-networks)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster for your organization. The current cluster is expected to host 10 nodes, with 20 Pods per node and 150 services. Because new services will be migrated during the next 2 years, planned growth is 100 nodes, 200 Pods per node, and 1500 services.  
  
You want to use VPC-native clusters with alias IP ranges while minimizing address consumption. How should you design this topology?

options.text: Create a subnet of size/25 with 2 secondary ranges of: /17 for Pods and /21 for Services. Create a VPC-native cluster and specify those ranges.

Create a subnet of size/28 with 2 secondary ranges of: /24 for Pods and /24 for Services. Create a VPC-native cluster and specify those ranges. When the services are ready to be deployed, resize the subnets.
Use gcloud container clusters create [CLUSTER NAME]--enable-ip-alias to create a VPC-native cluster.
Use gcloud container clusters create [CLUSTER NAME] to create a VPC-native cluster.

questions.explanation:
A /25 primary subnet supports the planned node count, while a /17 secondary range provides 32,768 Pod addresses and a /21 secondary range provides 2,048 Service addresses. These ranges exceed the planned requirements of 20,000 Pods and 1,500 Services without allocating substantially larger ranges. VPC-native GKE clusters use secondary ranges for Pod and Service addresses; the Service secondary range is fixed for the cluster lifetime.

**Learn more:** [VPC-native clusters](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/alias-ips)

What should you do in the GCP Console?

options.text: Create a new cloud storage bucket, and then enable Cloud CDN on it.
Create a new TCP load balancer, select the storage bucket as a backend, and then enable Cloud CDN on the backend.
Create a new SSL proxy load balancer, select the storage bucket as a backend, and then enable Cloud CDN on the backend.
Create a new HTTP load balancer, select the storage bucket as a backend, enable Cloud CDN on the backend, and make sure each object inside the storage bucket is shared publicly.

A Cloud Storage bucket is attached as a backend bucket to an external HTTP(S) Application Load Balancer, where Cloud CDN is enabled on that backend bucket. Public read access for each object allows the CDN-enabled load balancer to retrieve and serve all bucket objects.

You are migrating a three-tier application architecture from on premises to Google Cloud. As an initial migration step, you want to create a new Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) with an external HTTP(S) load balancer. The load balancer will send traffic back to the on-premises compute resources running the presentation tier. You must prevent malicious traffic from entering your VPC and using edge resources, so configure a policy that filters IP addresses and blocks cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Google Cloud Armor policy, and apply it to a backend service that uses an unmanaged instance group backend.
Create a hierarchical firewall ruleset, and apply it to the VPC's parent organization resource node.
Create a Google Cloud Armor policy, and apply it to a backend service that uses an internet network endpoint group (NEG) backend.
Create a VPC firewall ruleset, and apply it to all instances in unmanaged instance groups.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Armor security policies enforce IP-based Layer 7 filtering and preconfigured WAF rules, including protection against XSS, at the Google Cloud edge. For a hybrid deployment whose application backend remains outside Google Cloud, the external Application Load Balancer uses an internet NEG; attaching the policy to that backend service inspects requests before they are sent to the external backend.

**Learn more:** [Integrate Cloud Armor with hybrid deployments](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/integrating-cloud-armor?hl=en) · [Cloud Armor overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/cloud-armor-overview?hl=en)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are expanding your use of Cloud VPN between on-premises and GCP and need to handle more traffic than one tunnel supports. You want to increase the available bandwidth with Cloud VPN.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Double the MTU on your on-premises VPN gateway from 1460 bytes to 2920 bytes.
Create two VPN tunnels on the same Cloud VPN gateway that point to the same destination VPN gateway IP address.

Add a second on-premises VPN gateway with a different public IP address. Create a second tunnel on the existing Cloud VPN gateway that forwards the same IP range, but points at the new on-premises gateway IP.

Add a second Cloud VPN gateway in a different region than the existing VPN gateway. Create a new tunnel on the second Cloud VPN gateway that forwards the same IP range, but points to the existing on-premises VPN gateway IP address.

questions.explanation:
Cloud VPN can increase aggregate throughput by using multiple load-balanced tunnels. In the Classic VPN topology, this requires distinct peer VPN gateway external IP addresses; adding a second on-premises VPN gateway and creating a tunnel to its different public IP provides an additional tunnel for the same IP range.

**Learn more:** [Classic VPN topologies](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/classic-topologies) · [Add a VPN tunnel](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/how-to/adding-a-tunnel)

You are migrating to Cloud DNS and need to import your BIND zone file.  
  
Which command should you use?

options.text: gcloud dns record-sets import ZONE_FILE --zone MANAGED_ZONE
gcloud dns record-sets import ZONE_FILE --replace-origin-ns --zone MANAGED_ZONE
gcloud dns record-sets import ZONE_FILE --zone-file-format --zone MANAGED_ZONE

questions.explanation:
The `--zone-file-format` flag tells `gcloud dns record-sets import` that the input records file uses BIND zone-file format; without it, the command assumes YAML format. [`gcloud dns record-sets import`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/dns/record-sets/import)\
\

questions.question:
You are migrating to Cloud DNS and need to import your BIND zone file.  
  
Which command should you use?

options.text: Configure Packet Mirroring to match the source/destination IP addresses of the VMs.
Configure a firewall rule to match the source/destination IP addresses of the VMs, and use the goto_next action.
Configure a firewall rule to match the hostnames of the VMs, and use the apply_security_profile_group action.
Configure a firewall rule to match the source/destination IP addresses of the VMs, and use the apply_security_profile_group action.

questions.explanation:
Cloud NGFW Enterprise sends matching traffic to a firewall endpoint for Layer 7 inspection when a firewall policy rule uses the `apply_security_profile_group` action. Matching that rule on the VMs’ source and destination IP addresses directs the intended VM traffic to the security profile group for IPS inspection.

**Learn more:** [Intrusion detection and prevention service overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/about-intrusion-prevention) · [Global network firewall policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/network-firewall-policies)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],The organization uses a Shared VPC model. Service project owners need to manage their own DNS zones independently within service projects. Every service project workload must be able to resolve every private zone defined in other service projects. You need to create a solution that fulfills these requirements. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud DNS private zone in each service project. Use a Cloud DNS forwarding zone to forward queries to the Shared VPC in the host project.
Create a Cloud DNS private zone in each service project. Use Cloud DNS peering zones that target the Shared VPC in the host project.
Create a Cloud DNS response policy zone in each service project. Use Cloud DNS peering zones that target the Shared VPC in the host project.
Create a Cloud DNS private zone in each service project. Use cross-project binding to associate the zones to the Shared VPC in the host project.

questions.explanation:
Cross-project binding lets each service project create and administer its own Cloud DNS private zone while binding that zone directly to the Shared VPC network owned by the host project. Because all zones are associated with the same Shared VPC network, workloads in every service project using that network can resolve all of the private zones. [Cloud DNS zones overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones/zones-overview)

**Learn more:** [Cloud DNS zones overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones/zones-overview) · [Create a zone with cross-project binding](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones/cross-project-binding)

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently configured Google Cloud Armor security policies to control traffic to your application. You find that Google Cloud Armor is mistakenly blocking some application traffic. You need to identify the web application firewall (WAF) rule that is incorrectly blocking the traffic. What should you do?

options.text: Enable firewall logs, and view the logs in Firewall Insights.
Enable HTTP(S) Load Balancing logging with sampling rate equal to 1, and view the logs in Cloud Logging.
Enable VPC Flow Logs, and view the logs in Cloud Logging.
Enable Google Cloud Armor audit logs, and view the logs on the Activity page in the Google Cloud Console.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Armor writes per-request security-policy enforcement data to HTTP(S) Load Balancer logs in Cloud Logging. These records include the matched policy, rule priority, configured action, and outcome. Enabling load-balancer logging with a sampling rate of 1 ensures that every request is logged, making it possible to find the WAF rule that denied valid traffic.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Armor per-request logging](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/request-logging) · [Troubleshoot Cloud Armor issues](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/troubleshooting)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to build the network infrastructure to deploy a highly available web application across the `us-east1` and `us-west1` regions. The application runs on Compute Engine instances and does not need a database. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create one VPC with one subnet in each region.Create a regional network load balancer in each region with a static IP address.Enable Cloud CDN on the load balancers.Create an A record in Cloud DNS with both IP addresses for the load balancers.

Create one VPC with one subnet in each region.Create a global load balancer with a static IP address.Enable Cloud CDN and Google Cloud Armor on the load balancer.Create an A record using the IP address of the load balancer in Cloud DNS.
Create one VPC in each region, and peer both VPCs.Create a global load balancer.Enable Cloud CDN on the load balancer.Create a CNAME for the load balancer in Cloud DNS.

Create one VPC with one subnet in each region.Create an HTTP(S) load balancer with a static IP address.Choose the standard tier for the network.Enable Cloud CDN on the load balancer.Create a CNAME record using the load balancer’s IP address in Cloud DNS.

questions.explanation:
A global external Application Load Balancer provides a single global anycast IP address and distributes HTTP(S) traffic across healthy Compute Engine backends in multiple regions. It supports Cloud CDN and Google Cloud Armor. A Cloud DNS A record maps the application hostname to the load balancer’s static IPv4 address.

**Learn more:** [External Application Load Balancer overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/https) · [Cloud Load Balancing overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/load-balancing-overview)

You are designing a geo-redundant Partner Interconnect hybrid-cloud connectivity solution across two metropolitan areas. You want to follow Google-recommended practices for the following region/metro pairs:  
  
- (region 1/metro 1)  
- (region 2/metro 2)  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Router in region 1 with two VLAN attachments connected to metro1-zone1-x.Create a Cloud Router in region 2 with two VLAN attachments connected to metro1-zone2-x.
Create a Cloud Router in region 1 with one VLAN attachment connected to metro1-zone1-x.Create a Cloud Router in region 2 with two VLAN attachments connected to metro2-zone2-x.
Create a Cloud Router in region 1 with one VLAN attachment connected to metro1-zone2-x.Create a Cloud Router in region 2 with one VLAN attachment connected to metro2-zone2-x.

Create a Cloud Router in region 1 with one VLAN attachment connected to metro1-zone1-x and one VLAN attachment connected to metro1-zone2-x.Create a Cloud Router in region 2 with one VLAN attachment connected to metro2-zone1-x and one VLAN attachment to metro2-zone2-x.

questions.explanation:
Partner Interconnect 99.99% availability requires four VLAN attachments spanning two metropolitan areas, with one attachment in each edge availability domain (metro availability zone) in each metro. Each attachment must be associated with a Cloud Router in the corresponding region, so each region requires attachments to both of its metro’s zones.

**Learn more:** [Partner Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/partner-overview) · [Duplicate a VLAN attachment for redundancy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/partner/creating-redundant-vlan-attachments?hl=en)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are configuring a new Cloud Router instance in your Organization's Google Cloud environment to enable connectivity across a new Dedicated Interconnect to your data center. Sales, Marketing, and IT each have a service project attached to the Organization's host project.  
  
Where should you create the Cloud Router instance?

options.text: VPC network in all projects
VPC network in the IT Project
VPC network in the Host Project
VPC network in the Sales, Marketing, and IT Projects

questions.explanation:
For a Cloud Interconnect connection that uses Shared VPC, the VLAN attachment and its associated Cloud Router must be created in the Shared VPC host project. The host project's VPC network is shared with the attached service projects, enabling the Dedicated Interconnect connection to serve their resources.

**Learn more:** [Options for connecting to multiple VPC networks](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/enabling-multiple-networks-access-same-attachment)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are configuring your organization’s Google Cloud environment to connect with your on-premises network, which does not support Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). Your on-premises network contains 30 CIDR ranges that must be reachable from Google Cloud. Your VPN gateway creates a distinct child security association (SA) for each CIDR. You must make sure that the 30 CIDR ranges in your on-premises network can be reached from Google Cloud.  
  
Following Google-recommended practices, which two methods can you use to achieve this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a single Cloud VPN tunnel that uses route-based VPN.
Create a single Cloud VPN tunnel that uses policy-based routing with 30 CIDRs as the remote traffic selectors.

Create multiple Cloud VPN tunnels that use policy-based routing so that each tunnel has one CIDR block for its local traffic selector and one CIDR block for its remote traffic selector. Connect each tunnel to unique peer IP addresses.
Create multiple Cloud VPN tunnels that use policy-based routing with 10 CIDR per tunnel as the remote traffic selectors.

Create multiple Cloud VPN tunnels that use policy-based routing so that each tunnel has one CIDR block for its local traffic selector and one CIDR block for its remote traffic selector. Connect each tunnel to the same peer IP address.

questions.explanation:
Cloud VPN is incompatible with peer VPN gateways that create a separate Child SA for each CIDR when multiple CIDRs are used in a traffic selector. A route-based VPN uses `0.0.0.0/0` traffic selectors and can use more-specific static routes for the 30 remote CIDRs. Another supported strategy is to create multiple policy-based tunnels with one local and one remote CIDR per tunnel; tunnels on the same Classic VPN gateway must connect to unique peer gateway IP addresses.

**Learn more:** [Networks and tunnel routing | Cloud VPN](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/choosing-networks-routing)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have set up a Compute Engine virtual machine instance as a NAT gateway. You run the following command:  
  
```bash  
gcloud compute routes create no-ip-internet-route \  
--network custom-network1 \  
--destination-range 0.0.0.0/0 \  
--next-hop instance nat-gateway \  
--next-hop instance-zone us-central1-a \  
--tags no-ip --priority 800  
```  
  
You want the existing instances to use the new NAT gateway.  
  
Which command should you run?

options.text: sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
gcloud compute instances add-tags [existing-instance] --tags no-ip
gcloud builds submit --config=cloudbuild.waml --substitutions=TAG_NAME=no-ip

gcloud compute instances create example-instance --network custom-network1 \ --subnet subnet-us-central \ --no-address \ --zone us-central1-a \ --image-family debian-9 \ --image-project debian-cloud \ --tags no-ip

questions.explanation:
A custom static route with the `no-ip` network tag applies only to VM instances that have that matching network tag. Adding `no-ip` to each existing instance makes the route to the NAT gateway applicable to its traffic.

**Learn more:** [Use routes](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/using-routes?hl=en) · [gcloud compute instances add-tags](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/instances/add-tags)

questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and troubleshooting network operations
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization’s on-premises networking team reports frequent BGP session flaps to the Google Cloud environment. You need to examine the BGP configuration. What should you do?

options.text: Switch to static routing.
Increase the BGP hold timer to 36000 seconds max.
Ensure that graceful restart is enabled on the on-premises router.
Ask the on-premises team to enable Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD).

questions.explanation:
Enable BGP graceful restart on the on-premises router so it can process Cloud Router graceful-restart notifications and preserve forwarding while the BGP session is re-established during router maintenance or a control-plane restart. Google Cloud identifies graceful-restart support on the on-premises router as a configuration that prevents maintenance-related BGP flaps from causing disruption.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot BGP sessions | Cloud Router | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/support/troubleshoot-bgp-sessions) · [Manage BGP timers | Cloud Router | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/managing-bgp-timers)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],As part of your organization's modernization initiative, the application teams are migrating services to GKE on Google Cloud (GKE). The GKE clusters will reside in service projects. The teams have validated their applications and configurations in sandbox projects. When moving to production, you observed that GKE nodes were not being created. Users could create Compute Engine instances, but the operation failed when they attempted to create a GKE cluster. You need to enable the application teams to create those GKE clusters. What should you do?

options.text: Ensure that the service project's GKE service account has the compute.securityAdmin, container.hostServiceAgentUser and compute.networkUser IAM permissions in the host project.
Ensure that the service project's GKE service account has the compute.securityAdmin, container.hostserviceAgentUser and compute.networkUser IAM permissions in the service project.
Ensure that the service project's GKE service account has the compute.networkUser IAM permission in the service project.
Review the firewall rules configuration in the VPC. Identify what rule is blocking node creation.

questions.explanation:
For GKE clusters in service projects using a Shared VPC, the service project's GKE service account needs access in the host project: Compute Network User to use the host network, Host Service Agent User to perform network-management operations through the host GKE service agent, and Compute Security Admin to create and manage required firewall resources. Granting these roles only in the service project does not authorize use or management of the host-project network.

**Learn more:** [Configure clusters with Shared VPC](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/cluster-shared-vpc)

questions.domain: Designing and planning a Google Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a network administrator at your company who is planning a migration to Google Cloud and must complete the migration as quickly as possible. To simplify the transition, you decided to retain the same architecture as your on-premises network: a hub-and-spoke model.  
  
Your on-premises architecture has more than 50 spokes. No spoke has connectivity to any other spoke, and all traffic is routed through the hub for security reasons. You must ensure that the Google Cloud architecture matches the on-premises architecture. You want to implement a solution that minimizes management overhead and cost while using default networking quotas and limits. What should you do?

options.text: Connect all the spokes to the hub with Cloud VPN.
Connect all the spokes to the hub with VPC Network Peering.
Connect all the spokes to the hub with Cloud VPN. Use a third-party network appliance as a default gateway to prevent connectivity between the spokes.
Connect all the spokes to the hub with VPC Network Peering. Use a third-party network appliance as a default gateway to prevent connectivity between the spokes.

questions.explanation:
More than 50 VPC spokes would require more than 50 peering connections on the hub, which exceeds the default VPC Network Peering quota. A Cloud VPN hub-and-spoke topology can provide the required scale, but Cloud VPN supports transitive routing through the hub. A third-party network appliance acting as the default gateway can enforce the required isolation by blocking spoke-to-spoke traffic while permitting the intended hub-routed traffic.

**Learn more:** [Hub-and-spoke network architecture](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/deploy-hub-spoke-vpc-network-topology) · [VPC quotas and limits](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/quota)

questions.domain: Configuring, implementing and managing a cloud network security solution
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has recently expanded its EMEA-based operations into APAC. Users distributed globally report that their SMTP and IMAP services are slow.  
  
The company requires end-to-end encryption, but you do not have access to the SSL certificates.  
  
Which Google Cloud load balancer should you use?

options.text: SSL proxy load balancer
Network load balancer
HTTPS load balancer
TCP proxy load balancer

questions.explanation:
A TCP proxy load balancer supports non-HTTP TCP services such as SMTP and IMAP and can provide globally distributed traffic handling. It does not need the load balancer to terminate TLS, so the encrypted connection can remain end-to-end to the backend without configuring the service SSL certificates on the load balancer. Target SSL proxies, by contrast, require private keys and SSL certificates.

**Learn more:** [External proxy Network Load Balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/tcp) · [SSL certificates overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/ssl-certificates)

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is connecting its Shared VPC network to its on-premises data center by using Dedicated Interconnect to provide connectivity for all of its service projects. You must create a design to configure the VLAN attachments and Cloud Routers. You also want to attain a 99.9% Cloud Interconnect SLA based on Google Cloud's reference design. What should you do?

options.text: Create two Cloud Interconnect connections in different edge availability domains of two different co-location facilities in a project that will contain your connections. Create one VLAN attachment and Cloud Router for each physical interconnect in the Shared VPC host project.

Create two Interconnect connections in different edge availability domains of the co-location facility in a project that will contain your connections. Create one VLAN attachment for each physical Cloud Interconnect connection and a single Cloud Router in the Shared VPC host project.

Create two Cloud Interconnect connections in different edge availability domains of the co-location facility in a project that will contain your connections. Create one VLAN attachment for each physical interconnect and a single Cloud Router in the service projects.

Create two Cloud Interconnect connections in different edge availability domains of the co-location facility in a project that will contain your connections. Create a Cloud Router in the Shared VPC host project and the VLAN attachments in the Shared VPC service projects.

questions.explanation:
A 99.9% Dedicated Interconnect topology requires at least two connections in a single metro across different edge availability domains, with two VLAN attachments that each depend on a unique connection. At least one Cloud Router is required, and additional Cloud Routers do not improve this SLA. For Shared VPC connectivity, the attachments and Cloud Router are configured for the Shared VPC network in its host project, enabling its service projects to use the connectivity.

**Learn more:** [Establish 99.9% availability for Dedicated Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/tutorials/dedicated-creating-999-availability?hl=en) · [Use Dedicated Interconnect connections in other projects](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/using-interconnects-other-projects)

Your company has deployed a hub-and-spoke architecture in Google Cloud to host its workloads. It uses VPC Network Peering to connect the hub and spokes. You need to reproduce this design by using Network Connectivity Center. What should you do?

options.text: Choose a Network Connectivity Center star topology. Deploy the hub VPC in the center group. Deploy the spoke VPCs in the edge group.
Choose a Network Connectivity Center star topology. Deploy the spoke VPCs in the center group. Deploy the hub VPC in the edge group.
Choose a Network Connectivity Center mesh topology. Configure the hub and the spokes as Network Connectivity Center spokes.
Choose a Network Connectivity Center mesh topology. Configure the spokes as Network Connectivity Center spokes.

questions.explanation:
Network Connectivity Center star topology provides hub-and-spoke routing: the center spoke group can communicate with spokes in either the center or edge group, whereas edge spokes can communicate only with center spokes. Assigning the hub VPC to the center group and workload spoke VPCs to the edge group preserves the intended hub-and-spoke connectivity model.

**Learn more:** [Preset connectivity topologies | Network Connectivity Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/connectivity-topologies?hl=en)

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has one Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network deployed in Google Cloud, with on-premises access provided through Cloud Interconnect connections. The company must send traffic to Cloud Storage only across the Interconnect links, while accessing all other Google APIs and services through the public internet. What should you do?

options.text: Use the default public domains for all Google APIs and services.
Use Private Service Connect to access Cloud Storage, and use the default public domains for all other Google APIs and services.
Use Private Google Access, with restricted.googleapis.com virtual IP addresses for Cloud Storage and private.googleapis.com for all other Google APIs and services.
Use Private Google Access, with private.googleapis.com virtual IP addresses for Cloud Storage and restricted.googleapis.com virtual IP addresses for all other Google APIs and services.

questions.explanation:
A Private Service Connect endpoint for Google APIs gives Cloud Storage an internal IP address that is reachable from an on-premises network through the VPC and Cloud Interconnect. Retaining the default public domains for other Google APIs and services keeps their traffic on public endpoints. The private.googleapis.com and restricted.googleapis.com VIPs are private-access mechanisms, so assigning them to other services would not meet the public-internet requirement.

**Learn more:** [Access Google APIs through endpoints](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-service-connect-apis) · [Configure Private Google Access for on-premises hosts](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access-hybrid)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying HA VPN in Google Cloud and need to dynamically exchange routes between your on-premises gateway and Google Cloud. You have already created an HA VPN gateway and a peer VPN gateway resource. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Router, add VPN tunnels, and configure BGP sessions.
Create a Cloud Router, add VPN tunnels, and configure static routes to your subnet ranges.
Create a second HA VPN gateway, add VPN tunnels, and create firewall rules to allow BGP traffic to the Cloud Router.
Create a second HA VPN gateway, add VPN tunnels, and enable global dynamic routing.

questions.explanation:
HA VPN tunnels must use dynamic BGP routing. Create a Cloud Router, create the VPN tunnels, and configure BGP sessions so Cloud Router can learn and advertise routes with the on-premises gateway.

**Learn more:** [HA VPN topologies](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/topologies) · [Establish BGP sessions](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/how-to/configuring-bgp)

options.text: Create a design that uses the LOCAL_PREF BGP attribute to influence the egress path from Google Cloud to the on-premises environment.
Create a design that uses an equal-cost multipath (ECMP) with flow-based hashing on your on-premises devices.
Create a design that uses a BGP multi-exit discriminator (MED) attribute to influence the egress path from Google Cloud to the on-premises environment.
Create a design that uses the AS_PATH BGP attribute to influence the egress path from Google Cloud to the on-premises environment.

questions.explanation:
For a 99.9% Cloud Interconnect topology, on-premises routers advertise the same prefixes over each VLAN attachment and can use different BGP metrics, such as MED, to control path preference. Advertising a lower MED on the active attachment and a higher MED on the passive attachment makes Google Cloud prefer the active egress path while retaining the other attachment for failover.

**Learn more:** [Establish 99.9% availability for Dedicated Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/tutorials/dedicated-creating-999-availability)

Your organization needs to deploy an internal application named app-1 in VPC-1. The application will consume services from another internal application named app-2 in VPC-2. VPC Network Peering will connect the two applications. You must apply microsegmentation between these applications and VPCs. What should you do?

options.text: Assign network tags to these applications: secure-tag-app-1 to app-1 and secure-tag-app-2 to app-2. Configure a hierarchical firewall policy with an ingress rule that allows traffic from secure-tag-app-1 to secure-tag-app-2. Leave the default deny ingress rule and the default allow egress rule.

Assign secure tags to these applications: secure-tag-app-1 to app-1 and secure-tag-app-2 to app-2. Configure a hierarchical firewall policy with an ingress rule that allows traffic from secure-tag-app-1 to secure-tag-app-2. Leave the default deny ingress rule and the default allow egress rule.

Assign network tags to these applications: secure-tag-app-1 to app-1 and secure-tag-app-2 to app-2. Configure an ingress VPC firewall rule that allows traffic from secure-tag-app-1 to secure-tag-app-2. Leave the default deny ingress rule and the default allow egress rule.

Assign secure tags to these applications: secure-tag-app-1 to app-1 and secure-tag-app-2 to app-2. Configure a network firewall policy that is attached to VPC-2 with an ingress rule that allows traffic from secure-tag-app-1 to secure-tag-app-2. Leave the default deny ingress rule and the default allow egress rule.

questions.explanation:
Secure tags provide IAM-governed workload identity that firewall policies can use as ingress sources and targets. They can identify interfaces in VPC networks connected through VPC Network Peering, whereas network tags are meaningful only within their own VPC network and cannot be used in hierarchical firewall-policy rules. A hierarchical firewall policy using an ingress allow rule from app-1’s secure tag to app-2’s secure tag provides the required cross-VPC microsegmentation; implied ingress deny and egress allow rules preserve the baseline default behavior.

**Learn more:** [Secure tags for firewalls](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/tags-firewalls-overview) · [Hierarchical firewall policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies)

You are designing new network infrastructure for your customer in Google Cloud. The customer requires a connection between two Google Cloud VPCs that includes a VPN tunnel. You want to follow Google-recommended practices while ensuring the connection has maximum availability. Which VPN configuration should you select?

options.text: Policy-based VPN using Classic VPN between the two Google Cloud VPCs
Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)-based VPN using Classic VPN between the two Google Cloud VPCs
Route-based VPN using Classic VPN between the two Google Cloud VPCs
Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)-based VPN using HA VPN between the two Google Cloud VPCs

questions.explanation:
For high availability and a better SLA, Google Cloud recommends HA VPN with BGP. Connecting two VPC networks with HA VPN gateways and redundant BGP VPN tunnels supports the recommended highly available topology and can provide a 99.99% availability SLA. Classic VPN has a single interface and does not provide the same high-availability design.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for Cloud VPN](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/best-practices) · [HA VPN topologies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/topologies)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing your organization's network architecture. The organization has three developer teams: Web, App, and Database. Each developer team requires access to Compute Engine instances to carry out critical tasks. You are on a small network and security team that must provide the developers with network access. You need to retain centralized control of network resources, including subnets, routes, and firewalls. You want to minimize operational overhead. How should you design this topology?

options.text: Configure a host project with a Shared VPC. Create service projects for Web, App, and Database.
Configure one VPC for Web, one VPC for App, and one VPC for Database. Configure HA VPN between each VPC.
Configure three Shared VPC host projects, each with a service project: one for Web, one for App, and one for Database.
Configure one VPC for Web, one VPC for App, and one VPC for Database. Use VPC Network Peering to connect all VPCs in a full mesh.

questions.explanation:
A Shared VPC uses one host project to centrally manage the VPC network, including subnets, routes, and firewall rules, while attaching separate service projects where teams can create and manage eligible resources such as Compute Engine instances. Using one host project with service projects for Web, App, and Database provides centralized network governance without the management overhead of VPN-connected or fully peered VPC networks.

**Learn more:** [Shared VPC | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is designing a landing-zone architecture with these requirements:  
  
- No communication must be possible between production and non-production environments.  
- Communication between applications in the same environment might be needed.  
- Network administrators must centrally manage all network resources, including subnets, routes, and firewall rules.  
- Each application must be billed independently.  
- Developers for an application within a project must be able to create their compute resources, but must not create or modify networking resources.  
- Up to 1000 applications are anticipated per environment.  
  
You need to create a design that meets these requirements. What should you do?

options.text: Create a design that has one Shared VPC host project for the production environment, and another Shared VPC host project for the nonproduction environment. Associate the various applications' service projects with the corresponding environment's host project.
Create a design that has a Shared VPC for each project. Implement hierarchical firewall policies to apply micro-segmentation between VPCs.
Create a design that implements a single Shared VPUse VPC firewall rules with secure tags to enforce micro-segmentation between environments.
Create a design where each project in each environment has its own VPC with its own subnets, routes, and firewall rules. Ensure all VPCs are added as spokes to a Network Connectivity Center hub.

questions.explanation:
Shared VPC lets a host project centrally control VPC networks, subnets, routes, and firewall rules while attached service projects host application resources. Service-project administrators can be granted permission to create compute resources that use approved shared subnets without receiving network-administration permissions. Billing for resources using a Shared VPC is attributed to the service project containing the resource, enabling per-application billing. Separate Shared VPC host projects for production and non-production provide distinct networks, preventing direct communication between those environments; applications attached to the same environment host project can communicate as permitted by centrally managed firewall rules.

**Learn more:** [Shared VPC](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc) · [Decide the network design for your Google Cloud landing zone](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/landing-zones/decide-network-design)

You manage a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster that must communicate with a legacy monitoring service running in your on-premises data center. The on-premises network uses the `192.168.10.0/24` address range and connects to your VPC through Cloud VPN. The legacy monitoring service can accept traffic only from the GKE clusters’ node IP addresses, not Pod IP addresses. You observe that traffic from Pods is failing. You need to ensure that Pod traffic can flow seamlessly to the on-premises network. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a hybrid Cloud NAT gateway on the Cloud Router associated with the Cloud VPN tunnel.
Ensure that the ip-masq-agent is deployed and that 192.168.10.0/24 is not present in the nonMasqueradeCIDRs list in the GKE cluster.
Add 192.168.10.0/24 to the nonMasqueradeCIDRs list in the ip-masq-agent's ConfigMap in the GKE Cluster.
Configure a Public Cloud NAT gateway for the GKE cluster's subnet.

questions.explanation:
The GKE IP masquerade agent performs source NAT for destinations that are not in `nonMasqueradeCIDRs`, changing the Pod source IP to the node’s internal IP. Leaving `192.168.10.0/24` out of that list makes traffic to the on-premises monitoring service originate from a node IP, which meets the service’s source-address requirement. Destinations included in `nonMasqueradeCIDRs` retain Pod source IPs.

**Learn more:** [IP masquerade agent | GKE networking](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ip-masquerade-agent?hl=en) · [Configuring an IP masquerade agent in Standard clusters](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/ip-masquerade-agent)

You are setting up a Cross-Cloud Interconnect connection for your Google Cloud organization with two public cloud service providers (CSPs)—CSP 1 and CSP 2. The CSP 1 and CSP 2 environments are nearest to Frankfurt, Germany. You can select either of two shared colocation locations: Frankfurt or Munich. Your organization's Google Cloud infrastructure is deployed in the North American region, us-east4, located in Virginia, USA. The VPC dynamic routing mode is set to GLOBAL. Your organization needs 20 Gbps of protected bandwidth with a 99.9% Google Cloud SLA. You want to minimize costs where possible. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create two Cross-Cloud Interconnect connections to CSP 1, with 40 Gbps of total bandwidth (20 Gbps in zone 1 and 20 Gbps in zone 2) in a common co-location facility located in Frankfurt, Germany.2. Create two Cross-Cloud Interconnect connections to CSP 2, with 40 Gbps of total bandwidth (20 Gbps in zone 1 and 20 Gbps in zone 2) in a common co-location facility located in Frankfurt, Germany.3. Create two Cross-Cloud Interconnect connections to CSP 2, with 40 Gbps of total bandwidth (20 Gbps in zone 1) in a common co-location facility located in Frankfurt, Germany and (20 Gbps in zone 2) in a common co-location facility located in Munich, Germany.3. Create two Cross-Cloud Interconnect connections to CSP 1, with 40 Gbps of total bandwidth (20 Gbps in zone 1 and 20 Gbps in zone 2) in a common co-location facility located in Frankfurt, Germany.2. Create two Cross-Cloud Interconnect connections to CSP 2, with 40 Gbps of total bandwidth (20 Gbps in zone 1 and 20 Gbps in zone 2) in a common co-location facility located in Frankfurt, Germany.3. Create a Cloud Router in us-east4 (Ashburn, Virginia, USA), and configure two VLAN attachments for CSP 1 and two VLAN attachments for CSP 2.

questions.explanation:
A 99.9% Cross-Cloud Interconnect SLA configuration requires two redundant connections in different edge availability domains within one metropolitan area. To provide 20 Gbps of protected bandwidth, each redundant path must have 20 Gbps capacity; if either path fails, the remaining path still supplies 20 Gbps. Frankfurt supplies the closest common colocation location and its two edge availability domains satisfy the redundancy requirement without the added cost of using Munich. VLAN attachments for the Frankfurt Cross-Cloud Interconnect connections use a Cloud Router in europe-west3; GLOBAL dynamic routing allows the VPC to exchange routes with resources in us-east4. [Cross-Cloud Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/cci-overview) and [Cloud Interconnect best practices](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/best-practices).

You need to make sure that your personal SSH key works on every instance in your project, as efficiently as possible.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Upload your public ssh key to the project Metadata.
Upload your public ssh key to each instance Metadata.
Create a custom Google Compute Engine image with your public ssh key embedded.
Use gcloud compute ssh to automatically copy your public ssh key to the instance.

questions.explanation:
For metadata-based SSH access, a public SSH key added to project metadata can be used to access all VMs in the project, except VMs configured to block project-wide SSH keys. This provides project-wide access from one configuration point; instance metadata applies only to a single VM.\
\
**Learn more:** [Add SSH keys to VMs | Compute Engine | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/connect/add-ssh-keys)

questions.question:
You need to make sure that your personal SSH key works on every instance in your project, as efficiently as possible.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Enable Data Access audit logs of the VPC. Analyze the logs and get the source IP addresses from the subnetworks.get field.
Enable VPC Flow Logs for the subnet. Analyze the logs and get the source IP addresses from the connection field.
Enable VPC Flow Logs for the VPAnalyze the logs and get the source IP addresses from the src_location field.
Enable Data Access audit logs of the subnet. Analyze the logs and get the source IP addresses from the networks.get field.

questions.explanation:
VPC Flow Logs record sampled inbound and outbound VM network flows. Each record's `connection` field contains an `IpConnection` 5-tuple, including `src_ip`, so enabling flow logs for the subnet containing the VM provides the source IP addresses needed to investigate the incoming traffic. Data Access audit logs track API access rather than VM packet flows.

**Learn more:** [VPC Flow Logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/flow-logs) · [About VPC Flow Logs records](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/about-flow-logs-records)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company delivers software updates through a Cloud Storage bucket behind a global external HTTPS Application Load Balancer with Cloud CDN enabled. You uploaded a critical security patch as a file named `latest_update.zip`. The security patch removes a vulnerability that cybercriminals could exploit. You must ensure that users worldwide immediately receive the new version and that all previously cached copies of `latest_update.zip` are purged from the Cloud CDN network. What should you do?

options.text: Disable and then re-enable Cloud CDN for the entire backend bucket to flush the cache.
Modify the metadata of the latest_update.zip object in Cloud Storage to set the Cache-Control header to no-cache.
Run the gcloud compute url-maps invalidate-cdn-cache command, specifying the load balancer’s URL map and the exact path to the latest_update.zip file.
Change the Cloud CDN cache mode for the backend bucket from CACHE_ALL_STATIC to USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS and then back to CACHE_ALL_STATIC.

questions.explanation:
Cloud CDN can invalidate a single cached object by its exact URL path using `gcloud compute url-maps invalidate-cdn-cache` with the load balancer's URL map and the object's path. The invalidation removes the existing cached response from Cloud CDN so subsequent requests retrieve the updated object from the origin.

**Learn more:** [Invalidate cached content | Cloud CDN](https://cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/invalidating-cached-content) · [gcloud compute url-maps invalidate-cdn-cache](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/url-maps/invalidate-cdn-cache)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing networking for a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster that will host an internal, employee-facing application. The application must be reachable from your on-premises corporate network and from specific internal VPC networks in Google Cloud. You need to create a highly available and scalable load-balancing solution for ingress traffic that uses cookie-based session affinity, without exposing the application to the public internet. What should you do?

options.text: Use a GKE Gateway controller with an internal HTTPS load balancer. Configure DNS records to point to the load balancer's internal IP address from your on-premises network and peered internal VPCs.
Implement a GKE Service of type LoadBalancer to provision an internal TCP/UDP load balancer. Configure its forwarding rule to accept traffic from your internal VPC and on-premises IP ranges.
Expose the application using a Service of type NodePort. and configure an on-premises load balancer to target all the GKE node IPs as its backend.
Implement a GKE Service of type LoadBalancer to provision a regional TCP proxy load balancer. Apply firewall rules to restrict traffic to your internal source IP ranges.

questions.explanation:
A GKE Gateway with an internal HTTPS/Application Load Balancer provides private Layer 7 ingress, high availability, and scalable HTTP(S) routing. GKE Gateway supports cookie-based session affinity, including HTTP cookie and generated-cookie affinity. Publishing DNS records for the load balancer’s internal IP lets clients in connected on-premises networks and internal VPCs resolve and access the private endpoint without a public frontend.

**Learn more:** [Gateway traffic management | GKE networking](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/traffic-management) · [Configure Gateway resources using Policies | GKE networking](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/configure-gateway-resources)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has a subset of applications across multiple regions that need internet access. You must control application internet access to URLs, including hostnames and paths. The compute instances running these applications have an associated secure tag. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway. Use fully qualified domain name (FQDN) objects in the firewall policy rules to filter outgoing traffic to specific domains from machines that match a service account.
Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway. Use fully qualified domain name (FQDN) objects in the firewall policy rules to filter outgoing traffic to specific domains from machines that match the secure tag.
Deploy a single Secure Web Proxy instance with global access enabled. Apply a Secure Web Proxy policy to allow access from machines that match the secure tag to the URLs defined in a URL list.
Deploy a Secure Web Proxy instance in each region. Apply a Secure Web Proxy policy to allow access from machines that match the secure tag to the URLs defined in a URL list.

questions.explanation:
Secure Web Proxy enforces outbound web-access policies using URL lists that can match hosts, full URLs, and URL patterns, and its policy rules can match a workload’s secure tag. Enabling global access on one Secure Web Proxy allows clients in any Google Cloud region to use that proxy while preserving tag-based identity attributes for policy enforcement. Cloud NAT and FQDN firewall objects do not provide URL-path filtering.

**Learn more:** [Configure global access for Secure Web Proxy](https://cloud.google.com/secure-web-proxy/docs/configure-global-access) · [Use URL lists to create policies](https://cloud.google.com/secure-web-proxy/docs/use-url-list)
