questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s security team wants to restrict the types of inbound traffic that can reach your web servers to help protect against security threats. You need to configure firewall rules on the web servers in your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) for HTTP and HTTPS web traffic using TCP only. What should you do?

options.text: Create an allow on match ingress firewall rule with the target tag “web-server” to allow all IP addresses for TCP port 80.
Create an allow on match egress firewall rule with the target tag “web-server” to allow all IP addresses for TCP port 80.
Create an allow on match ingress firewall rule with the target tag “web-server” to allow all IP addresses for TCP ports 80 and 443.
Create an allow on match egress firewall rule with the target tag “web-server

questions.explanation:
Inbound connections to web servers require an ingress allow rule. HTTP uses TCP port 80 and HTTPS uses TCP port 443; targeting the `web-server` tag limits the rule to those instances while allowing the required web traffic from any IP address.

**Learn more:** [VPC firewall rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls) · [Use VPC firewall rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/using-firewalls)

You have the following firewall ruleset applied to every instance in your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC):  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783823451540-klh1waa1.png)  
  
You need to update the firewall ruleset by adding the following rule:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783823454548-2tg8ni46.png)  
  
You are using a new user account. Before updating the firewall rule, you must assign the appropriate Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles to this new user account. The account must be able to apply the update and view firewall logs. What should you do?

options.text: Assign the compute.securityAdmin and logging.viewer rule to the new user account. Apply the new firewall rule with a priority of 50.
Assign the compute.securityAdmin and logging.bucketWriter role to the new user account. Apply the new firewall rule with a priority of 150.
Assign the compute.orgSecurityPolicyAdmin and logging.viewer role to the new user account. Apply the new firewall rule with a priority of 50.
Assign the compute.orgSecurityPolicyAdmin and logging.bucketWriter role to the new user account. Apply the new firewall rule with a priority of 150.

questions.explanation:
VPC firewall rules are evaluated by priority, with the lower number taking precedence. The logging-enabled `/32` deny rule must use priority 50 to take precedence over the broader matching `/24` deny rule at priority 100; otherwise the existing rule applies and no log is generated. The Compute Security Admin role (`roles/compute.securityAdmin`) permits firewall-rule updates, and the Logs Viewer role (`roles/logging.viewer`) permits viewing firewall logs.

**Learn more:** [Manage VPC firewall rules logging](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/manage-vpc-firewall-rules-logging) · [Create regional network firewall policies and rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/use-regional-firewall-policies)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have the following Shared VPC design. VPC Flow Logs is configured for Subnet-1 in the host VPC. You also need to monitor flow logs for Subnet-2. What should you do?  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783862106085-trd451qr.png)

options.text: Configure a VPC Flow Logs filter for Subnet-2 in the host project VPC.
Configure VPC Flow Logs in the service project VPC for Subnet-2.
Configure Packet Mirroring in both the host and service project VPCs.
Configure a firewall rule to permit Subnet-2 IP addresses outbound in the host project VPC.

questions.explanation:
In a Shared VPC, subnets belong to the host project's VPC network. VPC Flow Logs must be enabled for the relevant subnet in that host project, and the resulting logs are reported in the host project; service projects do not own the shared network or access its flow logs.

**Learn more:** [About traffic flows](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/about-traffic-flows) · [VPC Flow Logs](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/flow-logs)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a hub-and-spoke network architecture for your company’s cloud-based environment. You must ensure that every spoke is peered with the hub. The spokes must use the hub’s virtual appliance to access the internet. The virtual appliance is configured in high-availability mode with two instances behind an internal load balancer at IP address `10.0.0.5`.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create a default route in the hub VPC that points to IP address 10.0.0.5.2. Delete the default internet gateway route in the hub VPC, and create a new higher-priority route that is tagged only to the appliances with a next hop of the default internet gateway.3. Export the custom routes in the hub.4. Import the custom routes in the spokes.

1. Create a default route in the hub VPC that points to IP address 10.0.0.5.2. Delete the default internet gateway route in the hub VPC, and create a new higher-priority route that is tagged only to the appliances with a next hop of the default internet gateway.3. Export the custom routes in the hub. Import the custom routes in the spokes.4. Delete the default internet gateway route of the spokes.

1. Create two default routes in the hub VPC that point to the next hop instances of the virtual appliances.2. Delete the default internet gateway route in the hub VPC, and create a new higher-priority route that is tagged only to the appliances with a next hop of the default internet gateway.3. Export the custom routes in the hub. Import the custom routes in the spokes.

1. Create a default route in the hub VPC that points to IP address 10.0.0.5.2. Delete the default internet gateway route in the hub VPC, and create a new higher-priority route that is tagged only to the appliances with a next hop of the default internet gateway.3. Create a new route in the spoke VPC that points to IP address 10.0.0.5.

questions.explanation:
An untagged custom `0.0.0.0/0` route using the internal load balancer as its next hop can be exported from the hub and imported into the spokes. A spoke’s system-generated default route to the default internet gateway is a local static route and takes precedence over an identical imported peering route, so that local default route must be deleted. A higher-priority, appliance-tagged route to the default internet gateway preserves outbound internet connectivity for the appliance instances themselves.

**Learn more:** [VPC Network Peering](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering) · [Routes](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/routes)

You correctly configured Cloud DNS forwarding zones to point to your on-premises DNS. You discover that you cannot query your on-premises Active Directory primary Domain Controller with `dig ad.company.int` through your Interconnect attachment. However, the query succeeds when you directly target the on-premises DNS server with `dig @10.10.10.53 ad.company.int`.  
  
You need to configure Cloud DNS correctly so that VMs and other resources can resolve DNS records in the on-premises DNS system. What should you do?

options.text: Make sure that the Cloud DNS source range is advertised over your BGP sessions towards the on-premises environment, and that the on-premises ingress firewalls allow traffic from this range on port 53.
Change the local DNS server in your Google Cloud VMs from 169.254.169.254 to your on-premises service, 10.10.10.53.
Use a nslookup query instead of a dig query.
Add an egress firewall rule in your VPC to allow DNS traffic on port 53 that is destined to your on-premises DNS server.

questions.explanation:
For an on-premises Cloud DNS forwarding target connected through Cloud Interconnect, Cloud DNS sends DNS requests from `35.199.192.0/19`. The on-premises network must have a return route for that range through the same VPC connection and allow both TCP and UDP port 53 from it. For Cloud Interconnect, advertise `35.199.192.0/19` as a custom BGP route and permit it on the on-premises ingress firewall.

**Learn more:** [Create a forwarding zone | Cloud DNS](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/zones/forwarding-zones) · [Best practices for Cloud DNS](https://cloud.google.com/dns/docs/best-practices)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying infrastructure in the `us-central1` region. Your on-premises data center is in New York City, and the Google Cloud region nearest to New York City is `us-east4`. Your Cloud Interconnect is located in Ashburn, Virginia (VA), United States.  
  
You need to use Cloud Interconnect to connect your application infrastructure to backend systems at your data center location. You do not expect application bandwidth to exceed 500 Mbps. You want to minimize latency and cost. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Router and VLAN attachments in the us-east4 region attached to your physical Interconnect in Ashburn, VEnable global routing in your VPC. Set the bandwidth on the VLAN attachments to 500 Mbps.
Create a Cloud Router and VLAN attachments in the us-east4 region attached to your physical Interconnect in Ashburn, VA. Enable global routing in your VPC.
Create a Cloud Router in the us-central1 region and VLAN attachments in the us-east4 region attached to your physical Interconnect in Ashburn, VA. Enable global routing in your VPC.
Create a Cloud Router and VLAN attachments in the us-central1 region attached to your physical Interconnect in Ashburn, VA.

questions.explanation:
Placing the Cloud Router and VLAN attachments in `us-east4` places the Interconnect termination in the Google Cloud region closest to the New York City data center, reducing latency. Global dynamic routing allows workloads in `us-central1` to reach on-premises routes learned through the `us-east4` attachment. Configuring the attachment capacity as 500 Mbps aligns its provisioned bandwidth with the expected requirement instead of using the default 10 Gbps capacity.

**Learn more:** [Create VLAN attachments | Cloud Interconnect](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/creating-vlan-attachments) · [Cloud Interconnect pricing](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/pricing)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You administer your company’s network security and have detected unusual outbound traffic from a Compute Engine VM in a production subnet. You suspect that the VM could be compromised because it is trying to communicate with a malicious external IP address. You need to capture detailed metadata for every IP connection to and from this particular VM, including the source/destination IP address, port, protocol, and volume of data transferred. What should you do?

options.text: • Enable VPC Flow Logs on the subnet containing the VM.• Set the sampling rate to 1.0 for maximum detail, and filter the logs in Cloud Logging for the VM's IP address.
• Navigate to Network Intelligence Center, and run a new connectivity test for the VM.• Analyze the report to see which configurations are allowing the traffic.
• Use Packet Mirroring to create a real-time copy of all network packets from the suspected VM.• Forward the copies to a collector VM for analysis.
• Create a new egress firewall rule with a priority of 65535 that allows all outbound traffic.• Enable Firewall Rules Logging on this new rule to capture all connection details.

questions.explanation:
VPC Flow Logs generate aggregated records for IP connections involving VM instances. Each record includes the source and destination IP addresses, ports, protocol, and estimated bytes sent; enabling the logs for the subnet and filtering in Cloud Logging isolates records for the VM. A secondary sampling rate of 1.0 retains all generated flow-log records after primary flow sampling.

**Learn more:** [VPC Flow Logs](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/flow-logs) · [About VPC Flow Logs records](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/about-flow-logs-records)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have the following private Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster deployment:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783823143410-qbl00os3.png)  
  
A virtual machine (VM) is deployed in the same VPC, in the `kubernetes-management` subnetwork, with internal IP address `192.168.40.2/24` and no external IP address assigned. You need to communicate with the cluster master using `kubectl`. What should you do?

options.text: Add the network 192.168.40.0/24 to the masterAuthorizedNetworksConfig. Configure kubectl to communicate with the endpoint 192.168.38.2.
Add the network 192.168.38.0/28 to the masterAuthorizedNetworksConfig. Configure kubectl to communicate with the endpoint 192.168.38.2
Add the network 192.168.36.0/24 to the masterAuthorizedNetworksConfig. Configure kubectl to communicate with the endpoint 192.168.38.2
Add an external IP address to the VM, and add this IP address in the masterAuthorizedNetworksConfig. Configure kubectl to communicate with the endpoint 35.224.37.17.

questions.explanation:
A private GKE control-plane endpoint is reached through its internal IP address, `192.168.38.2`. Authorized networks allow access based on the client source CIDR, so the VM's subnet, `192.168.40.0/24`, must be added to the authorized networks configuration. The control-plane range `192.168.38.0/28` and the cluster node range are not the VM's source network.

**Learn more:** [Creating a private cluster | GKE networking | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/legacy/network-isolation?hl=en) · [About network isolation in GKE | GKE networking | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/network-isolation)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are securing a newly provisioned 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect that links your on-premises data center to your Google Cloud VPC. Your company requires that all IP traffic between your private on-premises network and the VPC be protected with strong, end-to-end encryption at Layer 3 of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model. You need to implement the most direct and effective solution. What should you do?

options.text: Configure BGP sessions over the Dedicated Interconnect, and enable MD5 authentication.
Enable MACsec for Cloud Interconnect to encrypt all data frames between your on-premises router and Google's edge device.
Deploy HA VPN tunnels over the Dedicated Interconnect connections, and configure BGP sessions with on-premises routers to exchange routes.
Migrate your connection from Dedicated Interconnect to Partner Interconnect, and select a service provider that offers a private, encrypted connection.

questions.explanation:
HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect uses IPsec to encrypt traffic at the IP layer between the on-premises network and the VPC. Google Cloud specifically recommends HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect when IP-layer encryption is required. MACsec protects only the Layer 2 link between the customer router and Google's edge router, while BGP MD5 protects BGP session integrity rather than encrypting payload traffic.

**Learn more:** [HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/ha-vpn-interconnect) · [MACsec for Cloud Interconnect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/macsec-overview)

questions.question: You need to configure NAT to translate addresses between your on-premises network blocks and GCP. Which NAT solution should you use?

options.text: Cloud NAT
An instance with IP forwarding enabled
An instance configured with iptables DNAT rules
An instance configured with iptables SNAT rules

questions.explanation:
Cloud NAT’s Private NAT, including Hybrid NAT, provides managed private-to-private address translation between a VPC network and an on-premises network connected through Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect. It performs source NAT for outbound traffic and destination NAT for established response traffic.\
\
**Learn more:** [Cloud NAT overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/overview) · [Hybrid NAT](https://docs.cloud.google.com/nat/docs/about-hybrid-nat)

questions.question: You need to configure NAT to translate addresses between your on-premises network blocks and GCP. Which NAT solution should you use?

options.text: Provision a Partner Interconnect through your ISP.
Provision a Dedicated Interconnect instead of a VPN.
Create multiple VPN tunnels to account for the packet losses, and increase bandwidth using ECMP.
Use network compression over your VPN to increase the amount of data you can send over your VPN.

questions.explanation:
Partner Interconnect uses a supported service provider to provide private connectivity between an on-premises network and a VPC, avoiding the public-internet VPN path where packet loss can severely reduce TCP throughput. Its VLAN attachment capacity is selectable from 50 Mbps through 50 Gbps, so a capacity above the 1.5 Gbps peak can be provisioned without the cost and physical-circuit requirements of Dedicated Interconnect. [Partner Interconnect overview](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/partner-overview) [Choosing a Network Connectivity product](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/how-to/choose-product)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a highly dynamic e-commerce website that uses Cloud CDN to improve content-delivery speed for its global customer base. A new product was launched on the website with updated images and pricing information, and these changes were deployed to your Cloud Storage and Compute Engine instances behind a load balancer. However, customers still see the old product images and pricing on the website. You need to immediately and efficiently deliver the new content to users. What should you do?

options.text: Temporarily disable and then re-enable Cloud CDN on the backend services to force a cache reload.
Invalidate the specific URLs or URL prefixes corresponding to the updated product images and pricing information in Cloud CDN.
Configure a new backend service with the existing backends with Cloud CDN enabled to get the updated content.
Purge all cached content from Cloud CDN by performing a full cache flush for the entire CDN service.

questions.explanation:
Cloud CDN supports invalidating an individual URL or a URL-path prefix, which removes the affected cached entries so later requests refill from the updated Cloud Storage or Compute Engine backends. Targeting only the updated image and pricing paths minimizes unnecessary cache eviction and backend load.

**Learn more:** [Cloud CDN cache invalidation overview](https://cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/cache-invalidation-overview) · [Invalidate cached content | Cloud CDN](https://cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/invalidating-cached-content)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You deployed a new internal application that offers HTTP and TFTP services to on-premises hosts. You want to distribute traffic among multiple Compute Engine instances, while ensuring clients remain sticky to a particular instance across both services.  
  
Which session affinity should you select?

options.text: None
Client IP
Client IP and protocol
Client IP, port and protocol

questions.explanation:
Client IP affinity hashes the source and destination IP addresses without including the protocol or client port. Therefore, traffic from the same client is directed to the same backend instance for both HTTP (TCP) and TFTP (UDP). Affinity modes that include the protocol or port can select different instances between those services or connections.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Load Balancing feature comparison](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/features) · [Google Cloud backend services overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/backend-service)

questions.explanation:
With the default GKE Standard Pod allocation, every node receives a /24 Pod CIDR containing 256 addresses. Supporting up to three nodes requires three such blocks (768 addresses); a /22 range supplies 1,024 addresses and is the smallest listed range that accommodates them.

Your organization is deploying one project for three separate departments. Two departments need network connectivity to each other, while the third department must remain isolated. The design must establish separate network administrative domains between the departments and minimize operational overhead.  
  
How should you design the topology?

options.text: Create a Shared VPC Host Project and the respective Service Projects for each of the 3 separate departments.
Create 3 separate VPCs, and use Cloud VPN to establish connectivity between the two appropriate VPCs.
Create 3 separate VPCs, and use VPC peering to establish connectivity between the two appropriate VPCs.
Create a single project, and deploy specific firewall rules. Use network tags to isolate access between the departments.

questions.explanation:
VPC Network Peering provides private internal-IP connectivity between two VPC networks while keeping network administration independent for each VPC. Creating three VPCs and peering only the two that must communicate leaves the third VPC isolated, and avoids the additional tunnel and gateway management required by Cloud VPN.

**Learn more:** [VPC Network Peering](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering?hl=en) · [Virtual Private Cloud overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an application running on Compute Engine that uses BigQuery to generate results that are stored in Cloud Storage. You want to ensure that none of the application instances have external IP addresses.  
  
Which two methods can you use to accomplish this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable Private Google Access on all the subnets.
Enable Private Google Access on the VPC.
Enable Private Services Access on the VPC.
Create network peering between your VPC and BigQuery.
Create a Cloud NAT, and route the application traffic via NAT gateway.

questions.explanation:
Private Google Access lets Compute Engine instances that have only internal IP addresses access Google APIs and services, including BigQuery and Cloud Storage, when it is enabled on their subnets. Cloud NAT also supplies outbound connectivity for instances without external IP addresses, so the instances can access those service endpoints without public IPs assigned directly to them.

**Learn more:** [Configure Private Google Access](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access) · [Cloud NAT product interactions](https://cloud.google.com/nat/docs/nat-product-interactions)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a new global application with Compute Engine instances that will be exposed through a global HTTP(S) load balancer. You must protect the application from distributed denial-of-service and application-layer (layer 7) attacks. What should you do?

options.text: Configure VPC Service Controls and create a secure perimeter. Define fine-grained perimeter controls and enforce that security posture across your Google Cloud services and projects.
Configure a Google Cloud Armor security policy in your project, and attach it to the backend service to secure the application.
Configure VPC firewall rules to protect the Compute Engine instances against distributed denial-of-service attacks.
Configure hierarchical firewall rules for the global HTTP(S) load balancer public IP address at the organization level.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Armor security policies protect applications behind external Application Load Balancers from DDoS and web-based Layer 7 attacks. Attaching the policy to the backend service applies filtering at Google’s edge before malicious requests reach the Compute Engine backends.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Armor overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/cloud-armor-overview) · [Security policy overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/armor/docs/security-policy-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your on-premises data center has 2 routers, each connected to GCP through a VPN. All applications work correctly; however, all traffic traverses a single VPN rather than being load-balanced across the 2 connections as intended.  
  
During troubleshooting, you find:  
  
- Each on-premises router is configured with the same ASN.  
- Each on-premises router is configured with the same routes and priorities.  
- Both on-premises routers have a VPN configured to connect to one Cloud Router.  
- The VPN logs contain `no-proposal-chosen` lines when the VPNs connect.  
- A BGP session is not established between one on-premises router and the Cloud Router.  
  
What is the most likely cause of this issue?

options.text: One of the VPN sessions is configured incorrectly.
A firewall is blocking the traffic across the second VPN connection.
You do not have a load balancer to load-balance the network traffic.
BGP sessions are not established between both on-premises routers and the Cloud Router.

questions.explanation:
A `no-proposal-chosen` log entry means Cloud VPN and the peer VPN gateway could not agree on an IKE/IPsec cipher proposal. The affected tunnel therefore cannot establish, which also prevents its BGP session from coming up; traffic uses only the remaining operational VPN connection.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshooting Cloud VPN](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/support/troubleshooting?hl=en) · [Troubleshoot BGP sessions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/support/troubleshoot-bgp-sessions)

You are setting up load balancing for a standard three-tier application (web, application, and database). You have configured an external HTTP(S) load balancer for the web servers. You need to configure load balancing for the application-server tier. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a forwarding rule on the existing load balancer for the application tier.
Configure equal cost multi-path routing on the application servers.
Configure a new internal HTTP(S) load balancer for the application tier.
Configure a URL map on the existing load balancer to route traffic to the application tier.

questions.explanation:
An internal HTTP(S) Application Load Balancer provides private Layer 7 load balancing between the web and application tiers. Google Cloud’s three-tier web-services architecture uses an external Application Load Balancer for the web tier and an internal Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic across middleware application instances.

**Learn more:** [Application Load Balancer overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/application-load-balancer)

Your team is building an application that consumers worldwide will use. The application is currently behind a global external Application Load Balancer. You need to protect the application from possible application-level attacks. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Cloud CDN on the backend service.
Create multiple firewall deny rules to block malicious users, and apply them to the global external application load balancer.
Create a Google Cloud Armor security policy with web application firewall rules, and apply the security policy to the backend service
Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter with the global external application load balancer as the protected service, and apply it to the backend service.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Armor provides Layer 7 filtering and preconfigured web application firewall rules for common web attacks. A backend security policy can be attached to the backend service of a global external Application Load Balancer, so malicious requests can be evaluated and blocked before they reach the application.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Armor security policy overview](https://cloud.google.com/armor/docs/security-policy-overview) · [Create and manage Cloud Armor security policies](https://cloud.google.com/armor/docs/configure-security-policies)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have built a web application consisting of several containerized microservices and want to run the microservices on Cloud Run. You must also ensure the services are highly available to customers while providing low latency. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the Cloud Run services to multiple availability zones. Create a global TCP load balancer. Add the Cloud Run endpoints to its backend service.

Deploy the Cloud Run services to multiple regions. Create serverless network endpoint groups (NEGs) that point to the services. Create a global HTTPS load balancer, and attach the serverless NEGs as backend services of the load balancer.
Deploy the Cloud Run services to multiple availability zones. Create Cloud Endpoints that point to the services. Create a global HTTPS load balancer, and attach the Cloud Endpoints to its backend
Deploy the Cloud Run services to multiple regions. Configure a round-robin A record in Cloud DNS.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Run services are regional resources. Deploying each service in multiple regions protects against a regional outage, and a global external HTTPS/Application Load Balancer routes clients through serverless NEGs to the Cloud Run backends, providing globally distributed, low-latency access.

**Learn more:** [Serve traffic from multiple regions | Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/multiple-regions) · [Set up a global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/https/setup-global-ext-https-serverless)

questions.domain: Implementing a VPC network
questions.question:
You want to create a service in GCP that uses IPv6.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create the instance with the designated IPv6 address.
Configure a TCP Proxy with the designated IPv6 address.
Configure a global load balancer with the designated IPv6 address.
Configure an internal load balancer with the designated IPv6 address.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud supports IPv6 client access by assigning an IPv6 address to a load balancer forwarding rule. A global external load balancer provides a globally reachable IPv6 frontend and distributes traffic to healthy backends; internal load balancing is for private access only.\
\
**Learn more:** [IPv6 for Application Load Balancers and proxy Network Load Balancers](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/ipv6)

questions.domain: Configuring, implementing and managing a cloud network security solution
questions.question:
You want to create a service in GCP that uses IPv6.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Deploy a Cloud IDS endpoint in the production VPC, and configure the endpoint to inspect traffic from the specified VMs.
Configure VPC Flow Logs for the production subnet, set the sampling rate to maximum, and stream the logs to the IDS appliances for analysis.
Configure a Cloud Private NAT gateway for the production VMs, and route all egress traffic through the gateway to the IDS appliances.
Create a Packet Mirroring policy that selects the production VMs as mirrored sources and sets the internal passthrough Network Load Balancer as the collector destination.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Packet Mirroring clones the traffic of selected VM instances, including packet payloads and headers, and forwards the copies to a collector destination for out-of-band inspection. An internal passthrough Network Load Balancer backed by an instance group is the supported collector destination, allowing the IDS appliances to receive mirrored ingress and egress traffic without routing production traffic through them.

**Learn more:** [Packet Mirroring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/packet-mirroring?hl=en) · [Use Packet Mirroring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/using-packet-mirroring?hl=en)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your Google Cloud organization contains two folders: Dev and Prod. You need a scalable, consistent, and minimal-cost method to enforce these firewall rules for every virtual machine (VM):  
  
- Port 8080 must always be open for VMs in projects within the Dev folder.  
- All traffic to port 8080 must be denied for every VM in projects within the Prod folder.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create and associate a firewall policy with the Dev folder with a rule to open port 8080. Create and associate a firewall policy with the Prod folder with a rule to deny traffic to port 8080.

Create a Shared VPC for the Dev projects and a Shared VPC for the Prod projects. Create a VPC firewall rule to open port 8080 in the Shared VPC for Dev. Create a firewall rule to deny traffic to port 8080 in the Shared VPC for Prod. Deploy VMs to those Shared VPCs.
In all VPCs for the Dev projects, create a VPC firewall rule to open port 8080. In all VPCs for the Prod projects, create a VPC firewall rule to deny traffic to port 8080.
Use Anthos Config Connector to enforce a security policy to open port 8080 on the Dev VMs and deny traffic to port 8080 on the Prod VMs.

questions.explanation:
Hierarchical firewall policies can be associated with organization folders, and their allow or deny rules apply to VPC-network resources in projects under the associated folder. Associating distinct policies with Dev and Prod centrally enforces the respective port 8080 rules for all existing and future projects in each folder, without configuring every VPC individually.

**Learn more:** [Hierarchical firewall policies](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies) · [Create hierarchical firewall policies and rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/using-firewall-policies)

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are using Network Connectivity Center, and the hub is already configured. Every VPC in your environment must have network connectivity with every other VPC. All subnet ranges are unique. You need to configure the topology accordingly. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a star topology, add the VPC spokes to the hub, and specify all subnet ranges in the excludeExportRanges filter.
Configure a mesh topology, add the VPC spokes to the hub, and specify all subnet ranges in the excludeExportRanges filter.
Configure a mesh topology, and add the VPC spokes to the hub.
Configure a star topology, and add the VPC spokes to the hub.

questions.explanation:
A Network Connectivity Center mesh topology puts all VPC spokes in a single spoke group and exchanges their exported subnet routes, providing full connectivity among the VPCs. Unique subnet ranges avoid route-overlap conflicts. `excludeExportRanges` restricts subnet routes exported to the hub, so excluding all ranges would prevent the required connectivity.

**Learn more:** [Preset connectivity topologies | Network Connectivity Center](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/connectivity-topologies) · [NCC overview | Network Connectivity Center](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/overview)

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are implementing a hybrid connectivity solution between your on-premises data center and a Google Cloud VPC network by using Cloud Interconnect. The connection must automatically respond to network-topology changes and deliver high availability. You need to make sure that routes from your on-premises network are dynamically advertised to your Google Cloud VPC. You also need to make sure that routes from your Google Cloud VPC are dynamically advertised back to your on-premises routers. What should you do?

options.text: Implement a policy-based route in your Google Cloud VPC network to forward all on-premises destined traffic to a Network Virtual Appliance (NVA).
Use HA VPN on top of Interconnect to establish a BGP session to your on-premise router. Configure the Cloud Router to advertise all visible subnets.

Deploy a Cloud Router in your Google Cloud VPC network configured to advertise all subnets visible to the Cloud Router. Establish a BGP session over your Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachment to your on-premises router.
Use a Cloud Function triggered by network monitoring logs to automatically script and update static routes in the VPC route table for any detected on-premises subnets.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Router uses BGP over a Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachment to dynamically exchange routes with the on-premises router. It learns advertised on-premises routes for the VPC and advertises VPC subnet routes to the peer; advertising all subnets visible to the Cloud Router ensures the relevant VPC routes are announced and updates are propagated as topology changes occur.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Router overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/concepts/overview) · [Create VLAN attachments for Dedicated Interconnect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/how-to/dedicated/creating-vlan-attachments?hl=en)

In project `my-project`, you have two subnets in a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC): `subnet-a` with IP range `10.128.0.0/20` and `subnet-b` with IP range `172.16.0.0/24`.  
  
You need to deploy database servers in `subnet-a`. You will also deploy application servers and web servers in `subnet-b`. You want to configure firewall rules that allow database traffic only from the application servers to the database servers. What should you do?

options.text: Create network tag app-server and service account [email protected]. Add the tag to the application servers, and associate the service account with the database servers. Run the following command: gcloud compute firewall-rules create app-db-firewall-rule \--action allow \--direction ingress \--rules top:3306 \--source-tags app-server \--target-service-accounts sa-db@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

Create service accounts [email protected] and [email protected]. Associate service account sa-app with the application servers, and associate the service account sa-db with the database servers. Run the following command: gcloud compute firewall-rules create app-db-firewall-ru--allow TCP:3306 \--source-service-accounts sa-app@democloud-idp-demo.iam.gserviceaccount.com \--target-service-accounts sa-db@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

Create service accounts [email protected] and [email protected]. Associate the service account sa-app with the application servers, and associate the service account sa-db with the database servers. Run the following command: gcloud compute firewall-rules create app-db-firewall-ru--allow TCP:3306 \--source-ranges 10.128.0.0/20 \--source-service-accounts sa-app@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com \--target-service-accounts sa-db@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

Create network tags app-server and db-server. Add the app-server tag to the application servers, and add the db-server tag to the database servers. Run the following command: gcloud compute firewall-rules create app-db-firewall-rule \--action allow \--direction ingress \--rules tcp:3306 \--source-ranges 10.128.0.0/20 \--source-tags app-server \--target-tags db-server

questions.explanation:
An ingress VPC firewall rule can identify source instances by their service account and destination instances by their target service account. Allowing only TCP port 3306 from the application-server service account to the database-server service account restricts database access to the intended workload identities. Combining a source IP range with a source service account or source tag creates a union of allowed sources, not an intersection, so it would broaden access.

**Learn more:** [Use VPC firewall rules | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/using-firewalls) · [gcloud compute firewall-rules create | Google Cloud SDK Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/firewall-rules/create)

questions.domain: Configuring managed network services
questions.question:
You are implementing a global external TCP load-balancing solution and need to retain the source IP address of the original Layer 3 payload.  
  
Which load balancer type should you use?

options.text: HTTP(S) load balancer
Network load balancer
Internal load balancer
TCP/SSL proxy load balancer

questions.explanation:
A passthrough Network Load Balancer forwards the original client packets to the backends, preserving the client source IP address at Layer 3. Proxy-based load balancers terminate and re-establish connections, so they do not preserve the original packet source address.\
\
**Learn more:** [Cloud Load Balancing overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/load-balancing-overview) · [Choose a load balancer](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/choosing-load-balancer)

questions.domain: Configuring and implementing hybrid and multi-cloud network interconnectivity
questions.question:
You are implementing a global external TCP load-balancing solution and need to retain the source IP address of the original Layer 3 payload.  
  
Which load balancer type should you use?

options.text: Create a GKE private cluster with a private endpoint for the control plane. Configure VPC Networking Peering export/import routes and custom route advertisements on the Cloud Routers. Configure authorized networks to specify the desired on-premises subnets.
Create a GKE private cluster with a public endpoint for the control plane. Configure VPC Networking Peering export/import routes and custom route advertisements on the Cloud Routers.
Create a GKE private cluster with a private endpoint for the control plane. Configure authorized networks to specify the desired on-premises subnets.
Create a GKE public cluster. Configure authorized networks to specify the desired on-premises subnets.

questions.explanation:
A GKE private control-plane endpoint disables external control-plane access. Reaching that endpoint from on-premises networks requires routes to be exchanged between the cluster VPC and the Google-managed control-plane VPC, including custom-route export/import and Cloud Router advertisements for the on-premises prefixes. Authorized networks restrict access further to the specified on-premises CIDR ranges.

**Learn more:** [Creating a private cluster](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/legacy/network-isolation) · [Best practices for GKE networking](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/best-practices/networking)
